chapters.summary: Council staff calls the hearing to order, asks attendees to silence phones, and explains that those wishing to speak must fill out an appearance card with a sergeant. Staff also states that no one may approach the DA's chair.
chapters.title: Council staff opens hearing and announces procedures

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Hello, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Public Safety, joined with General Governmental Operations, State and Federal Legislation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, please silence all phones.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you wish to speak in today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with one of the sergeants.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Moving forward, no one is to approach the DA's chair.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Chair Feliz welcomes attendees to the Committee on Public Safety hearing on the Office of Community Safety. He thanks co-chair Gail Brewer and acknowledges Speaker Julie Menin, Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, and several council members.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz welcomes attendees and acknowledges co-chair Brewer

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Good afternoon everyone.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Azul Feliz, Chair of the Committee on Public Safety.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Good afternoon and welcome to today's hearing on the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: At today's hearing, we'll examine the newly created Office of Community Safety and other non-police solutions to reduce violence.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I would like to thank Councilmember and Co-Chair Gail Brewer and the Committee of Government Operations for co-chairing today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And I'd also like to acknowledge members who have joined us, including Speaker Julie Menon, Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, Council Members Riley, Wong, Morano, Nurse, and Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Before I begin my opening statement, I'd like to pass it on to Speaker Julie Menon.

chapters.summary: Speaker Julie Menin welcomes everyone and thanks Chairs Feliz and Brewer for convening the oversight hearing. She describes how the Office of Community Safety was established in March and lists the five mayoral offices moved under its umbrella.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin welcomes attendees and describes OCS creation

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I want to welcome everyone to today's committee hearing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm Julie Menon, Speaker of the New York City Council.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Let me begin by thanking Chair Feliz and Chair Brewer, chairs of these committees, for convening this very important oversight hearing on the Office of Community Safety and non-police solutions to reducing violence.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We will also be hearing three pieces of legislation that the chairs will discuss shortly.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: A crucial aspect of community safety is establishing and fostering trust between government and the people it serves.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That trust is earned over time through transparency, through ensuring impacted New Yorkers have a seat at the table, and mostly through proven results.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This past March, the mayor established

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: An Office of Community Safety tasked with developing citywide community safety strategies

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: and to supervise and coordinate the work of mayoral offices that operate in furtherance of community safety, including crime and violence prevention initiatives, victim assistant services, and community mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: As part of the establishment of OCS, five existing mayoral offices moved under its umbrella.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The Office of Crime Victim Services, the Office for the Prevention of Hate Crimes, the Office of Community Mental Health, the Office to End Domestic and Gender-Based Violence,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: the Office for Neighborhood Safety and the Prevention of Gun Violence.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: All of them were previously independent offices.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Some have existed for over a decade.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So it's important for us to come away from today's hearing with a greater understanding of why the offices were shifted from operating independently to being managed by the new OCS.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin raises concerns that key advocates and providers were not consulted before the restructuring. She cites Safe Horizon CEO Liz Roberts and Sanctuary for Families saying the move lacked meaningful collaboration.
chapters.title: Menin raises concerns about advocate consultation on office restructuring

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We also want to learn which advocates were consulted before the change was made and whether those organizations that have been working in these spaces for years are part of the decision making moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Certain providers have contacted us and have testified at prior hearings, particularly a hearing we held in the Gender Equity Committee

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: about the move of the office to end domestic and gender-based violence and voiced a concern at our hearing, Safe Horizon.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And CEO Liz Roberts said that she was concerned that they had not been contacted.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Prior to the restructuring and Sanctuary for Families specifically said that the move occurred without meaningful collaboration.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So one of the goals we have today is to understand what can happen moving forward to increase that level of collaboration and make sure that those organizations have a seat at the table.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin outlines the hearing goals: understand OCS's overarching approach and ensure collaboration moving forward. She cites rising crime statistics including a nearly 4% increase in reported rapes and an 11% rise in subway felony assaults.
chapters.title: Menin outlines hearing goals and cites rising crime statistics

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Most importantly, we want to understand the overarching goal of the office and what approach that it plans on taking moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we do want to say that the goal of keeping New Yorkers safe is obviously incredibly important.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We are concerned that compared to 2025, reported rapes have increased nearly 4%.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Subway felony assaults have climbed by 11% and hate crimes are up 13%.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So these are all questions that we plan on asking and we look forward to having a really fulsome hearing and conversation and I'll turn it back over to the chair for his opening statement.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker.

chapters.summary: Chair Feliz details Executive Order 15, which established the Office of Community Safety. He lists the five offices under OCS, including the Office for Neighborhood Safety and Prevention of Gun Violence and the Office of Community Mental Health.
chapters.title: Feliz details Executive Order 15 and offices under OCS

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Earlier this year, New York City Mayor Mamdani issued Executive Order No.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: 15, which established the Office of Community Safety, known as OCS.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Broadly tasked with developing citywide community safety initiatives, OCS is also empowered to supervise and coordinate the work of five existing mayoral offices that operate with similar safety-related goals.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: These offices are the Office for Neighborhood Safety and Prevention of Gun Violence, the Office of Community Mental Health, the Office to End Domestic and Gender-Based Violence, the Office for Prevention of Hate Crimes, and the Office for Crime Victim Services.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The executive order also directs OCS to coordinate citywide mental health crisis response programs, including the Be Heard program, an emergency response initiative that sends teams of mental health practitioners to certain mental health emergency calls.

chapters.summary: Chair Feliz explains that the hearing will examine the administration's plan for OCS, its accomplishments, and how it coordinates with other agencies including the NYPD. He asks how OCS will measure whether its efforts are improving safety.
chapters.title: Feliz explains hearing purpose: examine OCS plan and coordination

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Today's hearing is an opportunity for the council to examine the administration's plan and vision for the newly created Office of Community Safety, to better understand what OCS has accomplished since it was established,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: learn about how OCS plans to coordinate the work of the five offices under its jurisdiction, and other city agencies as well, including our New York City Police Department.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The Council also wants to know what changes have been made to existing programs and how OCS will measure whether its efforts are improving safety and connecting New Yorkers with needed services.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Through today's hearing, the committee seeks a clear understanding of OCS's authority, staffing, budget, and plans for the future.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Establishing an office is one step.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We need to know what it is doing, how is it working with the agencies and organizations responsible for delivering services, and what measurable results the city expects to achieve.

chapters.summary: Chair Feliz focuses on two specific areas he plans to examine: mental health emergency response and the crisis management system. He highlights the role of violence interrupters and asks how OCS evaluates their effectiveness.
chapters.title: Feliz focuses on mental health emergencies and crisis management system

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Two specific areas of OCS's work that I plan to closely examine include how we're responding to mental health emergencies and the crisis management system, which operates anti-violence initiatives citywide.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The committees will also examine how OCS is working with community-based organizations that deliver violence prevention services,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: notably via the crisis management system, which relies on community members and violence interrupters to mediate conflicts, connect people with services, and help prevent violence.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We want to understand how OCS is supporting these efforts, how it evaluates their effectiveness, and whether existing programs have the resources and coordination needed to reach the communities they serve.

chapters.summary: Chair Feliz discusses the two bills being heard: Intro 414 creating a gun violence intervention hotline and Intro 667 on community service in lieu of civil penalties for littering. He thanks his staff and the OCS leadership team.
chapters.title: Feliz introduces legislation and thanks staff

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Public safety is one of the most important responsibilities of city government, and we have to continue to explore new initiatives, but at the same time, we have to make sure that they're effective, so I look forward to a conversation on these new initiatives and this new office.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Finally, the committees will hear related legislation, specifically two bills being heard by the Public Safety Committee.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Introduction number 414, sponsored by Councilmember Riley, which will require the city to establish a three-digit emergency hotline known as the Gun Violence Intervention Hotline

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: to aid individuals seeking assistance with mental health and supportive services and programs related to gun violence intervention.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And introduction number 667, sponsored by Councilmember Williams, which will require that judges at the oath offer the option to comply.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: community service in lieu of paying civil penalties for violations given from proper disposal of garbage.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I would like to thank the leadership team at the Office of Community Safety and all the stakeholders who have joined us today.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I would like to thank also my staff, including the committee staff, Josh Kingsley, the senior counsel to this committee, Chad Benjamin, the policy analyst, Esperanza Diaz, my chief of staff, and Santiago Baena, my legislative director.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I look forward to a productive discussion, and I would like to now turn it to co-chair Brewer for her opening remarks before offering those bill sponsors an opportunity.

chapters.summary: Co-Chair Gale Brewer thanks Chair Feliz and introduces herself as chair of Government Operations. She notes OCS already has an acronym and mentions Intro 403 sponsored by Council Member Restler to create a Department of Community Safety.
chapters.title: Brewer introduces herself and notes Intro 403

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Council Member Felice, and we appreciate this bill.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I am Gail Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I chair the Committee on Government Operations, State and Federal Legislation, and it is important to talk about the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I notice it already has an acronym, OCS, and everything to do with non-police solutions to reducing violence.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We're obviously going to hear from Intro No.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: 403, sponsored by Council Member Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I want to give him credit for really working on creating a Department of Community Safety.

chapters.summary: Brewer discusses the mayor's campaign pledge to create a Department of Community Safety with a proposed $1.2 billion budget. She explains the vision to reduce police tasks and let health and social professionals lead on certain issues.
chapters.title: Brewer discusses mayor's campaign pledge for Department of Community Safety

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: He's been very focused on this to his credit.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: As you've heard, in March of this year, the mayor created this Office of Community Safety to develop safety strategies.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's made up of several already existing offices and was billed as the first step toward fulfilling the mayor's campaign pledge to create this department.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That pledge contemplated the creation of an agency with more experience

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: their powers and duties than those of the current Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And in proposing this, the candidate Mondami imagined a department that would fill the gaps of our programs and services and would address, more importantly, violence with a public health focus.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The Department of Community Safety, as envisioned by the mayor, was meant to help decrease the myriad tasks

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: police officers perform and allow trained health and social professionals to take the lead in addressing issues that have strained our social safety net.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: With a proposed budget of $1.2 billion, the Department of Community Safety would mark a drastic change in how New York City would deal with so many different safety issues.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We know that there are many of them.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Intro 403 would create a department, as you heard, of community safety based on a similar principle of removing police response from certain interactions.

chapters.summary: Brewer details Intro 403, which would create a department based on removing police response from certain interactions where services are the main need. She says the hearing will examine what works, what doesn't, and the consequences of expanding OCS into an agency.
chapters.title: Brewer details Intro 403 and public health approach to safety

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Where the main need is access to services, often mental health.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This new agency would build upon the infrastructure of non-police response currently exemplified in the Office of Community Safety, and that infrastructure is one that

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: advocates and members of the council have called on for years.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The Department of Community Safety contemplated by 403 would be tasked with promoting community safety, providing emergency responses that support

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: the preservation of public safety and health and welfare.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And it would involve collaboration with emergency responders, social service professionals, and public health officials, and the maintenance of field operations to facilitate the delivery of services.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Today, we will take a hard look at these

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: administration's efforts to take a public health approach to public safety.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This means examining how the Office of Community Safety has worked so far in its six months of existence.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We can analyze what works, what doesn't, where there needs to be more, and what we shouldn't do at all.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We will evaluate how this office meets promises made by the mayor and the goals of the council, look at what the consequences, good or bad, of expanding this office into an agency, and the creation of the Office of Community Safety

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: indicated a step toward a drastic change to both public safety and community safety in the city and the primary oversight authority in the city.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It is the council's job to make sure we are making that change right.

chapters.summary: Brewer highlights the gender aspect of community safety, mentioning a visit to a district attorney's office facility for women and families after sexual assault. She thanks government operations staff and her own staff.
chapters.title: Brewer highlights gender-based violence services and thanks staff

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I do want to say one thing about the topic that the speaker mentioned about the gender aspect to it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I visited the place at the district attorney's office where women and families go after some kind of horror sexual assault situation, and I hope that that...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Would be part of this discussion also.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Very important part of community safety.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: From government operations staff, I want to thank Joe Harry Frazier, Erica Cohen, and Samud.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Ameed and from my staff, Shuler, Puder, and I thank everyone.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'll turn it back over to Chair Felice.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from our public advocate, Jumaane Williams.

chapters.summary: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams thanks the chairs and members for holding the hearing. He describes how OCS was established to coordinate neighborhood safety, victim services, domestic violence prevention, hate crime prevention, and community mental health.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Williams thanks committee and describes OCS establishment

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Peace and blessings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Chairman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I just want to make sure I'm focused.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The Knicks have won two straight, and they're going to beat the 76ers tonight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Chair and Madam Speaker and Chair Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As mentioned, my name is Jermaine Williams, Public Advocate for the City of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I want to thank the chairs and the members of the committee for holding this very important hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In March of this year, the Office of Community Safety, OCS,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: was established to coordinate efforts across neighborhood safety, victim and survivor services, domestic and gender-based violence prevention, hate crime prevention, and community mental health.

chapters.summary: Williams says he is encouraged by the administration's desire to build a safer city and supports Intro 403 to codify a full Department of Community Safety. He emphasizes close coordination with agencies such as NYPD, FDNY, and DSS.
chapters.title: Williams supports Intro 403 and OCS coordination with agencies

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm encouraged by this administration's desire to build a safer city for everyone and want to see the office become its own department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I'm thankful to Councilmember Ressler's Intro 403, of which I'm a proud co-sponsor, would codify a full Department of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Building out OCS requires close coordination with agencies such as NYPD, FDNY, DSS, and others, ensuring adequate resources to centralize violence prevention and crisis response initiatives.

chapters.summary: Williams notes public safety wins such as downward trends in most major crimes but also cites increases in rape and sexual assault. He raises concern that citations for low-level quality-of-life crimes like turnstile jumping have increased by 12%.
chapters.title: Williams discusses public safety wins and low-level enforcement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The action our city takes to prevent violence and strengthen communities does not just impact everyone across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: They set a blueprint for what's possible across the entire country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Ten months into this administration, New Yorkers have seen genuine public safety wins like the continued downward trend of most major crimes, as we heard, unfortunately, some are up, including rape and sexual assault.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: However, citations for low-level quality of life crimes like turnstile jumping have increased by 12%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Any increase in police presence, especially when directed at commonplace low-level offenses, will by definition and intention increase the number of arrests for these incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: OCS can play an important role in providing the targeted services and programs that are more appropriate for addressing the underlying causes of many of the low-level offenses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So NYPD can focus on responding to and investigating more serious crimes.

chapters.summary: Williams says NYPD response to people in mental health crisis remains a major concern and cites the 2024 killing of Wynn Rosario. He argues OCS can strengthen initiatives like Be Heard but needs close collaboration across agencies.
chapters.title: Williams calls for strengthening mental health crisis response and Be Heard

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Additionally, the NYPD's response to people in mental health crisis continues to be a major concern.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In 2024, 19-year-old Wynn Rosario was killed during a mental health crisis by responding police officers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: NYPD officers agree that allowing clinicians to respond to those who need mental health care frees them up to do their jobs, investigating and responding to crime.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Our law enforcement should not be expected to service mental health professionals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: OCS has the opportunity to strengthen mental health response initiatives like Be Heard, but it will take close collaboration across agencies to make it successful.

chapters.summary: Williams says OCS represents an opportunity to align community safety initiatives under a single strategic vision. He expresses concern that OCS is not fully integrated across the administration and urges treating it as a full partner.
chapters.title: Williams urges full integration of OCS and CMS support

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The creation of OCS represents an important opportunity to align our city's current community safety initiatives under a single strategic vision to scale promising practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And deliver deeper impact for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: A fully operational office and eventually a department will enable us to build safer, thriving communities across

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I do want to say we're at a really critical time here, so I'm excited this office is built.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But wherever I see this working, there is full integration with the office, there's full coordination, there's full buy-in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I'm not sure that that is the case across the board in the administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I'm really hoping that we can figure out how we can have

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: OCS, not treated as an aside, but actually a full integrated partner when it comes to public safety, at the meetings, at the press conferences, at every place that they need to be, helping develop the strategy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I don't think that we've reached that point at this moment in time, and we're hoping that we can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And, of course, I did a lot of work around gun violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm very proud of the work CMS is doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Shout out to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I think some of that work has stagnated now, and so now is a great time to look at how we can build on that work that was there, continue to build on infrastructure, and build on it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The whole world, the whole country can see what New York City is doing, as they've done before, so I believe that we can get this right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And we have to get it right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I'm very much looking to this hearing to figure out how we can do this better and actually building some things so we can measure it even better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I want to shout out K-Bane, my brother from another who's not here now, but was very helpful and instrumental in helping build this out from CCD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'd also like to recognize Councilmember Stevens and also Councilmember Arriola, who has joined us virtually.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Councilmember Kevin Riley, who's Bill Introduction No.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
Council Staff
utterances.text: is being heard today.

chapters.summary: Council Member Kevin Riley presents Intro 414, which would establish a three-digit, 24-7 gun violence intervention hotline staffed by trained mental health professionals. He emotionally describes the shooting death of 15-year-old Javis Frimpong in the Bronx.
chapters.title: Council Member Riley presents Intro 414 for gun violence intervention hotline

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Feliz and Chair Brewer, for hearing my legislation, Intro 414, establishing a three-digit, 24-7 gun violence intervention hotline.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Let me start by saying what so many of us are feeling.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We are tired.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Tired of the shootings, tired of losing our young people, tired of families burying loved ones.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Just yesterday, 15-year-old Javis Frimpong was tragically shot and killed while walking to school in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The day before he marked, which would have been today, one year since he arrived from Ghana, a young boy with his entire future ahead of him, stolen by senseless gun violence.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: As a father, I am heartbroken, but most importantly, I'm outraged.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: No parent should have to bury their child.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: No child should fear for their life walking to school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: While shootings have declined citywide, those statistics mean little to a grieving family.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: One shooting is still one shooting too many.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Intro 414 will establish a 24-7 hotline staffed by trained mental health professionals, connecting New Yorkers to crisis counseling, conflict mediation, youth outreach, and intervention resources.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We cannot keep waiting until shots are fired to take action.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And this is not about replacing 911.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Law enforcement plays a critical role in keeping our communities safe, and community-based violence intervention strengthens those efforts.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We need both.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: working together to prevent violence and protect lives.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I want to thank my colleagues, advocates, and community partners for their support.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Our communities are tired of mourning.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: They're demanding safety, solutions, and action.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And today I want us to remember his name is Javits Frimpong, who is 15 years old, who was killed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: His family should be preparing for his future, not mourning for his loss.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: This is unacceptable, and we have to do more.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Intro 414 is just one more tool to intervene before violence escalates and helps prevent another family from experiencing this pain.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We owe Javits and his family and every child in this city more than condolences.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We owe them safety and we owe them action.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Riley.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Councilmember Lincoln Ressler, who also has his bill being heard today.

chapters.summary: Council Member Lincoln Restler thanks Chairs Feliz and Brewer and Speaker Menin for hearing his legislation. He thanks committee counsel Josh Kingsley and his chief of staff Molly Haley, and shares that community safety agency was a key campaign platform.
chapters.title: Council Member Restler thanks chairs and explains his vision for community safety agency

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Felice and Chair Brewer, for having this hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I really especially want to thank the Speaker for the opportunity to hear this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'd like to just also take a moment to thank Josh Kingsley, Committee Counsel, for his great work in drafting this bill, and my Chief of Staff, Molly Haley, who is absolutely brilliant and really the brains of our operation.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm really grateful to her on this and on everything.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I just want to start by thanking...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: All of the people who do the work of community safety every day.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: City workers, nonprofit workers,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: who help make our community safer and are helping people in need.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: When I ran for city council, the idea of a new community safety agency that could address issues in our neighborhoods in real time

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: and actually connect people to the help, to the solutions that they need, rather than just punitive enforcement, was a big part of my campaign platform.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We began the bill drafting process early in my term, and we were pleased to finally introduce the legislation last year, after the Department of Community Safety gained some traction on the mayor's campaign.

chapters.summary: Restler says the overwhelming majority of 911 mental health calls are responded to by NYPD rather than mental health professionals. He argues for a new city agency to ensure real-time response and connect New Yorkers to housing, health care, and other solutions.
chapters.title: Restler details need for new agency and bill support

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The overwhelming majority of 911 calls

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: for mental health assistance are responded to by NYPD officers, rather than mental health professionals, social workers, or others trained to handle and diffuse these challenging situations.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We ask our police to respond to every issue under the sun, and it distracts from their core work of preventing and solving violent crime.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We need a new agency.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: a new city agency that can ensure real-time response to mental health calls and other nonviolent issues and actually connect New Yorkers to the solutions that they desperately need, like housing and health care.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We all know that public safety is about much more than just policing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And to deepen public safety,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We must make greater investments in violence interrupting strategies to help our young people get on the right track.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We need to do so much more to help chronically homeless New Yorkers who are often dealing with mental illness, who are struggling daily on our streets and in our subways.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we also need to significantly improve coordination across our siloed city agencies so that New Yorkers will finally stop cycling through our jails and our hospitals and our shelters.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Making this a city agency in our charter will offer permanence and ensure that we can continue to provide robust council oversight through budget hearings, reporting, and more.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I am honored to have the support of 34 council members, a supermajority on this bill, and our distinguished public advocate.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I look forward to working closely with the Speaker, with my colleagues, with the administration, with many advocates and providers.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Doing the work on the ground every single day so that we together can refine the bill language and make sure that this agency is set up for success permanently.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Feliz calls the first panel from the Office of Community Safety, including Commissioner Delaney-Brumsey and several team members. Committee staff administers the oath, and Feliz warns the audience to remain quiet or be escorted out.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz swears in OCS panel amid chamber disruptions

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Council Member Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'll now call the first panel, representatives from the Office of Community Safety, Commissioner Delaney Brumsey.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Clifford LaRochell.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Edward Gill Hill.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Ranti Agunle.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Jija Ramjatan.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Michael Williams.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Evan Ellis, Santos Gores.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And Lakeisha Grant.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'll pass it to the committee council to administer the oath.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Can you just raise your right hand and just affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and to answer honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Please, quiet in the chambers.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You'll be escorted out if you cannot remain quiet.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you acknowledge that?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: This is the second warning, the third one.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You will be escorted out, so please quiet in the chambers.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We have a panel who will be testifying now.

chapters.summary: Commissioner Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey introduces herself and describes OCS's mission to advance a whole-of-government approach to preventing violence. She lists the five offices brought together under OCS and explains their shared goals.
chapters.title: Commissioner Delaney-Brumsey introduces OCS mission and component offices

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Feliz, Chair Brewer, and members of the Committee on Public Safety and Committee on Government Operations, State and Federal Legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I am Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey, Commissioner of the Office of Community Safety, or OCS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak today about OCS's work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Established through Executive Order 15 in March 2026, OCS advances a whole-of-government approach to preventing violence and promoting safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: OCS brings together five offices, the Office of Crime Victim Services, Office of Neighborhood Safety, the Office to End Domestic and Gender-Based Violence, the Office of Community Mental Health,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: and the Office for the Prevention of Hate Crimes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Our work recognizes that New York City needs multiple tools and strategies to build safer communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: This means investing in community-led solutions that prevent violence, intervening when conflicts and crises arise, and ensuring that victims, survivors, and families have the support they need to heal and recover.

chapters.summary: Delaney-Brumsey explains the rationale for integrating the five offices, noting that communities with high gun violence also experience high domestic violence. She says survivors often need mental health care and that people do not experience harm in silos.
chapters.title: Delaney-Brumsey explains rationale for integrating violence prevention offices

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Bringing OCS's offices together also recognizes that the challenges New Yorkers face do not exist in isolation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: For instance, research shows that communities with high level rates of gun violence also experience high rates of domestic violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: A survivor of domestic violence may need mental health care,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Communities affected by gun violence or hate crimes may also need immediate intervention and sustained support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Together, our offices work towards a city where New Yorkers can live safely and access the support they need.

chapters.summary: Delaney-Brumsey details the Office of Community Mental Health and the Be Heard program, which pairs EMS professionals with social workers to respond to eligible 911 calls. She reports that Be Heard responded to 8,524 calls in FY2026, with 42% receiving care in the community.
chapters.title: Delaney-Brumsey details Office of Community Mental Health and Be Heard program

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The Office of Community Mental Health, OCS, works to expand access to mental health care and improve behavioral health crisis response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The Office of Neighborhood Safety works to prevent gun violence among the people and neighborhoods at greatest risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The Office to End Domestic and Gender-Based Violence, NGBV, works towards a city free from domestic and gender-based violence, where survivors can access safety and support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And the Office for the Prevention of Hate Crimes works to prevent violence and bias and to build a New York where everyone feels safe and welcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Our approaches are grounded in research and evidence, informed by what we hear directly from survivors and communities about what they need to be safe and thrive, and implemented in partnership with our fellow government agencies and community-based partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: One way you can see this approach is in the work of the Office of Community Mental Health, or OCMH.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Which addresses gaps in the behavioral health system and expands

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: access to care for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: OCMH invests in community-based approaches that bring mental health support to where New Yorkers live, learn, and work, helping reduce stigma, promote early intervention, and strengthen community capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: One critical part of that work is ensuring that when New Yorkers experience a behavioral health crisis,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: they receive an appropriate response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Across the country, jurisdictions are increasingly bringing health professionals into 911 behavioral health crisis response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Research supports this approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: A study of Denver's STAR program, which pairs a mental health clinician with a paramedic to respond to certain 911 calls,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: found a 34% reduction in reports of lower-level offenses and no detectable increase in more serious crime.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Here, Be Heard, our signature 911 behavioral health response initiative, pairs two emergency medical services professionals with one social worker to respond to eligible calls, assess needs,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: de-escalate crises, and connect people to appropriate care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The program is operated by New York City's Fire Department, FDNY, and New York City Health and Hospitals, and is overseen by OCMH.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2026, Be Heard responded to 8,524 calls, with 42% of the individuals served receiving care in the community rather than being transported to a hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Also, among surveyed patients, 96 reported that BeHeard helped them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Expanding and strengthening Be Heard is a key priority for OCS and this administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are working in close partnership with FDNY and New York City Health and Hospitals to strengthen operations and expand the program's reach so that many more New Yorkers can receive a response from teams of EMS professionals and social workers.

chapters.summary: Delaney-Brumsey outlines the Office of Neighborhood Safety's work, including the Mayor's Action Plan for Neighborhood Safety and the Crisis Management System. She cites shooting declines, participatory budgeting results, and the ATLAS program for intensive therapeutic support.
chapters.title: Delaney-Brumsey outlines Office of Neighborhood Safety and violence prevention programs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Different public safety challenges require different approaches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: While OCMH focuses on improving behavioral health care and crisis response, the Office of Neighborhood Safety works to prevent community violence, assaults and shootings that typically occur outside the home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: New York City has seen declines in shooting incidents from 804 in fiscal year 25 to 673 in fiscal year 26.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: A 16% reduction, and a 61% decline from a recent peak of 1,741 incidents in fiscal year 2021.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: ONS contributes to the city's broader crime reduction efforts through complementary strategies focused on the people and places at greatest risk of violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Improving environmental conditions, interrupting conflicts, and providing intensive therapeutic and wraparound supports to people at risk, to support at-risk populations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: One way ONS works to advance a community-centered approach to public safety is through the Mayor's Action Plan for Neighborhood Safety, or MAP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Every year, MAP hosts participatory budgeting events designed to leverage the expertise of NYCHA residents in identifying and proposing local solutions to safety and well-being priorities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Through the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: This approach residents draw on their experience and local expertise to identify, propose, discuss, and vote on projects and initiatives most important to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Fiscal year 2026, 5,564 NYCHA residents participated in a participatory budgeting process, and $530,000 was invested back into communities through physical space improvements or community-based programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: By using evidence-based crime prevention through environmental design principles, MAPS also works with residents to improve their social and physical environment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: This includes enhancement and revitalization to gardens, playgrounds, basketball courts, lighting, and murals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Together, these efforts create vibrant neighborhoods that promote safety, build community cohesion, and address the immediate needs of residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Research supports this approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: A University of Chicago crime lab randomized control trial in New York City found that installing new lighting in public housing developments reduced nighttime outdoor index crime by 36%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Another randomized trial in Philadelphia found that restoring vacant land reduced gun violence by 29% in neighborhoods below the poverty line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: In addition to addressing broader environmental conditions, ONS works to prevent violence by identifying and intervening in conflicts before they escalate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: This includes supporting the Crisis Management System, CMS, where locally credible outreach workers and violence interrupters build trusted relationships with people at elevated risk of violence,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: mediate conflicts, and connect people to employment, education, mental health care, legal services, and other resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: In fiscal year 26, CMS providers conducted

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: 13,232 mediations and de-escalations, and served 1,636 participants on caseloads.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: ONS also works closely with individuals at elevated risk of violence, providing therapeutic supports and other supports that can help prevent future violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Through ATLAS,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: ONS connects participants to intensive therapeutic services and practical support, such as help accessing housing, employment education, and other essential resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: In fiscal year 26, Atlas engaged 1,127 participants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Research supports this approach as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: A Chicago study found that combining mentoring and cognitive behavioral therapy reduced arrests for up to five years into adulthood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Together, these strategies, along with others that ONS implements, addresses both immediate risks of violence and longer-term conditions that contribute to it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Recognizing the importance of this work, this administration invested an additional $14.8 million

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: in fiscal year 27 to expand community violence prevention and intervention, including bringing CMS to additional neighborhoods and increasing access to clinical and mental health supports for people at risk of or impacted by violence.

chapters.summary: Delaney-Brumsey describes the Office to End Domestic and Gender-Based Violence and the Office for the Prevention of Hate Crimes. She highlights investments including $15.7 million in NGBV and $26 million in hate crime prevention.
chapters.title: Delaney-Brumsey describes NGBV and OPHC programs and investments

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The Office to End Domestic and Gender-Based Violence, NGBV, also works to reduce future violence by working directly with people who have caused or are at risk of causing harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Here, however,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: the focus is on violence in intimate and family relationships.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Through the Abusive Partner Intervention Program, NGBV helps participants reflect on their behavior, take accountability for harm they have caused, and build healthier relationships.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: These programs respond to what survivors have told us they need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Options to stop abusive behavior, including when they are not ready, able, or willing to engage with law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Supporting survivors and their families is central to NGBV's work, not only to promote healing and well-being, but also to help interrupt cycles of violence and trauma.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Research shows that children exposed to domestic violence are nearly three times more likely to experience domestic violence as adults.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Childhood exposure to family violence is also associated with an increased risk of perpetrating domestic violence later in life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Through the family's five family justice centers and the Crime Victims of 66 program, CVAP, NGBV connects survivors of domestic and gender-based violence and victims of other crimes to advocacy, safety planning, counseling, legal services, and other supports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: NGBV is also expanding a community-based access to these services so survivors can receive support regardless of whether they engage with law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Recognizing the importance of this work, the administration invested an additional $15.7 million in NGBV in fiscal year 27 to expand programs including services for victims and survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Like NGBV, the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Officer of Preventative Hate Crimes, OPHC, works to address the needs of people who have been harmed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: OPHC takes a Big Ten approach to preventing hate and bias that can escalate into violence, working closely with government partners, government agencies, community-based organizations, and affected New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: In fiscal year 26, OPHC worked with 159 community partners, and its prevention programs served more than 280,000 participants, including over 7,500 young people reached through educational initiatives with programming delivered in

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: more than 20 languages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The administration has invested $26 million in new funding to expand hate violence prevention, education, community engagement, and support for affected communities.

chapters.summary: Delaney-Brumsey concludes by emphasizing partnership and says OCS will use data and community feedback to assess progress. She expresses support for the intent of Intro 414 but notes it would require federal authorization and suggests leveraging 988 and the NYC Hope Hotline.
chapters.title: Delaney-Brumsey concludes testimony, supports bills, and plans for department

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Across all of OCS's work, partnership is essential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: No one can do the work of building safety alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: OCS works closely with city agency partners, community-based organizations, service providers, and New Yorkers directly affected by violence and trauma.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: At its core, OCS is built on the understanding that safety is something we create together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: As OCS grows and evolves, we will continue using data, research, and community feedback to assess progress, address gaps, and strengthen our work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We look forward to continued collaboration with the Council and all our partners to ensure all New Yorkers have the support and opportunities they need to be safe and thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Also, we support the intent of 414 to connect you New Yorkers affected by gun violence with intervention and support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Establishing a new three-digit emergency number of this kind would require federal authorization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Additionally, we believe that existing resources such as 988 and the New York City Hope Hotline could be leveraged more quickly and efficiently to connect New Yorkers to needed services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We welcome the opportunity to work with Council, our city agency partners, and community-based organizations to expand access to those resources and ensure they meet the needs of people affected by gun violence, advancing the bill's goals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Finally, our goal is to establish a Department of Community Safety and we are currently working collaboratively with the Council to amend

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: 403 to align our shared goals and advance this effort.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I welcome any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you for being here.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Great to see you again.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Also want to recognize Council Members Justin Sanchez and Chio Se who have joined.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: This is obviously a new office and this is the first hearing that we have on this matter, so we have many questions.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'll pass it first to Speaker Julie Manon for her questions.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin asks about OCS's FY2027 budget of $271 million and how many staff members report to the commissioner. Delaney-Brumsey confirms the budget and breaks down funding across the five offices, noting $67 million in new resources.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin questions OCS budget and staffing structure

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I have a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: OMB testified that your fiscal year 2027 budget was $271 million.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What are those numbers?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is that an accurate number?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What are the numbers today, and how many staff members do you have?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, that is accurate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Our budget is $271 million, not including our discretionary funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That represents an additional $67 million that this administration invested in the work of OCS and the component offices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that breaks down as follows.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: $29 million for Office for Prevention of Hate Crimes, $157 million for the Office of Neighborhood Safety,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: $75 million for NGBV, $7 million for OCMH, and $2.9 million for OCS staffing needs.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So how much represents in total new resources rather than existing programs that were transferred into your office?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: $67 million are new resources since this administration started.

chapters.summary: Menin asks about the division of responsibilities between the deputy mayor for community safety and the commissioner. Delaney-Brumsey says her office has about 100 staff, she reports to the deputy mayor, and the deputy mayor's team has eight staff.
chapters.title: Menin asks about deputy mayor vs commissioner roles

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And what is the division of responsibilities between the deputy mayor for community safety, the commissioner of community safety, and how many employees report to each?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: My office is approximately 100 staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: My role as the Commissioner of the Office of Community Safety is to manage the office, to build out the office and the component offices that are part of it, to ensure that we have a strong strategy

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: that knits together the existing work of these offices into a comprehensive approach for addressing violence and preventing harm, and also to support people in the aftermath of harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I report to the Deputy Mayor of Community Safety, as other commissioners report to deputy mayors across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Her role is to support the office, but also to build out work across New York City that expands, that advances community safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: As I noted in my testimony, the work of community safety is something that is both held by the Office of Community Safety, but held by all of our government partners, our community partners, and many others.

chapters.summary: Menin notes subway felony assaults are up 11% and subway murders increased from four to seven this year. She asks if OCS deploys personnel into the subways; Delaney-Brumsey says OCS does not currently have such a program.
chapters.title: Menin questions subway violence and OCS deployment

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: A couple questions first on subway violence.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So subway felony assaults are up 11% so far this year, and subway murders have increased from four to seven this year.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Just this month, Daryl Rodriguez was fatally shot on an E train platform in Midtown.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is your office deploying personnel into the subways, and how are you working with the NYPD to prevent attacks?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Our office works very closely with NYPD on a number of initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are in a process right now of ensuring that across all of the work, there are existing relationships with NYPD at the ground level and all the way up to senior leadership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And the work that we are doing is around making sure that the work we have around violence prevention, domestic and gender-based violence, mental health, and hate crimes is both informed by and in partnership with NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Those relationships exist and we continue to build on them in a deliberative way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: But are you deploying...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are not currently...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just want to make sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is your office deploying personnel into the subways?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We do not currently have a program that deploys personnel into the subways as part of our work.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

chapters.summary: Menin asks how often OCS meets with the NYPD. Delaney-Brumsey says there is daily contact across the office and weekly leadership meetings.
chapters.title: Menin asks frequency of NYPD meetings

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And how often do you meet with the NYPD?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We work at different levels across the entire office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: As I said, there's 100 people in within OCS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so I don't have a literal number of exactly how often we're meeting, but we are in daily contact with OCS of NYPD across our entire office.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Do you meet with them every week on a leadership basis?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We certainly meet with them every week on a leadership basis, and we're meeting with them on a daily basis throughout the office.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Menin cites an IBO finding that only 33% of eligible mental health calls received a Be Heard response in Q3 2025 and asks for the current percentage. Lakeisha Grant says about 8,500 of 10,945 eligible calls received a Be Heard response last fiscal year.
chapters.title: Menin questions Be Heard response percentage

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: For mental health response, so the Independent Budget Office found that only 33% of eligible mental health calls received a be heard response in the third quarter of 2025.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What is the percentage today?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Our most recent percentage, I'll turn to our Deputy Executive Director for Office of Community Mental Health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: What I will say is that the goal of this administration and the goal of the Office of Community Safety is to strengthen and expand Be Heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We know that the necessity of providing a 911 mental health response to more New Yorkers is crucial to our work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so we are in the moment of expanding the work that has existed for some time so that we can over time build it so we're responding to more and more calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That work for some time had been stagnant, but now this administration is providing the support necessary and the office, the agencies we are working with,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: FDNY, New York City Health and Hospitals, as well as NYPD and others, has continued to advance that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And we've made some significant advances in just the last few months on increasing staffing, improving how we are triaging calls, and we are in a moment of working towards expansion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: We'd have to do some math on the exact percentage, but there were about 11,000 calls that were eligible for a be heard response last fiscal year, 2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And of those, about 8,500 received a be heard response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: There are about

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: 150,000 overall 911 mental health calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And so we just have to do the math on how much that calculates to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: But of those, over 8,000 received a be heard response.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I'm sorry, you're saying 8,000 of what is the overall amount?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: So 8,500 calls received a be heard response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: There were about 10,945 calls that were eligible for a be heard response.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

chapters.summary: Menin asks how much Be Heard relies on ambulances given EMS staffing shortages. Delaney-Brumsey says FDNY remains a core component, and Grant describes a recent integrated training class of 27 personnel.
chapters.title: Menin asks about EMS role and Be Heard training

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Given EMS staffing shortages and rising ambulance response times, how much does Be Heard rely on ambulances and

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: has the administration made any decision regarding EMS and its role in Be Heard?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The administration has made the decision that FDNY is a core component of Be Heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are working very closely with FDNY and EMS to operate Be Heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Right now, the program is a partnership between FDNY and New York City Health and Hospitals as managed by OCS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
