utterances.text: while we are working very closely with FDNY to ensure that we have the resources necessary, both staffing and vehicles, to make sure that this program operates and can expand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: In fact, I'll also turn it over to Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Grant to talk about some recent improvements we've been able to make with staffing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Yes, we just earlier this month completed the latest class of Be Heard teams, which included over about 27 personnel across EMS and H&H combined.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: They underwent a four-week integrated training where the staff learned techniques such as motivational interviewing, suicide prevention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: They also, for the first time this year, were able to hear from other jurisdictions that are operating similar programs across the country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And also for the first time during this training class, received a workshop on what peer support means and the principles of peer support,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: including a peer panel where they got to hear directly from peers who have been impacted by the 911 mental health response system.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So EMS will, just from what you're saying, it sounds like you're saying EMS will remain involved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Okay, understood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Also, I will say that that training was the first training that Be Heard has had for integrated training since 2024.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we are in the process of...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: filling staffing gaps and have been making significant progress on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We're on track to have additional trainings early in next year as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And those will include both EMS and New York City Health and Hospital social workers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Menin expresses concern about the decision to remove the commissioner for NGBV from that leadership position. Delaney-Brumsey says Commissioner Sloane remains with NGBV and Deputy Commissioner LaRochelle reports a 25.3% vacancy rate.
chapters.title: Menin questions removal of NGBV commissioner and vacancy rate

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm very concerned about the decision to remove the commissioner for NGBV.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: From that commissioner leadership position that was made in the spring.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Why was that decision made?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Commissioner Sloane is still a significant and important member of the Office of Community Safety's leadership team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: She remains with NGBV.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The decision that was made was to combine these five offices into one office, and that was made in order to strengthen the work of all of the component offices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that was a reflection of the recognition that the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: A necessity to prevent violence and harm requires all of the component offices working very closely together, and I'm really excited to continue that work in partnership with the commissioner, with her team, as well as the rest of the team.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I just think, and I said this at the gender equity committee we had on this, I just think it sends the wrong message to victims of domestic violence, survivors,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: when there's not an independent office that's dedicated to this and there's not that commissioner level when they're basically made an executive director.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we heard from Safe Horizon and Sanctuary for Families.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: voicing concerns about that decision.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: How many vacancies are currently in that particular office?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I'll turn to Deputy Commissioner Hill for the exact number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: However, one thing that I will note is that since NGBV has become part of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: OCS, we have made, the administration has made the largest investment in programs under NGBV that was made since 2018, 15.7 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And in addition, we've been able to fill some longstanding vacancies, including vacancies such as the head of the Staten Island Family Justice Center, which is

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer, one of the places that I believe you mentioned, where people, families, individuals who've experienced harm can receive services and walk in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: So NGV currently has a headcount of 79.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: There are currently 59 staff members at the agency, and so the vacancy rate is 25.3%.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Right, that's what our data is showing too.

chapters.summary: Menin notes reported rapes are up nearly 4% and asks what OCS is doing. Delaney-Brumsey and Deputy Commissioner Hill describe NGBV's Family Justice Centers and the Crime Victims Assistance Program integrated with sexual assault centers.
chapters.title: Menin asks about rising rape rate and NGBV programs

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, that is concerning why there is such a high vacancy rate for a

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: an entity that is obviously serving such a critical mission.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then I also want to say, I mean, reported rapes are up in the city, nearly 4%.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: A woman was recently sexually assaulted in Central Park.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So what is going to be done to really address the vacancy rate?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We share your concern about the vacancy rate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Some of that vacancy rate is longstanding related to hiring freezes, and we are working right now to ensure that we are filling

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: key positions because we know that the charge of the Office of Community Safety is to grow, to expand, and ensure that we have the people and the staff to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We cannot do that without a robust team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we are working very hard right now with the leadership to ensure we are doing that work.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And what specific efforts is the office doing to address the rising rape rate in the city of New York?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I will turn it to Deputy Commissioner Hill to talk about some of the programs that we have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: However, the work of the Office of NGBV has existed in this city for 25 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: focus of that work is both on preventing harm and supporting individuals in the response

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: in the aftermath of harm and addressing people who themselves have caused harms to interrupt that cycle and the team has a robust set of resources from supporting the New York City Hope hotline which is a 24-hour hotline

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: to support survivors of domestic and gender-based violence as well as other crimes we have the family justice centers that I mentioned we have we

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: to provide mental health services within New York City shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: There is a range of work that's happening within NGBV that addresses the needs of people who have been sexually assaulted or who have experienced other victimization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And I'll turn to Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll add on to what the commissioner noted, that we do in fact have family justice centers in each borough that provide services to victims of rape and other sexual violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And in addition to that, we have the CVAP program, which is in every precinct in New York City, and they have dedicated staff for the sexual assault centers that the district attorneys operate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And so that CVAP is integrated into that program to offer deeper support for victims of rape and sexual violence that are interacting with the criminal justice system.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Menin notes hate crimes are up nearly 13% and asks about the Office for the Prevention of Hate Crimes reportedly having only three employees in June. Delaney-Brumsey confirms the small staff and describes new $26 million investment and PATH program expansion.
chapters.title: Menin questions hate crimes and OPHC staffing

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: On hate crimes, so hate crimes are up nearly 13% in the city year to date with more than half targeting Jewish New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It was reported that the Office for the Prevention of Hate Crimes had just three employees in June.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I will turn to our executive director to double check my numbers, but the Office for Prevention of Hate Crimes had an approximately $3 million budget before the budget was increased and adopted in preliminary by $26 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we are in the process right now of expanding that office both in terms of staff as well as in terms of the programs and initiatives that we work on to address hate, hate violence, and hate crime.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I will say that we are working very closely with our partners in the mayor's office to combat anti-Semitism as well as our community-based partners to ensure that as we are expanding this office, we are paying attention to all communities who experience hate, violence, and bias.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so we recognize that to do this work, we need good staff internally, we need good partnerships across the city, and we need good partnerships with our community-based partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We recently are one of the first programs that we were able to increase is the PATH program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We doubled that budget so that we can meet more New Yorkers, and we also invested recently a million dollars to support security initiatives for houses of worship, including

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: synagogues and other culturally sensitive locations in recognition of the urgency of this need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that is just the very first type of investment that we are working on, and you will have seen that announced in the mayor's office to combat anti-Semitism's report, because we worked very closely with our colleagues in that office on designing and building that out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Can I turn to you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We recognize that hate crimes continue to be a concern, but also, too, I think with that, we are grateful for the additional investment that was made to this office by this administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For the first time, by over 800%, our office finally has the resources to put meaningful work on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And as the Commissioner mentioned, each of our anchor partners, as part of the PATH initiative program, has received an additional 153% increase in funding to make sure that we are taking this work across the five boroughs, but across

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: communities that historically have not been given the resources to make sure that they feel safe and they can live and thrive here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And what I would add is that we're talking about a team that has been quite small that we are building, but now with OPHC being part of OCS, we can rely on each other for support as we are building out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So Executive Director Vijay has worked very closely with LaQuisha and her team to think about how we build in mental health support to the work that OPHC is expanding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that is the kind of coordination and support we are seeing across our office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So while we're talking about teams being...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Being small, one of the things that I also want to escalate is that building this work together makes us stronger.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I guess with the three employees you have, since you do have this significant new investment, then what are the plans in terms of, why are there still just three employees?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What are the plans there?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are actively in the process of crafting and posting job descriptions and intend to be hiring very shortly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And in the meantime, we are working with existing staff to support the office.

chapters.summary: Menin asks whether expanding community safety can replace the need for additional NYPD officers. Delaney-Brumsey says the city has relied on law enforcement for social service needs outside their expertise and describes a comprehensive response vision. Menin then asks about benchmarks and deadlines.
chapters.title: Menin asks about community safety replacing NYPD and accountability benchmarks

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, just two more questions, I'll pass it to the chair.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So the mayor had in the budget originally supported adding 580 police officers before reversing course of budget adoption.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What is your view in terms of believing expanding community safety, do you believe it can replace the need for additional NYPD officers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I believe as many of you testified that we have relied on law enforcement for too long to respond to social service needs that are really outside of the scope and expertise of law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And the vision of the Office of Community Safety is to build out a set of responses that will be a core component of our public safety and public health system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And as we do that work, we will continue to be able to meet people in moments of crisis, in moments of distress, after they've experienced harm with the kinds of responses that are both specific.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: specific and flexible, whether that's a behavioral health response, whether that is connecting them to a victim's advocate, whether that is connecting them to a violence interrupter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That is the work that the Office of Community Safety does, and that's the vision.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So because you mentioned that the budget is around $271 million, so

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: where the city then is investing hundreds of millions of dollars in the office, yet we have the increase in rapes and subway assaults and hate crimes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So what benchmarks and deadlines should the office be held accountable for moving forward?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are holding ourselves accountable and we should be held accountable for the idea that we are going to have a comprehensive approach to violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we are in the midst right now of a strategic planning process, which is helping us to think even more sharply about how all of these offices work together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: For example, there is victim services support across every single one of the offices that you see represented here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so we're doing the work to think about how do we knit those together so that we have a single place where people can go to get victim services, that those services are responsive to the needs of people who've experienced assault, those responsive to the needs of people who've experienced gun violence,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: responsive to the needs of people who also have behavioral health needs or experience hate crime.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So the work that we're being held accountable for is to knit all of those two together to be able to expand and to reach more and more New Yorkers over time.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much, and I'll pass it over to the chair.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Speaker, for the questions.

chapters.summary: Chair Feliz follows up on the OCS leadership structure, asking how the deputy mayor, commissioner, and offices under them are organized. Delaney-Brumsey explains the leadership team includes leaders from each of the four component offices.
chapters.title: Feliz asks about OCS leadership structure

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So I just wanted to follow up on some of the questions that the Speaker asked.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: This is obviously the first hearing that we have in the office, so I'll start with general questions related to the staff structure and the budget.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How is the leadership team structured?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: There's obviously a deputy mayor, a commissioner, and then offices under it.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Can you elaborate on the general office structure?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So the office includes myself and the leadership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: team includes leaders across each of the four offices, Office of Neighborhood Safety, Office to End Domestic and Gender-Based Violence, which includes our Office for Victims of Crime, the Office of Community Mental Health, and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: the Office for Prevention of Hate Crimes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are in the midst of both the strategic planning process, as I noted, and that will inform our future structure, because what we want to do is make sure we are building a structure that is responsive to this work, but also responsive to the goal of becoming

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: an independent department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And part of that work is also building out operations, because as you know, mayor's offices, all of their operations are usually embedded within other agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so we are also building out the operational capacity to become our own department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So the structure of this team will shift over time, but the core work of this team will be maintained and continue to grow.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks what the deputy mayor of public safety supervises versus the commissioner. Delaney-Brumsey clarifies she reports to the deputy mayor of community safety, whose team has eight staff and whose role is to build out community safety across city government.
chapters.title: Feliz asks about deputy mayor vs commissioner roles and team size

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Currently, who does the Deputy Mayor of Public Safety supervise versus you, the Commissioner of the Office of Community Safety?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And what is the difference between the two positions?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So the Deputy Mayor of Community Safety supervises me, and we have a first Deputy Mayor who oversees a number of offices and departments across the city, including some of our other public safety departments.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How large is the Deputy Mayor's team?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I have to double check my math, but the deputy mayor's team has five staff right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Her role is to oversee the office community safety, but also to build out the work that is going to be outside of the office community safety to improve how New York City in general improves community safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Because it is not just the work of one office to do community safety work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The work of all of city government focuses on improving safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So when we think about how lighting is, where we light New York City, where there are access to parks, all of that work affects community safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so the deputy mayor's role is not just to support our office, which is crucial, but also to think about how this entire administration is focused on community safety.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks how much of the $271 million budget is for staff versus programs such as cure violence. Delaney-Brumsey says she cannot do the math on the fly but will provide the exact split later.
chapters.title: Feliz asks about budget split between staff and programs

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, and earlier you mentioned the total budget for the Office of Community Safety is approximately $271 million.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How much of this is for staff versus for programs such as cure violence programs?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I would have to get back to you, and we can get back on the exact split between personnel versus OTPS.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Could you give us a rough ballpark?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Would you say 50-50 or 70-30?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: No, it can't be 50-50.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: There's about 100 staff total across OCS, which are paid for by the $271 million.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Would you say it's like 70% to 80% being super?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I will not be able to do that math on the fly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I will definitely make sure that we get back to you with that split.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks where OCS is headquartered and whether it plans a stronger presence in affected communities. Delaney-Brumsey says most staff sit at 253 Broadway, with some at family justice centers, and OCS is contemplating locations through its strategic planning process.
chapters.title: Feliz asks about office location and community presence

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: This is, again, obviously a new office.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Does the Office of Community Safety currently have a permanent work location?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Where is it headquartered?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And also, what is the plan to have a stronger presence in the communities that are disproportionately affected by the issues that we're all working on, safety and mental health?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The bulk of our team, the vast majority of our team, sits across the street into 53 Broadway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We also have staff members who sit within our family justice centers across the five boroughs, but the vast majority of our team are within our central office, which is 253 Broadway.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Are there any plans to have a stronger presence in the communities that are affected by these issues?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And if yes, can you elaborate on those plans?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So what I will say is that this, the Office of Community Safety and the teams that work within it have a really strong connection to the communities that we serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We have our family justice centers, which are in all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We have our CVAP program, our Crime Victims Assistance Program, where our staff members are, our contracted providers are located within precincts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The goal of this office is to ensure that we are in very close contact with community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so as we are building out our strategic planning process, one thing that we are contemplating is where we need to be located across the city so that we can make sure that we are doing the work of being embedded within community and we are able to reach the community members that we need to connect with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: However, even with the work as it is structured now, our team is frequently on a daily basis in the field across the city working with communities and with our community-based partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: to do the work of improving safety.

chapters.summary: Feliz notes that about 40% of city shootings occur in the Bronx and suggests OCS should be headquartered in a disproportionately affected community. Delaney-Brumsey agrees on the importance of close community contact and says OCS has significant Bronx work through the Office of Neighborhood Safety.
chapters.title: Feliz suggests OCS headquarters in Bronx or affected community

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, thank you for that information.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'll certainly be interested in continuing that conversation offline.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You know, when I see an office like this one, whose role is, you know, improving safety in the city of New York, especially gun violence, and when I see numbers including, for example, approximately, you know, 40% of the shootings that occur in this city

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: happen in communities in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I don't see a reason why an office like this one wouldn't be headquartered out of a community that is disproportionately affected by these issues.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So I'll be interested in chatting offline about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We would love to speak about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And I will say that we have...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: A significant amount of work that we do in the Bronx through the Office of Neighborhood Safety, which I can turn to Executive Director LaRochelle to talk about, but we are in agreement that the need to be in close communication and in close contact with the communities we support is essential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that's embedded in the way we work right now, and it will continue to be embedded in the work as we build out our office.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks whether OCS has established any new functions or if it has simply reorganized existing programs. Delaney-Brumsey begins to answer by describing the combination of work as essential to success.
chapters.title: Feliz asks if OCS created new functions or just reorganized

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, so there's five offices under the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Would you say the Office of Community Safety so far has established any new functions, or at least at this point it was simply a reorganization and a consolidation of programs that already existed, at least at this point?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know there's plans to expand and a total, but at least these past seven months, have there been any new functions established?

chapters.summary: Delaney-Brumsey explains that OCS has created new ways of working together, such as NGBV and ONS coordinating on emergency housing transfers. She says this makes offices stronger by avoiding silos.
chapters.title: Commissioner answers on new ways of working and expansions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So there's a few ways that I would like to tackle that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The first is I would characterize the combination of this work as essential to our success.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So, and I mean that on a...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Micro level, for example, we have right now the Office to End Domestic and Gender-Based Violence and our Office of Neighborhood Safety thinking very carefully about how we support emergency housing transfers for people who are

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: either victims of crime or at risk for retaliation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so while that isn't a new function, it is a new way of working together that makes those offices stronger because they are not having to think in silos or utilize only their own resources to address really crucial public safety needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: In addition to that, during this time, since the office has launched, we've expanded several of our initiatives, and I can turn to a couple of my team members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I'll ask Ed to speak some about some of the expansions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: that NGBV has had to our culturally specific services, to some of our other services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we are continuing to do that expansion as we

chapters.summary: An NGBV official describes expansions under the new budget, including mental health services at Family Justice Centers and homeless shelters, and increased funding for the relationship abuse prevention program in schools.
chapters.title: NGBV official details expansions in mental health and prevention programs

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So in recent, under the new budget, we're able to expand our mental health services at the Family Justice Center and also at

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: homeless shelters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So there's more additional funds for that to expand those services and get them out to more people so more people can be served.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There is also...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I apologize, give me just one second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There's also been increased funding for our relationship abuse prevention program, which works with

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: middle school and high school students, in addition to staff and their parents, to raise awareness about

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: relationship abuse and what a healthy relationship should look like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And in addition, that program also offers group counseling and individual counseling to students who are identified through the program as already experiencing relationship abuse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that's just one example of the way we've been able to expand and deepen some of the work.

chapters.summary: Executive Director LaRochelle describes expanding Crisis Management System services to Bushwick, Inwood, and Harlem. He notes CMS operates in 49 catchment areas across 33 precincts and highlights Bronx assets including street outreach and mobile trauma units.
chapters.title: ONS Executive Director LaRochelle details CMS expansion into Bushwick, Inwood, Harlem

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I'd also like to turn to Executive Director LaRochelle to talk about some of the expansions we've seen in our neighborhood safety work over the years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: the last several months.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you so much, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: So we recently expanded CV and CMS services to Bushwick, Inwood, as well as Harlem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: So again, just expanding the footprint of the crisis management system throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Just some, you know, at a glance here, we're in 49 catchment areas across 33 NYPD precincts, spanning 20 neighborhoods across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: So we have a footprint in each of the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And Chair Felice, you mentioned the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: I just want to talk a little bit about, you know, the assets that we have in the Bronx, which includes street outreach teams, mobile trauma units, hospital-based violence intervention programs, and a host of therapeutics.

chapters.summary: Feliz follows up, noting the programs existed before and asking specifically about new functions. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS is expanding and strengthening existing work as the foundation for future new initiatives.
chapters.title: Feliz follows up on new functions and expansions

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, yes, thank you for all that information.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You know, these are all obviously very important programs, programs that I think all of us here support.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But I'm just wondering, though, have there been any new functions, though?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Because these were things that were already there.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They're being expanded, but they were already in the works.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So I'm just wondering if there's been any new functions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We've been working on making sure we are expanding and strengthening the work that exists because that will be the foundation for which we build out any new functions or any new initiatives as we expand and grow.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, thank you for the information.

chapters.summary: Feliz questions the Be Heard program, asking how large the team is and which precincts are eligible. Grant explains Be Heard operates in 31 precincts, fully in the Bronx and parts of Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens, selected based on 911 mental health call data.
chapters.title: Feliz questions Be Heard team size, precincts, and eligibility

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'll move on to a few questions related to the Beat Heart program, and then I'll pass it on to Chill Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And then colleagues, thank you everybody for being patient on this Friday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So the Be Her program, obviously a very important program, obviously a very important program.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We want to make sure that if New Yorkers are facing emergencies, we want to make sure that they receive the help that they need.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: In this case, it's individuals facing mental health emergencies, something that obviously requires mental health professionals.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You kind of touched on it earlier today, but briefly, how large is the Be Heard team and what precincts are Be Heard eligible and how do you determine eligibility?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So I will turn to Deputy Executive Director Grant to talk about some of the precincts that we're in as well as the size of the program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: But the way that Be Heard was developed and the way it's expanded is focusing, utilizing our 911 call system data to identify the precincts with the highest rates of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: 911 behavioral health crisis calls and prioritizing those for the initial launch and then subsequent expansions of Be Heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that's the kind of work that we will continue to do as we expand the program, looking for where there's high needs, where we go next, and then continuing across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Be Heard currently operates in 31 precincts in the surrounding areas, so it's fully operational in the Bronx

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: and then operational in parts of Manhattan, all of Upper Manhattan from Harlem up through Washington Heights, in Brooklyn, neighborhoods in Brooklyn, including East New York, Brownsville.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: parts of Queens as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And as the commissioner mentioned, we identified those neighborhoods, those precincts using 911 mental health call data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And so the precincts where Be Heard operates have some of the highest rates of 911 mental health emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I want to recognize Council Members Dinowitz, Banks, and Caban who have joined.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What are calls that are eligible for a be heard response and what are calls that are not eligible?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know, for example, if there's violence or weapons that that wouldn't be eligible.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So you could give us a summary on those calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: So be heard response to what we call low acuity mental health calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: So those are calls where there's an indication of a mental health need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: There is no violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: There is no known violence, no known weapons and no imminent risk of serious harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: So an example of that might be someone who is in the middle of the street in a very dangerous situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And so calls that would not be eligible are calls where the caller is indicating that the person in crisis has a weapon or is actively violent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And again, that's because we send EMTs and social workers to those calls without police.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: So we don't want them to be in situations where.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: there's already an indication of safety concerns and danger.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: If the caller does not know whether or not the person in question in crisis is violent or has a weapon, we'll still send Be Heard to those calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Those calls are still eligible for Be Heard while we try and get more information about what's happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And if the teams do need support from police, they have that available.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks about total 911 call volume and what percentage are Be Heard eligible. Grant says there are about 150,000 mental health calls per year, 10,945 were eligible, and Be Heard responded to 8,524. Commissioner adds total 911 calls are about 1.6 million.
chapters.title: Feliz asks about 911 call volume and Be Heard eligible numbers

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How many 911 calls do we receive every year, and what percent would you say are Be Heard eligible?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Could you provide some data on the last two years?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And also, how many calls are you able to respond to?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So how many 911 calls, how many Be Heard eligible, and how many are you able to respond to out of those that are eligible?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: So there are about 150,000 calls that are mental health calls per year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Of those, typically around, if...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We had, and last year it was 10,900.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: How many was it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Yep, 10,945 calls were eligible for Be Heard, and then Be Heard responded to 8,524.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, and how many down-home calls do we usually receive per year?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Do you have any data on that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: It's about 1.6 million.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: 1.6 million.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks about the Be Heard budget and the plan to make it 24-7. Delaney-Brumsey says the budget is $35.3 million, the program operates 9 a.m. to 1 a.m. 365 days a year, and OCS is working with FDNY, H&H, and OMB to assess expansion costs.
chapters.title: Feliz asks about Be Heard budget and 24/7 expansion plans

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, some final questions.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What is the current Be Heard budget?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Is the plan to get it up and running 24-7?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: My understanding is that it's not 24-7 currently.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And how much would it take?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What would be the cost for getting it 24-7 and also in the areas that...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: That you're planning based on the many needs that we have in the city related to mental health and other...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So our goal is to make sure that we are responding to as many behavioral health calls as possible, and we are doing that, and we are expanding across the city so that more and more New Yorkers can receive access to Be Heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Right now, the program operates 9 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: To 1 a.m., 365 days a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And we...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: You asked the question was...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Oh, how much would it cost?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Or what the budget is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The budget is $35.3 million across both teams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: As we are working on this expansion, we are in very close contact with both FDNY and H&H to determine when and if there are additional resources needed, and we'll work very closely with our OMB colleagues to request those resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I don't have a specific estimate right now because we are in the process of doing that work of assessing exactly how many calls there are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: are that we would need to be expanding to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We're working on a joint data analysis as well as a staffing and expansion plan across all of those teams, and that will give us a more precise determination of the necessary resources, and we will work with all of those partners and OMB as we need.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks about Be Heard response time and what the response includes. Delaney-Brumsey explains teams consist of two FDNY EMS professionals and one H&H social worker who assess medical and behavioral health needs, de-escalate, and connect people to care or hospital.
chapters.title: Feliz asks about Be Heard response time and team composition

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Final question, how large is the, or talk to us about the response time for those that are eligible for Be Heard, for Be Heard response, and what exactly does the response include?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know it includes FDNY or paramedics and mental health professionals, but what exactly would the response include?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So the teams conclude two FDNY EMS professionals and one New York City Health and Hospital social worker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: They work together in pairs to respond to these calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's a necessary combination of staffing because we want to make sure that when we do show up to the call, we have the expertise to assess if someone's also in a medical crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So some may be aware that sometimes a panic attack may look like a heart attack or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So the EMS professionals are essential to be there to clear someone medically, and the social worker is there to support their behavioral health needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The way I just described that makes it actually sound significantly more separate than it is because those teams work really closely together to ensure that they are supporting the patient, helping to de-escalate the situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And the response on the ground includes a very robust clinical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: intervention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The social worker will assess what the person's needs are, they will connect with them about what their

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: past history is, they will provide de-escalation and calming techniques, they will assess whether or not the person needs to go to the hospital, or whether they can reconnect them to existing community-based services or other services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So it is a flexible response, but it is a behavioral health response.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I have many more questions, but I'll pause for now.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'll pass it on to co-chair Gilbrewer.

chapters.summary: Co-Chair Brewer praises Be Heard and asks what happens to a person after they are serviced, noting difficulty finding quality follow-up care. Delaney-Brumsey acknowledges the gap in disposition options and says OCS is working with DOHMH and H&H on an interagency working group.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about Be Heard disposition options and next steps

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have been out with Be Heard a couple of times, and I would absolutely second the fact that they're excellent.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This is the issue.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What do you do with the person who has been serviced by Be Heard?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My understanding is it's hard to find a place that that person gets quality services.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What's really needed, and Dr.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Katz agrees, is 24-hour OT, nurse, and psychiatric.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Only one place in East Harlem has such a location.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I'm just wondering, are you aware of that situation?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Where do you say they go?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And what are you doing?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I just want to say, this is a great hearing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You have the most important topic in the whole city.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What the hell are we going to do with people who need help?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so I'm just excited to hear this, but your shoulders have to be very big to carry all this.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Be heard.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Where are you going to put everybody?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because they need help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, myself and the team is acutely aware of both the importance of this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: and the responsibility that has been placed on this office to build out the work in a way that is effective and responsive to what New Yorkers need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And I will say that this is the work of our office, but it's the work of the entire city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So to your question about where else do you take people, this has been a challenge that we are continuing to work on, not just in Be Heard, but with our partners at DOHMH and New York City Health Hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We were just yesterday connecting with DOHMH on their plans around improving access to serious mental illness services because that's the kind of work that you need to have so that you can reduce the likelihood that people go into crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we right now are engaged in an interagency working group to think very clearly about what are the other, we call them disposition options, but what are the other places that we can connect people to when a Be Heard team connects with them that is not the hospital

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: and is not their home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Now, one of the great things about Be Heard is we...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Have we are able to bring such effective clinical care to people that we are often able to support them in their home in school in shelter support them in that moment and let them stay there safely

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: but there are a group of people who need additional care but it's not quite as acute as going to a hospital and we are trying to work on that gap sometimes we are able to take people to supporting connection centers we are sometimes able to connect people to respite

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: centers but there is a gap in the system that we are working to fill and that's exactly the kind of challenge we are working towards and would like to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Love to continue discussing.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about utilization of Family Justice Centers, which she says seem underused. Officials explain that post-COVID, 40-60% of visits are remote, and the FJCs served about 16,200 people and 64,000 visits last fiscal year.
chapters.title: Brewer questions Family Justice Center utilization

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, I love doing what Dr.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Katz says.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What we need is what I just listed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I go with Dr.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Katz.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Oh, always, always, always.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number two, when I go to the family centers, there's not a lot of people there.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I'm just wondering, how are you going to utilize them?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What is their plan for them?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're beautiful.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're, you know, well laid out, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Children, families, everything's there.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Casework, location, so on.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But they don't seem to be extremely well utilized.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how are we, is that true?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Or is it just me going on the wrong day?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And how do you look at it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The Family Justice Centers, I'll turn to Deputy Commissioner Hill for some numbers on utilization, but those centers are a core part of OCS's work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: One of our goals is to make sure not only that they continue to remain strong, but that we are continuing to connect as many people as possible to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I will say, especially post-COVID, one of the things that has been a big shift in the behavioral health space and the social service space is the shift to many services remote.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We find that that actually really is helpful for survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so often when you're going to a physical location, you're not necessarily seeing the people that we are.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They were telling me people are remote, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, but we have been seeing really significant, strong utilization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So I'd like to turn to the commissioner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As the commissioner noted, pre-COVID, all services at the FJC had to be done in person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We had no remote services at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Of course, responding to COVID, that changed literally overnight, over a week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Last fiscal year, the FJCs served about 16,200 people, about 64,000 visits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's actually increased since 2024.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And about...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Depending on the FJC, because it varies across the five, but somewhere between 40 and 60% of visits are done remotely.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, I mean, as time goes on, I guess real estate is always an issue because it's beautiful space, and people are going remote.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Even the caseworkers were remote.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Everybody was remote when I was there.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question would be, what are you going to use it for if fewer people are there?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Not now, but I would like to hear that because the space is phenomenal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: No, those spaces are beautiful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: They're a real asset to the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: They're an asset to the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And one of the conversations that we have been having to Chair Felice's question is how do we ensure that we're utilizing any physical resources that we have to ensure that we are

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: having space for our contracted providers, for others to operate out of them and serving more and more people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Because we want to make sure that we're meeting people where they are, if that's in their home, if that's remotely, if that's physically, but completely agree with you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that is absolutely a space where we will be.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: To put that on your strategic list.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what it means to take a public health approach to violence. Delaney-Brumsey says it means recognizing how lived environment, social networks, and access to resources affect violence, and LaRochelle adds it means leveraging data and addressing root causes.
chapters.title: Brewer asks what a public health approach to violence means

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What does it mean to take a public health approach to violence?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because that is, I think, the core of your work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That is the core of our work, and I will also ask Executive Director LaRochelle to speak to this, but when I think of a public health response to violence, that to me

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: talks about recognizing that the places that we live, the resources that we have access to, the people in our networks, those all affect our likelihood for experiencing violence,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: and that to address violence, prevent it, we need to make adjustments in all of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We need to think about the lived environment, we need to think about the social environment, and we need to connect people to resources that have been shown by evidence as well as what we hear from our partners and from survivors is necessary to reduce violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: No, thank you so much, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And I think for us, the public health approach to violence means leveraging data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: We know that resources are limited, so we want to make sure that the data is helping to inform the populations and areas that we need to be in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: It also means really understanding and recognizing the antecedents to violence, right, the root causes of violence,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: whether it's health, whether it's housing, employment, education, and that we're addressing those needs because we know when we address those needs, invariably, violence goes down.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about specific metrics used to determine if OCS is helping make communities safer. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS uses crime data, program data, and satisfaction surveys, and is building out a broader data and evaluation framework.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about metrics for measuring community safety

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, those are good answers.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Hard to implement.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have specific metrics that you're using to determine whether you are helping make the community safer, either with the violence interrupter?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Or any of these other programs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think I know all your programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: You do know all our programs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Every one of them, and I've been to every one of them.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's amazing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We really appreciate your partnership and support around this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I mean, and the way that we think about metrics across the team, there's a few, there's different kinds of metrics we use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Certainly we look at crime data from our NYPD partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's one kind of metric that we use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We also use metrics such as program data around how we're supporting people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So you heard me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Quote numbers about how many mediations our crisis management service system providers have had, how many people we are serving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We also look at whether or not the people that we are serving are satisfied with our work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So you heard me quote numbers from Be Heard about patient satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Similarly, we get numbers from our Family Justice Center around satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so we look across all of that type of data to understand whether we're having an impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: However, one of the things that I will say is that as OCS builds and develops, one of the things we want to do is take the work that we have right now around data and evaluation and expand and grow that because we know that to be

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: effective and stewards of this vision and of New York City's taxpayers'dollars, we need to be able to show both what we're doing and the impact that we're having.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so building out that data and evaluation framework is something we're actively engaged in.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what OCS is doing to learn from other cities. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS has had calls with leadership from cities across the country, including Baltimore and Tucson, and is actively learning from other jurisdictions.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about learning from other cities

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I used to be on the...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: the large cities board chair of the National League of Cities.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so Albuquerque, and I know my friend who's the mayor of Baltimore, he gets lots of great press.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't know if he's doing a great job, but he thinks he's doing a great job.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And the press does too.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question to you is, what are you doing to look at other cities to see if what they're doing is helpful, if at all?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Oh, we're doing so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Actually, we just set up a meeting with Baltimore leadership to make sure that we are connecting with them about what they're doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We have...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: All of this team here has had calls with leadership from cities across the country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We have worked with various jurisdictions to learn from them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We've looked at places like Tucson that has a really strong mental health crisis system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So part of the work of building out what happens in New York City, we are of course an extremely unique city, not just because of our size, but our structure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: But that is also about making sure that we are learning from other jurisdictions, and we're doing that actively.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: You cannot do this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Kind of with your blinders on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: You have to be able to hear what is happening in other jurisdictions, as well as talk to the people who've been doing this work in New York for so long to learn from people there too.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'll give you the mayor's cell phone in Baltimore.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks if OCS work might decrease police overtime. Delaney-Brumsey hopes it will allow the city to rely less on police for safety and crisis issues. Brewer also asks if other agencies might come under OCS; Delaney-Brumsey says OCS partners with many agencies.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about police overtime and other agencies under OCS

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My other question is, overtime for PD is always an issue, comes up every year.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you think the work you're doing might help to decrease overtime at PD?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is that one of your metrics?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I will say that I'm really hopeful that the work that we do allows New York City to say that we have a really robust

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: community-based response to lots of different types of safety and crisis issues, and that we have stopped relying only or solely on police in those situations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that is what I'm hoping that we will be able to see over time.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have ideas about other agencies coming under your umbrella, or is this it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I would say that we are really excited to partner with other agencies who do work that is essential for us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we are in active partnership with, I hesitate to even try to name agencies because that means we will leave people out, but active relationship, as you've heard, health and hospitals, DOHMH, Department of Social Services,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: parks, sanitation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Probation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Probation, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So the fact is that everything can't live with under one umbrella, but we can do this work comprehensively and we can do it in partnership.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about overlap between OCS and the Mayor's Office of Criminal Justice. Delaney-Brumsey says they work very closely, including joint meetings and data sharing, recognizing their work is part of an ongoing continuum.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about OCS overlap with Mayor's Office of Criminal Justice

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, last question.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you overlap in the work between you and Mark J?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Mark J has a lot of contracts working also in trying to reduce
