utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: challenges and keeping people out of the criminal justice system, etc.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How do you work together?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We work together very, very closely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I was actually just on a call this morning with Justine Olderman, the criminal justice coordinator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We have

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: joint meetings with Mach J, we work with their data team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We recognize that for the work that Mach J is doing to be successful, our work has to be successful and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so we recognize ourselves to be part of an ongoing continuum and a project of building out safety together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, co-chair Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, I'll pass it on to public advocate Williams.

chapters.summary: Chair Feliz asks if OCS tracks what happens after connecting individuals to services. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS tracks where people are taken, but does not yet have a metric for long-term outcomes, though H&H community health workers follow up with patients.
chapters.title: Feliz asks about tracking outcomes after Be Heard assistance

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But before that, just curious.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So I'm actually impressed by the amount of be heard calls that you were able to respond to.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know you mentioned about 10 or 11,000 were be heard eligible and you were able to respond to about 8.5.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: That's impressive based on the budget that you have.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Just curious though, do you have

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Do you keep track of what happens after you connect these individuals to other services?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So what we do is we track where we take people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So if we are taking them to the hospital, whether we're connecting them to another type of community-based service, whether we left them, say, at their home but with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: referrals and support, because that's really the goal of Be Heard is to respond in that moment and to take that moment of crisis and change it into a moment where we are supporting people and helping people heal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We don't yet have a metric where we track exactly what happens to people afterwards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Sometimes we're taking people to private hospitals that are outside of the city's purview.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: However, one thing that we do have is New York City Health and Hospitals has community health workers who will call patients to check in with them, conduct the patient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: survey and see if there is any support that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Anything you'd like to add to that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Yeah, just as part of that follow-up, they are also asking if they made it to the appointments that were set for them or if they used the referrals that were provided.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks if there is a plan to keep information on what happens after assistance to avoid people cycling back to square one. Delaney-Brumsey acknowledges the challenge and says OCS is working on an MOU to track from call through response.
chapters.title: Feliz asks about plans to track follow-up after services

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Is there a plan to, I guess, keep information related to what happens after you assist someone?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Because I'm just wondering whether, you know, one thing is for us to be able to connect them to services and be able to have enough capacity to do that for everybody that helps to be...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Needs to be connected to services, but then after they're connected, nothing happens, and then we're back to square one, and we don't make any progress.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, you're pointing to a really, a real challenge for the system and for crisis response in general.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And I think the way that we are approaching it now is really around the way that we follow up with the patients to see if they have connected to their provider.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We do a lot of work on the ground to make sure that any disposition that we are giving really is helpful for people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: But what we also want to make sure that we are doing is...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: What's the word?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm losing my train of thought.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: But what we do right now is that kind of follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And we also are right now doing the work of merging agency, getting an MOU so that we can see more clearly what's happening from the point of call all the way through our response, which will help us get even more precise about how we're understanding the program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: But what you are raising around making sure we're interrupting that cycle is a very real challenge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And I would just add, as the commissioner mentioned earlier, we do have an interagency working group that's looking at kind of what are the options in the community for when we bring someone to someone who

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: had a visit from a Be Heard team, as we're referring them to different community-based options, kind of, they have raised this question around

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: on the need to understand what is happening after that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And so that is something that we're actively thinking about with our partners in the health department at H&H and other health care agencies in the city.

chapters.summary: Delaney-Brumsey corrects earlier numbers: the deputy mayor's team has eight staff, and about 5% of OCS's budget is for city staff. She also notes the budget split between personnel and programs.
chapters.title: Commissioner corrects deputy mayor staff count and budget split

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, I just got two notes from people who are faster on their feet with numbers that I misstated a number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: You asked previously, Chair, about how many people were on the deputy mayor's team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: It might have been someone else, but you asked previously how many people were on the deputy mayor's staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: It's actually eight staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And someone else was able to do the math on this for me as well, the question about how much of OCS's budget is for city staff versus programs and OTPS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Approximately 5% of our budget is for city staff.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks which programs OCS would most want to expand based on needs. Delaney-Brumsey declines to pick one or two, saying all programs are essential, and cites flexible grants for violence survivors and school-based consent education.
chapters.title: Feliz asks which programs need expansion

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, thank you for that information.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And also going back to the earlier question, based on the New Yorkers that you've been able to help this past year, you connect them to services, depending on the needs that they have,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What would you say are programs that we absolutely have to think about expanding based on the needs that you continue to confront?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's a really good question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I would say that that's actually a hard choice because we help New Yorkers across every single one of our programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so to me, it's not about picking just one or two.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: It's about recognizing that all of the work that we do is essential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I think about the funding that we were able to provide for flexible grants for people who've experienced violence to make sure that if they, say, for example,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: need money to buy new furniture for a new apartment, that that's a kind of need that we had not been able to serve in the way we needed, and so we were able to expand into that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I think about the kind of work that we are doing with young people in schools to address bias

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: and the necessity of teaching young people how to interact with each other with respect and the necessity of teaching young people how to go into their first relationships in a way that allows them to recognize what consent

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: looks like and should look like and what it should feel like to be in a loving relationship.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: All of that work is essential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so I wouldn't want to pick just one thing or two things.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from public advocate Jumaane Williams.

chapters.summary: Public Advocate Williams asks about the frequency and level of OCS meetings with NYPD leadership. Delaney-Brumsey says she and the deputy mayor met with the police commissioner early in her tenure and she has regular contact with NYPD leadership.
chapters.title: Williams asks about NYPD leadership meeting frequency

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I thank you, Commissioner, and the entire team for being here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I wanted to drill down a little bit because I, like,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I am so appreciative of the office being here and appreciative of the work that's being done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But I have to say, from afar, when I've traveled to other cities that have been successful in this, the synergy is a lot better than what I see.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I just want to go back to when I believe a speaker asked how many times you meet with PD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So my question is very specific.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'd like to know what a definition of leadership is, of who's meeting with who, and when was the last time the commissioner or you or the deputy mayor has met with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: the commissioner of the police department or the chief of department?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So the deputy mayor and I met with the police commissioner early on in our tenure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We've continued to have conversations and meetings at the leadership level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That includes with the first deputy commissioner, a variety of deputy commissioners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I meet regularly with deputy commissioners across NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The way we're doing this work is that for any particular program, we're working with the leadership who's most closely related to that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that also includes the leadership here who's working with their counterparts across NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I don't want to put anyone in difficult situations, but I'm going to keep pressing because I appreciate what you said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But it sounds like the last time the deputy mayor or you, the commissioner, met with the police commissioner or the chief of department was roughly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I came on board in late May.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The last time that I met with the police commissioner herself was sometime after that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I'd have to get the exact date.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: But since then, I have been in regular, weekly, sometimes more than weekly contact with her leadership team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It's important to me because I want to differentiate you meeting with civilian leaders in the police department and operational police leaders in the police department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And so it doesn't seem like the latter is happening in any regularity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I just want to make sure that's on the record.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I think that's a part of the problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And I will say also, and I'll turn to Executive Director LaRochelle to talk about some of the ways that we are working very closely with senior members of NYPD's uniform service across Office of Neighborhood Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I know you're very familiar with that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Public Advocate Williams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: So we've been working very, very closely with NYPD around data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: So we get police alerts, for instance, on a daily basis, which helps to inform how we operationalize cure violence and our CMS groups.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: We work with them on special activations like Labor Day and Juve, for instance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: So we're very, very closely with them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And I think the important thing to understand is that the roles are distinct but different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Our role, obviously, is to make sure that we are advocating and supporting civilian-led and community-based approaches to violence prevention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And their job is law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: But it's very important to make sure because we operate in the same neighborhoods, the same communities, and we interface with the same populations that we're working together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: We also make sure that we are talking to their leadership on an almost weekly basis around data that they can offer to us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Again, so we could trickle it down to our folks on the ground who are doing this work and help out with their operations.

chapters.summary: Williams asks if OCS is invited to CompStat and CrimeStat briefings. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS was invited to one CompStat before Juve but is not currently attending CompStat or CrimeStat briefings regularly.
chapters.title: Williams asks about OCS attendance at CompStat and CrimeStat briefings

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Is OCS invited to CompStat meetings and crime briefings?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We were invited to the CompStat that was prior to Juve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We were really happy to be able to participate in that, just as we had had, remind me of the inspector's name, at Alvergia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We had an, well, yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we worked really closely with NYPD leadership, both uniform and civilian, around the Juve deployment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so we were invited to the CompStat before that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And then they were participating in our Juve preparation, which we were doing at that point on a, I want to say, weekly basis, and the deputy mayor's team was managing that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Wait, it sounds like there's not CompStat meetings regularly that you're invited to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are not currently attending CompStat meetings regularly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And CrimeStat briefings?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I'm not currently attending crime stat briefings regularly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Williams discusses the disparity between OCS's $271 million budget and NYPD's roughly $60 billion budget. He argues the city needs a structure compatible with NYPD's 24-hour operations and urges building out OCS infrastructure and funding.
chapters.title: Williams discusses budget disparity and need for integrated OCS structure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And the reason is, I'm bringing this up because we are, if you say $275 million is the budget.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The police department, the city is, without the federal funding, is roughly maybe $60, $65 billion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And so I think we're at a point now where people actually understand more than they did 15, 16 years ago why we need alternatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And so we've reached that point, which is a success.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Now we're at a point where we have to stand up a structure that can be compatible with what the police department is doing at $60 billion and is 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And in order to do that, we really have to push the envelope and make sure that when people think of the Office of Community Safety, they think of the way they think of other safety measures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And so when you mentioned NYPD, when you mentioned FDNY, those things conjure something in people's minds that I don't think is where we want to be right now for the alternatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And so we need the funding and we need the structure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The funding is going to come hopefully soon, sooner than later.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We'll build a bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I don't know when we'll get to $60 billion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Imagine if this office had $1 billion, what it can do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But we can build out an infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: That respects the work of OCS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I haven't seen that yet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And that's part of the questions that we have here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: No, I appreciate the concern.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And I would say that this is part of that process of building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: You know, nothing...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: that we do that's strong, that works well, is built overnight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And the fact is that the Office of Neighborhood Safety, OSU, all of these do work with NYPD at different leadership levels, both uniform and non-uniform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And we are continuing to build that relationship, and we will continue to strengthen that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I don't want to overstate my welcome because the chair allowed me to squeeze in, so there's more questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I just want to make it clear that I want to not be confused.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: You have a different function in the police department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But they are, wherever they are, they're going to be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The lack of a better word, guerrilla in the room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: That's what everybody looks at.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So we want to make sure that coordination is happening not just with them, but so many others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We want to stand up CMS workers, some of whom have lost their lives in doing this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And we lift off Antoine, who released a loss of life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: There's not job open mobility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: There's not the pensions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: There's not the things that people think about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And we have to stand that up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And this administration has been very good at standing up things very quickly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I want to push them to really envelope on this as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So thank you so much for being here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I'll continue to push some very difficult questions as efficiently and effectively as I can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Thank you for your support and your push.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Councilmember Sandy Nurse.

chapters.summary: Council Member Sandy Nurse asks about the expansion of Be Heard and whether peers with lived experience are being deployed with teams. Delaney-Brumsey says 27 new staff are responders, and H&H has hired an associate director focused on incorporating peers.
chapters.title: Nurse asks about peers in Be Heard teams

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you for all your testimony here today.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I have a few questions, but based on some of the conversations that have happened, I'm glad to hear the expansion of, I think you said, 27 new staff for...

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: The Be Heard project, that's really, really great.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: We'd love at some point maybe in the follow-up to get where those folks are at.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Is it in calls?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Is it out on the ground?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: What that would be?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: You don't have to detail all of that here just for the sake of time.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: But the only other thing I wanted to mention on that is over the last couple of years, a lot of the community groups and advocacy groups have really called for the deployment of peers with these teams in the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And so wondering if you've had any conversations about exploring that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And I will say, just to answer your question quickly, because it's an easy answer, those 27 staff are the staff that will be responding to calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's the training that we were doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Those are not, that's not necessarily administrative folks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So that's what those staff are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We have had not just conversations, but we're making strides towards how do we incorporate peers into Be Heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: New York City Health and Hospitals did hire a person who is their associate director, who is on Be Heard, who is focused on how do we build in peers to that program, and that work is currently underway right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And we're looking forward to working with our partners and to the advocates who've really pushed this work as we structure that role.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I'd really love to hear that.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks how youth and impacted communities are informing OCS strategy. Delaney-Brumsey describes a listening tour with over 1,400 young people and says the strategic planning process will solicit feedback from impacted communities.
chapters.title: Nurse asks about youth and community input in OCS strategy

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And my other question was really about, could you list out some of the specific opportunities or intervention points where youth and impacted communities are going to be informing or are currently informing?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: informing the overall strategy of where this office is going?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, no, thank you so much for asking that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's such an important question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so from the beginning of this office, that has, well, since before the creation of this office, because all of these offices work so very closely with impacted communities and as with youth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: But we started off the work, the deputy mayor began her tenure with her and myself a listening tour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that listening tour began with young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: It was across New York City schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We had more than 1,400 young people talking to the deputy mayor about what they understand and see as their major safety concerns and what they need to be safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And we are expanding that work as we are going to our partners who support people with behavioral health needs, organizations that support people who have experienced domestic and gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that's part of how we are informing that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We're also in the midst of launching our strategic planning process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And as part of that, we are both going to be hearing from, of course, our staff, council, other government agency partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: But we will be also soliciting feedback and thoughts from impacted communities, both youth and otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I think you've answered all my other questions.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: The one thing I will comment on is that while we applaud the expansion of funding into an organization like the WIC over

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: In North Brooklyn, the Bushwick community does not feel that that is serving Bushwick specifically.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So that was a lot of feedback I'm getting, that that is Williamsburg, the area is that.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So I just want to flag that for you all as that caused a little bit of, it ruffled some feathers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: No, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And I appreciate the correction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I should have said, you know, focus on Bushwick houses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We also know that that is a concern and a criticism that has been raised.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And we'd like to continue to work with our partners with the WIC and otherwise to make sure that we are meeting the needs of all the communities that we're looking to serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Councilmember Murano.

chapters.summary: Council Member Frank Morano says he is not opposed to non-police approaches but worries about bureaucracy. He asks for one measurable public safety improvement from OCS's creation; Delaney-Brumsey cites the first Be Heard integrated training since 2024 and CMS expansion.
chapters.title: Morano asks for measurable public safety improvement from OCS creation

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I know it's Friday afternoon and before Halloween and Election Day, I'm sure you're eager to get the weekend started.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to start by saying that I'm certainly not opposed to non-police approaches to public safety.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I think if we can prevent a shooting or get somebody mental health treatment before a situation becomes dangerous, I think that's a great thing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I am concerned about creating additional layers of bureaucracy.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We've seen something similar in the past with Thrive NYC, where the city assembled numerous programs under one umbrella, spent a lot of taxpayer dollars, and struggled with accountability.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony describes the accomplishments of five existing offices, most of which were operating long before your office was established in March.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Can you identify one measurable public safety improvement that's occurred specifically because the Office of Community Safety was created rather than because of programs that already existed?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: What I will say is that because the Office of Community Safety is created, we have been able to advance programs that have been either stuck or that needed a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: additional support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So for example, you heard that this year was the first year that we were able to hold a Be Heard integrated staff training since 2024.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That is in part because our office was created to advance the goals of Be Heard, and that's a public safety outcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Whether or not we are able to staff an initiative that responds to 911 calls at the rate that it should.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: You also heard that we were able to expand CMS into three additional neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So part of, bless you,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Part of what we are doing is that work of expanding and building out additional programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we are not doing this from a place where we hover above the work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are doing the work of implementing these programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And the fact is that some of these programs have existed for a long time because they are effective and that we don't want to jettison that and we want to invest more deeply.

chapters.summary: Morano asks how many of the 14,232 CMS mediations involved credible threats and how the city verifies them. Delaney-Brumsey says providers report data and OCS conducts site visits, and LaRochelle explains the specific definition of de-escalations and conflict mediations.
chapters.title: Morano questions CMS mediation numbers and independent verification

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony says that in fiscal year 2026, your crisis management system providers conducted 14,232 mediations and de-escalations,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: and I think that's a really impressive number.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But I have a question about what that number actually means.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many of those 14,232 interventions involved a credible threat of imminent violence, and how many were routine disputes that might never have escalated?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And as you answer that, how does the city independently verify that these interventions actually

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: occurred.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I'll turn to my colleague for more details, but what I will say is that we think it is important to intervene at any level of dispute that we are seeing, whether it's a dispute that might be relatively minor or a dispute that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: is significant while we are seeing it, because we know that something that's minor can over time become more significant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we do not want to constrain ourselves to saying that there's only certain types of disputes that we should be intervening in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: However, what I will also say is that the staff of the crisis management system, these are people who have both deep expertise in their communities and who have been trained as credible messengers and as people who can de-escalate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: They are trained to identify when there is a challenge that can be significant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: They are working in jurisdictions where we have selected them because they have high rates of gun violence, and we are working, therefore, at the deep end of that need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so we both collect information from the providers directly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We also conduct site visits to make sure we are getting an independent review of what is also happening.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But are we relying on the organizations receiving taxpayer funding to report their own accomplishments?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Well, you know, just like any program that we operate, we do rely on our provider to report what they are doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: However, we ourselves conduct site visits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We also have a technical assistance partner who conducts training and otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we have other kinds of information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We also talk to our partners who are working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: with our crisis management system partners and get feedback.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we make sure that we are hearing from a variety of people around what our contractor providers are doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And Councilmember, to the Commissioner's point, we do frequent site visits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: We also have frequent touch points in various ways with our providers on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: They are trained in conflict mediations and de-escalation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And these are folks who obviously understand the dynamics in their communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And when we talk about de-escalations and conflict mediations, there's a very specific definition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And these are either incidents that could become a little bit more serious and might lead to community violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And so when that happens, our folks are able to track every single conflict mediation or de-escalation between either individuals or groups, and then they report that back to us.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: May I continue briefly, Chair?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is there an independent auditing mechanism to verify these numbers, or are we essentially accepting what the contractors tell us?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Well, I think the site visits is one way where we do independent auditing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The other thing that we also do is we have over at various points in time, and we will start to do this again as we have conducted third-party evaluations of our work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: as well because that's also a way that we ensure that the work that we are doing is effective.

chapters.summary: Morano reads the fiscal impact statement for Intro 403, which says the cost is $0, and asks how that squares with expanding programs. Delaney-Brumsey says she is not familiar with that statement and does not anticipate expansion would cost no dollars.
chapters.title: Morano questions fiscal impact of Intro 403

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioner, I read the fiscal impact statement for Intro 403.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It says the cost of establishing a Department of Community Safety is $0.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yet the legislation calls for offices in every borough operating 24 hours a day, seven days a week, with personnel conducting field operations.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Meanwhile, your testimony references additional investments of $14.8 million in neighborhood safety programs, $15.7 million in domestic violence services, and $26 million in hate crime prevention.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How can we tell taxpayers that creating this department costs nothing when we're simultaneously talking about expanding these programs and potentially adding a whole new level of administration?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I'll have to check on that fiscal impact statement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We certainly would not anticipate that expansion of initiatives would cost no dollars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We're really supportive of Intro 403 and the intention to create a Department of Community Safety that is independent and have already spoken with Council Member Ressler about working closely with any potential

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: amendments.

chapters.summary: Morano asks how many Be Heard patients required another emergency response within 24 hours, seven days, or 30 days. Delaney-Brumsey says that is not a metric she has data on, and says she would think about publicly reporting such outcomes going forward.
chapters.title: Morano asks about Be Heard repeat emergency calls and outcome reporting

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: One final question, and I appreciate the chair's patience.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony cites the Be Heard program, which you, again, just referenced, which responded to 8,524 calls last fiscal year.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: year, you report that 42% of individuals served received care in the community instead of being transported to a hospital.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I think that raises an important question, which is how many of those people required another emergency response within 24 hours, seven days, or 30 days?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Because avoiding a hospital trip isn't necessarily a success if the person ends up in another crisis the next day.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Are we tracking repeat emergency calls, subsequent violent incidents, or whether people actually receive ongoing treatment?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The ability to support someone in their home in that moment, I would characterize as a success.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We want to make sure that if someone is in a crisis and we are able to support them right then and there and help them connect to services and stay at home, that's a success.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: When necessary, we take someone to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: One of the things that we are doing as part of the build of the Office of Community Safety and ongoing support, but now even more robust support that OCMH is providing that program,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: is building out our capacity to look at data across agencies and answer some of the longer-term questions that we have not been able to answer to date.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But do we know how many are repeat calls?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That is not a...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Metric that I have data on.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But going forward, would you support publicly reporting those outcomes rather than simply reporting how many calls the program answers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I think that's a really interesting and important question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I would love to think about that and connect with you about that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Chair Feliz asks whether OCS knows how many individuals were served versus repeat calls, and whether services are sufficient. Delaney-Brumsey says she does not have disaggregated numbers but H&H tracks frequent contacts and tries to provide additional support.
chapters.title: Feliz asks about repeat clients and root causes of crisis calls

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Murano.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: A quick point.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So as we know, we are in a well-documented public health crisis and mental health crisis.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We see it in our subways.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We see it in our streets.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We see it in our homes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And the big question is, what are steps that we have to take to truly but truly resolve the issue?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Are we simply not reaching enough people, or is it that we're reaching people, but after we reach them, we connect them, but then things fall through the cracks, given that the services that we have are not enough to resolve that?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So I'm wondering, and I don't know if this is a very similar question that Councilmember Murano asked, but you mentioned that you responded to about 8,500 calls.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Do we know how many individuals were served?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Or were reached through those 8,500 calls that you responded to?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'm just wondering the repeat client number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I don't have that number disaggregated by individual clients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: However, what we do is New York City Health and Hospitals does have a part of their work where they look at people who we have seen

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: more frequently and connects internal to that team because that is the health side of the team and we want to make sure that we're protecting patients'health information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And they see, is there something that we can provide to that person outside of the space of a 911 call to reduce the likelihood that they call back?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we are attuned to the fact that some people, we are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: are having repeat contact with, and we are focusing on those folks and providing additional support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I just don't off the top have that specific number of like the individual patient contact versus the overall number, but that is a really, that is something we are both attuned to and working on.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Yeah, and that's a very important piece of data just so that we could really think about what is the root of the problem.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Is it that we're not reaching people?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I mean, obviously, we could always expand those programs, but whether after we reach them, the things that we connect them to are not enough, and therefore, we're back to square one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And I will say that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Be Heard is an important initiative, an important part of New York City's behavioral health and mental health system, but it's not the only piece of work that needs to happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: In order to build out a comprehensive crisis system, I utilize the SAMHSA framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: You need someone somewhere to call, someone to come to you, and somewhere to go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so, for example, we have 988 in the city, which is an amazing resource.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: It operates 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: It's available by phone, by text, by chat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Some of the work that the Office of Community Mental Health is doing right now with DOHMH is trying to ensure that more and more New Yorkers know about 98.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Because it exists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: It's a three-digit number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: It's 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: There are trained counselors that staff that center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We want to make sure that more people are actually utilizing that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's just one gap in the system that we are also working in close partnership to address.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: But what your question speaks to is,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: the ways in which we want to shore up our entire system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So complete agreement around that.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So next is going to be Councilmember Wong and then Wilson and then Ressler.

chapters.summary: Council Member Phil Wong notes the five offices existed for years and asks why OCS is needed. Delaney-Brumsey says combining them allows a comprehensive approach because people experience violence and harm in interconnected ways. Wong then asks about budget transfers and extra management layers.
chapters.title: Phil Wong questions why OCS needed if offices already existed

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I have read, actually read the committee report regarding the five officers.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: This is victim services, neighborhood safety, and prevention of gun violence, offers to end domestic and gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Office of the Prevention of Hate Crimes and Office of Community Mental Health.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: They've all been existed for a while.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So like you mentioned, the Office to End Domestic and Gender-Based Violence has been around for a decade, two decades, 25 years.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So what I'm...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You mentioned Be Heard many, many times, but it is my understanding that health and hospitals and FDNY retains operation control of Be Heard.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Be Heard is operated as a partnership between FDNY and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: health and hospitals, they staff it, they are deployed together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: However, OCMH manages, OCS manages programmatic control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we convene the agencies on a weekly and more than weekly basis to ensure that the program is operating effectively.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We also engage our other partners, whether it's NYPD, OT,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: who are involved in the 911 system to make sure that this initiative functions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: When you have a cross-agency initiative like this, it's important to have a single point of responsibility for that work, and that is our team.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I'm just confused.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: They already existed.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: These offices that I mentioned already existed, and so was FDNY and health hospitals, and the services they offer existed before your office.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So why can't the existing agencies continue delivering these services?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Why do we need OCS?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The existing agencies are continuing to deliver these services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The goal of combining all of them within OCS was that so we can have a more comprehensive approach to violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Because, and this I mentioned in my testimony, what we know is that people don't experience violence and harm in silos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: People who have experienced domestic violence have significant behavioral health needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Neighborhoods with higher rates of gun violence also have higher rates of domestic violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Combining these offices together allows us to have the resources and the expertise across all of these offices supporting New Yorkers as one.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Your budget of $270 million, there's funding that's transferred from these existing programs.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We're not adding, this budget is not adding in addition to these offices.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So I don't see how you're enhancing these offices.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You're taking funding away from them.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But what, I mean, explain, can you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Because then they have less budget to work with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: No, all of the offices have their budget to work with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The staff within the offices exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: They are doing the work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Their programs and contracts exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: This administration invested an additional $67 million in the offices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are now just under one home and one roof.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so these teams are continuing to do the work with the resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Our goal as an administration, my commitment as a commissioner, is to ensure that we are continuing to ensure that we have the resource available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we are not taking away from these offices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We have only added to the offices.

chapters.summary: Wong asks if $260 million was taken from existing offices and if OCS is just an extra layer of management. Delaney-Brumsey says the offices still have their funding and OCS has added $67 million, and rejects the comparison to Thrive NYC.
chapters.title: Wong continues on budget transfers and extra layer of management

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, but isn't it true that the $260 million was taken away from the existing funding from these five offices?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The offices, it hasn't taken away because those offices still have their funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: They are just now part of OCS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So that funding, the $157 million of ONS funding is ONS's money and supports their programs, and it's now just part of OCS.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Again, it seemed to me that you're asking for, we're paying for another layer of management to get existing officers to do their jobs.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I don't see that as any beneficial to what we already have.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So unless you can convince me otherwise, you know, this is, I see it as an extra layer of red tape.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You know, it's like this reminds me of Thrive NYC from a couple of years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I appreciate that concern.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I'd like to actually turn it to some of my team members to talk about how they have worked across the office to support some of the work that they're doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I might start with the Office for Prevention of Hate Crimes, which you heard was quite small and is now working very closely with some of the offices to enhance the work that they are doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner, and thank you for your concern, but I'll say that now that we are part of this larger network of providers and people, we are able to do wraparound services when it comes to hate crimes and occurrences of biases in communities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Additionally, being in office with three staff, now we have an additional 97 staff members, I would say, to collectively help us to do our work as well and to reach New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Previously, we wasn't able to do so.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I've saved my next set of questions for round two.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Feliz asks briefly about the different ways to get a Be Heard response. Grant says the primary way is through 911, but police on the ground can request Be Heard, and 988 counselors can escalate calls to 911.
chapters.title: Feliz asks about ways to get a Be Heard response

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So next is Councilmember Wilson, but briefly, what are the different ways that we can get a be heard response?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Obviously, the most obvious one is calling 911.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'm wondering if the NYPD, for example, relates different...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Data and incidents and other different agencies as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Yeah, the primary, as you mentioned, the primary way to get a be heard response is through 911.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: However, if police on the ground respond to an incident that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: they find to be a mental health related incident and they think be heard would be beneficial, they do have a mechanism to be able to request be heard from the ground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: There are some calls that might come into

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: 988 for instance and if the call if the 988 crisis counselor determines that a 911 response is needed

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: the 988 counselors know how to escalate a call to the 911 system and then those calls could potentially also get a be heard response thank you uh next council member wilson and then russell

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Council Member Carl Wilson asks how Be Heard coordinates with contracted outreach teams and nonprofits to avoid duplication. Delaney-Brumsey says Be Heard is built into the public hospital system, allowing providers to see if patients are connected to other services.
chapters.title: Carl Wilson asks about Be Heard coordination with outreach teams

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I also have a couple questions about Be Heard.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: The city has a lot, spends a lot of money on contracted outreach teams.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: that aren't necessarily contracted for serious mental health episodes, but oftentimes that does overlap.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And there's also nonprofits and CBOs that also do this kind of outreach work.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: How does Be Heard coordinate with those folks so that...

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: You know, if one of them has a personal relationship to people, that we're not duplicating work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So one of the really strong aspects of the way the program is operating and designed is that it is built into our public hospital system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So because it's co-managed by New York City Health and Hospitals and FDNY, it means that our health and hospital providers are able to, for example, if someone's already a health and hospital patient, look in their charts, see if they have other providers that they're in contact with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: They are also able to connect with our DOHMH colleagues to see if someone has already been, say, part of an ACT team or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So the social workers in that program are highly trained to ensure that they are gathering information about the kinds of resources and programs that people are already connected to and making sure to reconnect them.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: What about like...

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: DSS, like are you coordinating with like Breaking Ground and Urban Pathways and all these groups that are out there doing that work?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And we coordinate with those organizations in a variety of ways, both in terms of ensuring that as we're building out programs or policies, we're in the room with them to make sure that we are talking about what we're seeing, what they're seeing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I can also turn to Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Grant to talk about some of the interagency work that she manages across that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Because we are acutely aware that we are part of a system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are not the system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We must make sure that we are coordinating with our partners, and we're doing that frequently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And as it relates to Be Heard, one of the referral options that Be Heard teams make is very often to the Joint Command Center that's operated by DHS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: So if they do encounter someone who needs housing support, they facilitate that connection directly with the JCCs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Outside of Be Heard, as you know, our office does a lot of work with the other social service agencies, such as the health department, H&H, DHS, around quality of life concerns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: in specific neighborhoods, especially those neighborhoods that have, you know, a high presence of people who appear to need behavioral health support or housing support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And so we will continue to do that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: We'll continue to grow that work under OCS.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks what happens when a person in crisis refuses service. Grant explains that if someone meets the threshold for involuntary transport, the social worker arranges it with a warm handoff to the hospital; otherwise the team offers referrals and a palm card.
chapters.title: Wilson asks about refusal of service and involuntary removal

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: If Be Heard responds and the person that's experiencing the crisis refuses service or is not

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: well enough to understand that they are in need of service,

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: How do you deal with that?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And what is...

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: What's the next step in that engagement?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And what happens to that person who refuses service?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: It depends.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: If it rises to the level of, you know, an involuntary transport to the hospital,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: then the Be Her team, there's a social worker there to make that assessment and that determination that a person actually does need to go to the hospital imminently for

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: an additional psychiatric evaluation and will make arrangements for that to happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: They'll also call ahead to the hospital to do a warm handoff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: So it's particularly if it is an H&H hospital so that the hospital knows that this individual just met with the Be Her team and the Be Her team is recommending additional evaluation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And so we try to ensure that that process happens as smoothly and the best way for the patient as possible.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Do you have data on how many Be Her responses have resulted in an involuntary removal?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: We can get that data, but I do know that it does not happen frequently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: The social workers are so skilled at being able to de-escalate and support individuals during a mental health crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And so the need for an involuntary transport is quite minimal.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: If someone doesn't meet the threshold for involuntary removal,

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: and refuses service, is there like a caseload that they get added to?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Is there a follow-up with that person after this particular engagement has concluded?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: The Be Her team will attempt to give that individual a referral to ongoing care, to an additional service if they do not wish to be served by a Be Her team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Every person that a Be Her team comes in contact with gets a little palm card with information about available services in their community and also an attempt from the team to make a referral to services.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks if OCS sees a link between mental health crisis and housing crisis and what it is doing. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS recognizes the overlap and works with DSS on supportive housing, rapid rehousing, and services for survivors of gender-based violence.
chapters.title: Wilson asks about link between mental health and housing crisis

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I have one more question, Chair, if I may.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And you touched on this a second ago with your response, but I happen to believe that there is a pretty direct link between

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
