utterances.text: mental health crisis and our housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And I am wondering if OCS shares that view, and if so, what are some of the tools or data sharing or advocacy that you're doing

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: to help build more supportive and affordable housing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We recognize that there is a significant overlap between people with mental health needs and people who are experiencing homelessness or who are unstably housed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That is absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That is something that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: we understand and that we support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we work closely with DSS and our partners across the city to identify ways in which we can be supportive of the efforts that the city is making, whether that means,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: as we do, sitting on the committees where the city is thinking through how to expand access to the housing, whether that means

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: funding services like our rapid rehousing work, whether that means ensuring that we are supporting providers who are also connecting people with behavioral health services with housing, we know that this is

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: absolutely an intersect that we can and should address.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: Yeah, and I would just add that being a part of OCS, having all of these different offices under this one umbrella also means that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: not only are we thinking about it from a mental health perspective, we're thinking about it in terms of how does housing help to prevent violence?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: How does housing help to make ensuring that, you know, supportive housing options support people who may be victims of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lakeisha Grant
utterances.text: And so this just gives another opportunity to elevate more of those voices and concerns as we think about housing for people who have mental health needs.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And then just a comment and I'm done.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: When you're contemplating the expansion, we would really like it in lower Manhattan, midtown and lower Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Manhattan, I think one of the biggest calls I get to my office are people concerned about folks that appear to be experiencing mental health crises or appear to be unhoused, very resistant to services.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And we, you know, around big transit hubs like the Port Authority bus terminal and Penn Station, where we see a lot of this.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Please come down to Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, no, we appreciate that that is, you know, Lower Manhattan is an area that we have also received very similar.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So thank you for that ask, and we look forward to working with you.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, Councilmember Althea Stevens.

chapters.summary: Council Member Althea Stevens discusses a recent shooting of a student in her district and asks how OCS coordinates prevention, education, and support for young people. LaRochelle says ONS is working with NYC Public Schools and will deploy CMS teams around schools.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about coordination for youth safety and school safety after shooting

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I will try, well, I don't know if I'll be brief, but if we could just, I have a lot of questions, so if you could be succinct as possible.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I want to just start with, I know Councilmember Riley spoke about Jarvis, who was on his way to school, and he's a young person from my district and in a school that's in my district.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This is actually the second shooting involved.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Your microphone, sorry, your microphone might be off.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: No, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Oh, it's very far.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Can't hear?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Is it better?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I've never been accused of being not loud, so that's the first.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So this is the second shooting, and, you know, this is a school that's outside of a catchment area, which is one of the things that I've been yelling about, like the catchment areas of, like, what does that really look like in the expansion?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But just also just thinking about how's the office ensuring that coordination to across prevention, education, interventions, and support for young people and communities.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Is a house being done within the school communities as well?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, what does that look like?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I know we have some, like, safe pastures programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: There are some programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But, again, like, in a tragedy where a young person is gunned down and there was a shooting outside the school, and then they're telling me that they're, you know, they did get positive money and now they're not on a list.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And, like, what does that look like other than, like, the interventions being poured in for one day?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What is the long-term solutions for these people?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, no, I mean, there's just had so many tragic incidents in the last few days, and I just really want to send condolences to the families and friends of everyone who's been affected because it has been a really, these have been really awful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And our team has been on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Obviously, we want to respect the privacy of the people affected, so we won't talk about the literal specifics, but we can talk about the ways in which we support young people and their families and the aftermath of incidents like this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We work very closely with schools as well as with other agency partners to do the work of responding in the moment, but also the long-term work of supporting people in the aftermath of these kinds of incidents, whether that means,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: well, I'll turn to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Yeah, no, thank you so much, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Hi, how you doing?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Haven't seen you in a while.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Hi, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: So I was just on a call with New York City Public Schools yesterday, last night actually, to figure out how we can extend resources to the young man and his family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And we're looking at...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: various things that might be cost neutral.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Like you mentioned, even if we're not in that school, this is information that we're receiving from New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And so what we're going to be doing in the days and weeks ahead is to be working very closely with our sites in the Bronx on the ground, and not only in the Bronx, but the other five boroughs, to figure out, okay, operationally,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Where do we need to be canvassing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Who do we need to be engaging?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Even if this is not a yes school, a youth enrichment services school, you know, how do we engage with these young people?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Making sure that, you know, when young people are going to school in the mornings and, you know, they're let go in the afternoons, that CMS and our folks on the ground have a presence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: So this is something that we're working very closely with New York City Public Schools right now to accomplish.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks if there is already a plan in place for school safety programs and how many schools participate. LaRochelle says the YES program is in 50 schools, chosen based on level four and five cases involving suspensions and weapons.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about plans for schools and YES program

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And is there already a plan that's in place that already exists, or is this something that you guys are still in the process of developing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Yeah, so the plan in place and the interventions that we have right now are yes, which is funded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: But that other plan.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How many schools is that in?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How many schools is that in?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's in 50 schools?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Could you send, you probably don't have it now, but if you can send over a list to the committee so that we can look at the schools.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And how are those schools picked?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: They're picked through New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: They provide us a list of level four and level five cases that are cases that involve suspensions, young people who might

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: bring weapons to school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And whatnot, and we go ahead and operationalize from there.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Interesting.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I have some thoughts, so I'll call you because I have more questions.

chapters.summary: Stevens raises concerns about juvenile justice programming and coordination between agencies like DYCD, ACS, and OCS. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS participates in the Youth Justice Task Force and works closely with DYCD and ACS.
chapters.title: Stevens questions juvenile justice programming and coordination

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The next question I have is I've been a one-woman band around juvenile justice, and I have been raising the alarm because one of the things, especially with talking to the judges and folks, is just around programming.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I know that you guys have a set of programming.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You guys do program in these CMS groups and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I'm trying to get a better understanding of, like, why we're not using some of these programs for these young people and how is that connection happening.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I know there's an expansion with, like, ADT and ADI programs, but I know that you guys have specific programs that have funding attached to it with stipends and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And my big concern is that no one is talking to anyone, and we have all these programs, and they're working in silos.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So DYCD has a set of programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I know you guys used to be under DYCD.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So the...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Things used to be a little bit more coherent around programming and integrating into them.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I'm trying to understand what is the connection and through line of these programs and young people having access.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because, again, I've been meeting with judges and they're like, there's no programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I'm like, what are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: There are programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, we have certainly, and I'll, of course, turn to Cliff to describe more, but we absolutely do have programs that work with youth who are in the juvenile system, both youth who are in detention as well as youth.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: No, I know you guys have programs, but what I am saying is how is this all being connected?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because when I am talking to judges, they're saying that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: There's no programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I know, and I know for a fact, because I've been doing this for 20 years, and I'm here, and I see all of these things, which is why I have ACS and DYCD.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How are these things being connected, and how are people knowing to refer people to these programs?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And, like, I'm trying to understand how are you guys all working together, because, again, it seems very disconjoint.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I know DYCD has programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You guys have programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: ACS has programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Everybody got programs, but every time I turn around, everybody's like, there's no programs for these kids.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I think one of the challenges of working in a place like New York City is that it is so large and that it is really hard to know everything that is going on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: But one of the goals that we have is to make sure that we are in very close coordination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So, for example, we're at Office of Neighborhood Safety as well as the rest of the Office of Community Safety as part of the Youth Justice Task Force that is being run right now to ensure that this administration is making improvements to the youth justice system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And we are in very close contact with our partners at DYCD and ACS and otherwise as we continue to...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That's a good show because I have another question.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The issue isn't you guys talking, everyone else needs to know and so that's the issue.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You guys having a meeting and I'm a part of the justice working group, don't get me started, but if people who are supposed to refer the kids are not knowing about these programs, nobody cares.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so I need us to figure out a way, I mean I have legislation around it, but this is a real problem when I am in these spaces and judges are saying these kids are being detained because there's no programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so if you have not heard that, I don't know how people are not hearing that because I'm hearing that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That is something we need to work on.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: as a city because that is really important.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so I just have another question.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks about the hotline bill and how caller information would be protected from NYPD. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS supports the intent but suggests leveraging existing resources like 988 and the NYC Hope Hotline.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about hotline bill and data privacy for callers

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: One of the, my last question, I'm so sorry, Chair, and I will be done, is just around, you guys had mentioned that you were in support of Councilmember Riley's hotline bill, the hotline bill.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Do you have a plan on how you'll be protecting Carlos'information on the hotline from like NYPD and things like that?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And is there a plan in place that you guys are thinking about to make sure the information that's being shared on this hotline is protected?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we are in support of the intent of the hotline bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are suggesting that there are resources already within New York City, like 988 and the New York City Hope hotline, that could be utilized more effectively and more quickly and more efficiently to meet the goals of the bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And we would really welcome conversations with the council member to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And to your point about making sure that the judges and others are aware, we would really welcome, you know, working with you and working with others to make sure we are getting the word out because we want to make sure that when there are gaps in people understanding what exists, that we are filling those gaps.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Trust me, I've been yelling about it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I will continue to yell about it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I've also been promoting these programs because I'm telling you, people are pretending like they don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so I know for a fact because I know the work, but there are a lot of people who do not know that you guys have these programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And as you're seeing gaps, I know the team is aware of those.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: I know we would love to just continue working on it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That is part of the work is making sure that the people who make decisions are aware and utilize these programs.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, Councilmember Ressler.

chapters.summary: Council Member Lincoln Restler thanks the chairs and asks about Be Heard staffing and goals. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS convenes agencies weekly, ran the first training in over a year, and is building a data sharing agreement to expand the program.
chapters.title: Restler asks about Be Heard staffing and expansion goals

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Felice.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I really just want to thank you again for your flexibility in accommodating this bill in the hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really appreciate it and the opportunity for Interpora 3 to be heard.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And Commissioner, I just have to say I think that you're–

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Testimony today has been clear and compelling.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You've demonstrated a really impressive command of the range of issues that OCS confronts, and I think it's been really helpful for the council to hear the benefits of consolidating these offices

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: and the opportunities that the new investment that the Mondani administration is making and how that can help us address the surge in hate crimes that we're experiencing and other challenges.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'd love to just touch on a few general areas.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Maybe I'll start with Be Heard just because it's gotten so much attention today, and I know this is something that, an area where you have a lot of expertise.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And the mayor has rightly said that Be Heard is a top priority.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The MMR, you know, as you've noted today, I think, and the deputy executive director noted, there were just 8,500 calls that were responded to on Be Heard last year.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's down, I think, 40-odd percent from two years ago.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I was disturbed by the police and fire departments kind of competing in somewhat inconsistent testimony at our budget hearings earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it felt to me it was indicative of a program that had been orphaned.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I was hoping you could elaborate further on kind of how you're, as you're looking to ramp Be Heard back up,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: are there new goals in terms of people that we're hoping to serve and calls that we're kind of hoping to divert from the NYPD that...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: EMTs and social workers can respond to, you know, recognizing that we have a major staffing crisis with EMTs that I'm sure is making that challenging.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, we'd love to kind of understand as you look ahead, kind of the universe of people that we're hoping to serve with this program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We, you know, as you noted, there was a decrease, you know, the calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We're proud of every single call that we respond to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We think that's important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: But we also know we're not responding to as many calls as we need or want to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that is really the goal, to make sure we are increasing day every day, week every week, so that we are responding to more and more calls and that we are doing that effectively.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So one of the things that had been a challenge and that we've addressed with the agencies is ensuring that we have a clear point of leadership within the city across this program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Because any program that's managed by two different agencies, there still needs to be a clear point of leadership, and that point of leadership is OCS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so we are able and do convene the agencies on at minimum a weekly basis, but quite frankly, nearly a daily basis in the moment to make sure that we are expanding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That means identifying locations from which we can send our teams out of as we are going across.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The city, that means increasing staffing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: As you heard, we ran the first training that we had run in over a year for staff, so to fill staffing gaps and to ensure we have enough staffing to do this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are currently right now building out our data sharing agreement so that we can see with more specificity what the calls are, how we're responding to those.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: All of that work is happening right now and is going quickly, and we will continue to build on this program, making it more and more coherent, making it more and more effective over time.

chapters.summary: Restler notes the troubling increase in youth detention and asks what OCS is prioritizing to address gun violence affecting teens. Delaney-Brumsey cites the Youth Justice Task Force, CMS providers in detention centers, and summer youth employment.
chapters.title: Restler asks about youth detention and violence prevention initiatives

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I wish Councilmember Stevens was still here for this, but we've seen this deeply troubling increase during the Adams administration of youth in detention.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Well over twice as many kids are incarcerated today as at the beginning of Eric Adams'term.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And just wondering,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: What kind of initiatives you all are prioritizing now to address the rise in gun violence that is impacting our teens

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: and helping us to drive down the population that we're experiencing in Horizons and Crossroads?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So I will turn to my colleague for more details, but not only are we sitting on the Youth Justice Task Force, which is focused on improving how the justice system works, including the real crisis

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: in the detention centers and making sure that we are bringing to bear any resources we can to support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We also have our CMS providers in the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: attention centers to address and support violence because we know that for the youth who are there that is essential and we all have work where we are also providing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: support to young people who have been justice involved including summer youth employment because we know that employment is one of the key

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: preventative factors for being engaged in the justice system and what would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Yeah, no, thank you so much, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And so we work very, very closely still with the YCD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And so we work very closely to be activating public spaces like our cornerstones and beacons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: We have employment programs to the Commissioner's point, AGVP, which is our anti-gun violence employment program, as well as SYEP, summer youth employment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Working very, very closely to add additional slots there to extend to young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: You'll find us, again, in New York City public schools, as I mentioned earlier, as well as our ACS facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: And our Mayor's Action Plan for Neighborhood Safety also has a youth leadership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifford LaRochelle
utterances.text: Component where we are engaging young people again just to extend resources make referrals to them and make sure that we're invariably reducing their risk of being involved in community violence

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm gonna try to just I want to try and get through a few more topics if I can I appreciate those responses

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: and hope this is an area, I'll just say, hope this is an area where OCS, in partnership with other agencies, can really rebuild the landscape of programs that were obliterated during the Adams administration that are serving

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: this young adult population and are effective preventative tools that we really need.

chapters.summary: Restler asks about short-term goals and metrics for success. Delaney-Brumsey says programs include metrics on people served, support provided, and satisfaction, and OCS is building capacity to measure reductions in violence and increased access to care.
chapters.title: Restler asks about metrics and success for OCS

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think the Department of Probation in particular needs a lot of help.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Metrics and success.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: As you're thinking about kind of measuring the success of this office,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Are there short-term goals and targets that you might want to highlight or data points or metrics that you're prioritizing for success kind of for this fiscal year that you might want to highlight for us?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: All of our programs include, or I would say that our programs include a set of programmatic metrics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So usually when I think about those, what I talk about is like the number of people we're serving, what kind of support we're able to provide, what their satisfaction is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: All of those are essential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: But also as we're building that out, we are also continuing to build out our ability to look and say at things like for neighborhoods where we are operating, what are, are we seeing reductions in violence?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Are we seeing increasing access to care among the people we're serving?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So that's the kind of metrics and building out that we will continue to do.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: Restler asks about the internal work to set up OCS for success. Delaney-Brumsey describes building out administration, HR, payroll, and contracting, and notes OCS has launched an interagency task force to plan the transition to a department.
chapters.title: Restler asks about internal work to set up office for success

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I thought this section in the MMR this year was helpful, and hopefully that's something where more metrics can be added and elaborated on.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I fully appreciate that setting up a new office in government is far from easy.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's, I would probably say, often painful, especially when contracting is involved.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you share with the council today a little bit more about what you've undertaken to make sure that the office is kind of set?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: structure to be successful and just elaborate a little bit on kind of that internal work that might not be super sexy but is really important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: No, thank you so much because people, you know, often don't ask about the behind the scenes work of ensuring that this office functions and then is ready to be a department and that is, I say, equally as essential as the programming that we do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: So right now we are a mayoral office so our staff lines as well as our contracts are embedded within other agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The back end, things like administration, HR, payroll, contracting is all managed by other entities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: The process of building that out, the process of going from office to an agency has happened in New York City before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We're thinking about NISIM if you're thinking about the Department of Veteran Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: That often takes years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And our goal as we're doing this is to ensure that when we're making that transition, we're doing so in a way that allows us to make sure there are no gaps in our ability to pay the people who are contracted providers, to pay our own staff, that we continue to be able to manage the data that we have in a way that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: is in line with all data protection and security protocols.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And to do that, we have already launched the work with an interagency task force to help us plan out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that task force includes not only the agencies here, but the agencies that serve as our back end, so DSS for NGBV, DYCD for ONS, and so forth, but it also includes the agencies across the city that manage some of the operational functions of the city, like

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: DCAS, Mayor's Office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: of contracts, OTI, others, to help us make sure that we have the staffing, the infrastructure, and the technology resources necessary to do that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: And we are already doing it because we know that it will take time, but we want to do it as quickly and as effectively as possible.

chapters.summary: Restler asks about the long-term vision for OCS as a direct service provider and coordinator. Delaney-Brumsey says the agency will need to do all of that and describes how OCS can address gaps for people cycling through Rikers, hospitals, and shelters.
chapters.title: Restler asks about long-term vision and gaps in service

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's great.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: As you look ahead a little bit more to a longer-term vision, I know you mentioned that you're undertaking a strategic planning process.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Interested in kind of how you see the agency.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I recognize you've got a variety of existing programs that are kind of under your umbrella, but how do you look at kind of the agency as a direct service provider?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: First and kind of providing its own standalone response for serving as a coordinating force between existing programs?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is it all of the above?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, we will need to do all of that in order to be an effective community safety department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We will need to be able to directly serve people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We will need to coordinate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey
utterances.text: We will need to be able to speak to policy and research, and that work exists, but we will need to make sure that we are doing that even more so.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I'm interested in just your assessment on kind of existing gaps that we see today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I will say I often encounter situations in my district where there are individuals who are struggling with mental illness on our streets, in our subways, and they don't appear to be getting the help they need.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I can say that's me being generous.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: not getting the help they need by the existing programs that the city offers.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I'm interested, you know, we often get inadequate responses from non-police agencies.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The police get called in, and their involvement doesn't address the problem or the challenge or the condition that somebody's facing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Folks often are cycling through Rikers, hospitals, shelters, one versus the other to the next.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I'm just interested in generally how you think the...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Department of Community Safety can help to address this particular challenge?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: That challenge of people who are cycling, the fact that when people are cycling, we're seeing them often in the street, not without, and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: we have not yet been able to connect with that person in a way where we have provided what they need, whether that is housing, whether that's support for serious mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: The thing that I am most, one of the things I'm most hopeful about is having this kind of combined expertise within the office and a charge to address those really thorny problems will help us move the needle on closing some of those gaps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: You can't, if we are able to really address gun violence and access to mental health services at the same time, we're closing a gap.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: If we're able to do so in a way that addresses victim services and domestic violence, we're closing a gap.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: So part of what we are going to be doing and continue to do is think about how do we get into those really sticky problems where people are falling through the gaps and either ourselves provide services or work with our community partners to do that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: And so one of the great things about having, well, I'll pause there because I know you have other questions.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yeah, no, look, I want to be mindful.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The chairs were gracious to give me some extra time.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I thought two things I just want to repeat that you said earlier that I thought were helpful.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Kind of your role.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In overseeing the operations day to day and making the work of the Office of Community Safety successful and the Deputy Mayor's role in kind of serving as a core

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: across city government to help bring in other partners and make sure that they're collaborating and supporting with that work as effectively as possible, I thought was really clear and beneficial to understand.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And the second thing that you talked about, like how each of these five offices provide victim services in one form or another, and how do we better integrate those efforts because

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: oftentimes as a victim of violence in one form or another, it might cut across multiple offices, and yet siloing these things out doesn't necessarily help the people who need it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so I think it just provided some really helpful color in why things are being structured the way that they are, and so appreciate your testimony today and very much look forward to working with you and your team on this effort.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Likewise, thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Feliz shares a story about a Brooklyn neighborhood transformed by a community-based safety hub and asks what it would take to headquarter OCS in a high-need community like the Bronx. Delaney-Brumsey agrees on the importance of community presence and LaRochelle lists Bronx assets.
chapters.title: Feliz advocates for OCS headquarters in affected community like Bronx

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you so much, Councilmember Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So a quick question and then we'll hear from Councilmember Banks and then we'll do a second round.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So as someone who represents the Bronx, I'm always talking about public safety.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I don't see how anybody who represents a neighborhood like the one that I represent where about 40% of the shootings and shooting incidents

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: in the city, happened in the Bronx, you know, very difficult to talk about anything else when that is such a big problem in the borough.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And not too long ago, I was visiting Brooklyn, and I was speaking with a Brooklyn elected official.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We were talking about the history of the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They basically said that back in the 90s, that specific neighborhood,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: would get crushed by issues related to violence, including gun violence.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They created new programs and they were able to bring

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: A new building with basically everything related to issues related to violence, including a building with a one-stop shop, services for victims, counselors, programs for children, teen dating violence, hate crimes, and so much more.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And one thing that they said was that that, by having it directly in the community that was disproportionately affected, that basically completely transformed that community permanently, basically, practically, you know, crime is almost non-existent.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: It also brought jobs to families that needed them the most.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Obviously, we know the correlation between high unemployment rates and lack of opportunity and crime and violence and mental health issues.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I think this says a lot about the difference that we can make when we have programs like the ones that we're talking about today directly embedded in the communities that need them.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So I'm just wondering what would it take to have an office like the Office of Community Safety headquartered out of a neighborhood like the ones that need it the most, such as a disadvantaged community in Brooklyn or the Bronx and et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I mean, you know, obviously, as we know, the real work gets done in the communities facing these issues.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So I'm just wondering what would that take?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, you could not have said it better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: The work gets done when you are in the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: So we absolutely are in agreement that in order to do this work, we have to work in the communities with the highest needs, that we have to work closely with partners that are already embedded in that community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: And as we grow, we will look at where we need to be positioned within the community, whether that's physically or otherwise in terms of being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: supporting community-based partners that are already doing that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: So completely agree on the statement.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, sounds good.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll definitely be interested in having conversations about how we could support the partners already there.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But also, given that this office is going to be working on these issues, you know, having the office in the community is disproportionately affected by these issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We love City Hall and the region, but, you know, we're talking about safety.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Have them have these services directly in the communities affected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: And I would say, you know, we've started, or not just started, we've for a long time and continue to fund services in the Bronx because we know that the Bronx is a place with significant rates of violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: And so our team is doing work all the time in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: My guess is that there are several team members currently right now in the Bronx doing work with our providers on any given day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: That is the case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: And I can certainly turn to Executive Director LaVoschel to talk about some of the resources we already have in the Bronx that we would be building on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: Yeah, Chair Felisa.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: So I just want to, you know, at a glance, let you know exactly what type of assets we have in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: First of all, we serve 11 cashman areas across eight precincts, and our crisis management system investment is roughly $22 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: And that includes street outreach work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: That includes work directly with our hospital-based violence intervention programs, ACS, our mobile trauma units.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: And we even have investments through our mayor's action plan for neighborhood safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: So look at.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: Patterson, for instance, with that unfortunate incident that happened a few days ago, we were fully mobilized there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: So I just want you to rest assured knowing that we do have assets in the Bronx, and obviously there are ways for us to hopefully increase our presence and footprint there, but we are working very closely with our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: Base partners and civilians in the Bronx to make sure that we're lowering rates of community violence.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But I guess the overall point is, and yes, we absolutely appreciate the expansion of the programs in the Bronx, but I guess the overall point is, if this is where most of the issues are at, why not be headquartered out of there?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, we definitely appreciate the point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, Councilmember Banks, and then we'll go for a second round.

chapters.summary: Council Member Chris Banks asks when CMS contracts will transfer from DYCD to OCS. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS has programmatic control and is building a contracting team to manage the transfer without funding gaps.
chapters.title: Banks asks about CMS contract transfer from DYCD to OCS

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When it comes to the CMS contracts, when can we expect the transfer of responsibility from BYCD to OCS?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: So in terms of the CMS contracts, as well as all of the other contracts within ONS, we are...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: myself, Cliff, all of us are in programmatic control of those contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: In terms of literally moving the contracts, we are in the process right now of working really closely with DYCD, with others, to ensure that we can build out a contracting team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: So we need staff, we need equipment, we need all of our technology, all of that to make sure that we are actually able to manage the contracts and that we do so in a way that we are not, there's no gaps in our ability to provide funding because that's also

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: something that we want to be very careful about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: And so we are working right now to work towards that transfer, but in terms of programmatic operations, we are doing that, and then we are in very, very close contact with DYCD on a, I would say, probably daily basis around making sure that the contracts are continuing to move and operate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: So we are making sure that even in this kind of transitional space, we are managing that work.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how OCS will ensure CMS providers have adequate and reliable funding to retain workers. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS is working on a new RFP to modernize the work and continue investments, and LaRochelle notes providers now receive a 50% advance at the top of the fiscal year.
chapters.title: Banks asks about adequate funding for CMS providers

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How will OCS ensure that the CMS providers and other community-based violent prevention organizations have adequate and reliable funding to retain experienced workers,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: mediate conflicts, and prevent shootings and retaliation?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Well, one of the things that we are doing, of course, is making sure that we are continuing to ensure that the contract is managed and that as we're doing this transition, we are able to continue to fund our partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Another thing that is happening is that as the current contract is set to expire, we are working right now on releasing a new RFP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: The focus of that RFP will be to ensure that we are making continued investments in the CMS work, but also making adjustments to modernize the work, which has existed in New York City for a great deal of time and is really strong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: And we want to make sure that we are reflecting the changes that have happened in the system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: So, I mean, no surprise to you, but of course, when COVID happened, it changed a lot about how people operate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: And we want to make sure that we are also reflecting that in our new work and that that work is invested in the CMS providers and that they can do their work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: work effectively.

chapters.summary: Banks asks about delayed payments and contract funding gaps. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS works closely with DYCD to address issues and is building an effective contract shop to provide consistent, on-time funding.
chapters.title: Banks asks about delayed payments and contract funding gaps

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And when it comes to the delayed payments and the gaps in the contract funding, how are we addressing that?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Especially on the delayed payment side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, so we work really closely, and I'll let Cliff speak to this, we work really closely with DYC to identify when there are issues with delayed payments or any other issues in the contract to make sure we are addressing those.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: As we are building our OCS, one of the principles that we are building out our contract shop with is to be as effective as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: We know that making sure that we are providing consistent funding and on-time funding to our contracted providers is essential for us to do our work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: Yeah, no, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: And to the Commissioner's point, one thing that we're doing is working very closely to identify the organizations and providers that need additional assistance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: One thing that is happening, one thing that recently happened is that the providers are now receiving a 50% advance at the top of the fiscal year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: And again, that's directly related to their feedback to us around what they needed to be fully operational at the top of the year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: But we also understand and we want to be very equitable in making sure that we are applying resources to our providers who need them the most.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how OCS coordinates with DYCD and DOE to connect youth to employment, mentorship, and mental health services. LaRochelle says OCS works with DYCD on SYEP slots, runs an anti-gun violence employment program, and keeps public spaces like cornerstones open.
chapters.title: Banks asks about coordination with DYCD and DOE for youth services

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How will the OCS coordinate with DYCD, DOE?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: and other city agencies to connect young folks most impacted by violence to employment, mentorship, mental health services, and safe after-school space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: Yeah, so we're working very, very closely with DYCD to make sure that summer youth employment slots or SYEP slots are being allocated directly to our population of young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: We also, as I mentioned earlier, have our anti-gun violence, violence employment program that we're extending to folks as well, to young people particularly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: And we're working very closely to make sure that public spaces like cornerstones and beacons, satellite lights remain open and available to serve as secure and safe spaces for young people to congregate and to interface.

chapters.summary: Banks asks what outcomes OCS tracks to evaluate youth safety investments. LaRochelle says CMS partners track conflict mediations, de-escalations, and referrals, and OCS is working across offices to tell a comprehensive story and keep score.
chapters.title: Banks asks about outcomes tracked for youth safety

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And what outcomes will the OCS track to evaluate whether it's investments or improving

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: youth safety, including conflicts, mediated, retaliation prevention, and just...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What's being done to?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: Yeah, so right now we're tracking, our CMS partners track conflict mediations, de-escalations, referrals that are made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: We really want to be able to tell a comprehensive story about the work that's happening, and we want to effectively be able to keep score.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: So we're working very closely with the other offices within OCS right now to see how we can collaborate and coordinate a lot better.

chapters.summary: Banks asks about OCS's role in protecting youth from the criminal legal system. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS works to prevent violence and system contact, places CMS providers in detention facilities, and connects youth to jobs and other supports.
chapters.title: Banks asks about OCS role in protecting youth from criminal legal system

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And my last question.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We know this administration and the council have been vocal about the dehumanizing conditions at the youth detention centers.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And I think Althea touched on this a little earlier, the lack of citywide support for our children.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Can you please describe the role that you believe your office will play in protecting our youth from the criminal legal systems?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, I think there's a few different roles, and we share the concern, and we recognize the urgency of the issue, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: So thank you so much for raising that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: One thing that we do is by preventing violence and working with young people who are at risk is we're preventing them from coming into contact with the system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: And then in addition for young people who are in the system, our CMS providers, especially in the detention facilities, we have CMS providers in the detention facilities to address conflict and reduce violence there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: And then you also heard from Executive Director LaRochelle about all of the work that we do to connect young people to jobs, to other supports that reduce the likelihood that they cycle back in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: And we do focus on connecting with young people who have either had

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: contact with the juvenile system or young adults who've had contact with the criminal justice system and people who are at high risk so that we

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: We are doing our part to make sure that we are both being preventative and addressing the needs of people who have come into contact with the system.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner, for your responses and your team.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Banks.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Back to Chair Brewer.

chapters.summary: Co-Chair Brewer says there is a feeling that gender-based violence is not being covered, especially since the NGBV head is not on the leadership team. Delaney-Brumsey says Commissioner Sloane remains part of her leadership team and NGBV work is essential.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about gender-based violence and NGBV leadership

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Two quick things.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One is, again, back to the gender-based and the centers and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: There's a lot of interest.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I co-chaired the council's women's caucus.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I speak at a lot of women's events, and this comes up constantly.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I guess what I'm saying is I think as time goes on, if you could make it clear what you are doing in that domain.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because there's a feeling that it's not being covered.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Whether it is or isn't, that's how it feels.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And because the individual who was head of that is not part of your leadership team,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think you're doing a great job.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Everybody up here is saying, oh, she's really good.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But that issue is still hanging out there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, I will say Commissioner Simone is still part of my leadership team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: She testified with me at the last hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: She just happens not to be available today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: But the work of NGBV is so essential to the work of the office, and it is important for us to tell the story of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: So I appreciate that feedback.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: We will continue to work on that.

chapters.summary: Brewer raises mental illness and street homelessness as a top issue and asks for the city's response. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS is working closely with DSS on street outreach and behavioral health access and agrees it is an essential issue.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about mental illness, encampments, and Be Heard expansion

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, and then just secondly, the great, I mean, Council Member Ressler talked about it, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Across the board, the mental illness in our districts is huge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so I know you can only be heard in certain districts.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We'd all love to have B-Hurt.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I assume it'll hopefully something like it or it will move to other districts.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But again, it's sort of on you because the street homeless outreach can't handle them in many cases.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: People don't want to move.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I often say to them, because these are encampments or something like that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I got two-year, ten-year encampments.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's what we got.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're not going anywhere unless something miraculous happens, and DSS is trying.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But the issue would be try to come up as soon as possible with what the city's response is to this mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because it is, I think, the number one issue on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, I will say I'm working really closely with DSS, too, as they are doing the work of figuring out how to address

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: street outreach and homeless encampments, recognizing that our part is to support them to make sure that we are thinking about how do we support any work they're doing around expanding access to behavioral health care and helping to knit in a focus on community safety within that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: And we've been really excited to be able to work with that team to do that because we agree that is a really essential issue.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's hard.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're not.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Easy to, I always say to them, did you grow up in Central Park West?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What the hell's with you?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because they are so intractable.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so I don't know the answer, but I can say everybody's looking to you and DSS for help.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Phil Wong returns for a second round, asking how expansion will be financed given budget deficits and whether OCS saves police overtime hours. Delaney-Brumsey says OCS will work with OMB and City Hall and that the goal is to provide effective non-police responses. Wong also asks about administrative costs; answer is $2.9 million for OCS staff.
chapters.title: Phil Wong second round on funding expansion and administrative costs

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Co-chair, we're going to go back to Council Member Wong for a second round of questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cliff Rosenthal
utterances.text: Thank you, Chas.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My next round of questions regarding who's going to pay and what gets cut.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I read today's political playbook, which reports that this bill on creating this office does not specify the department's funding and that the city...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Faces budget deficits, big deficits heading into the next budget process.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So my question regarding to how any expansion would get financed, like what, here's my question, what pays for any expansion beyond the existing programs?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Are we going to get higher taxes or cuts to other services or savings you expect to achieve?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please answer that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, so this administration has made a commitment to the Office of Community Safety and to the expansion of the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: And as we do that expansion, we'll be working very closely with Office of Management and Budget and with City Hall to identify any necessary resources that would be needed to support that expansion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: To date, the administration has invested an additional $67 million in this work.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Now, I also, okay, granted.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I also heard from you that you work with NYPD, and are you actually saving police office hours by working with them?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Or, like, how many net police office hours have actually been saved after accounting for backup?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And repeat responses.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Can you talk about that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: I don't have data on exactly how many hours might be saved, but what I will say is that the work that we are doing is meant to build out a response that is effective for people with needs when what we know, both in New York City, you'll hear this also from

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: across the country, including law enforcement themselves, that we have been asking law enforcement to take on functions that they are not part of their purview, that they're not best positioned to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: So bringing in behavioral health providers, community violence interrupters, victims advocates to that work is essential for providing an effective response to the people in need.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, okay, do I have time for, yeah, one final question.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You mentioned the structure of the OCS, that you report the deputy mayor and supervising five existing offices, but what is the administrative cost that will be involved?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I'm talking about other than the programs and the frontline employees that already existed.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What is the annual cost of this additional management structure of the OCS?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Across, I may not be hearing your question correctly, but across OCS's budget, about 5% of OCS's budget goes to staffing.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But what about the management structure that you mentioned that you report to the deputy mayor and you have staff?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: So the deputy mayor is not on my budget.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: All the deputy mayors are part of City Hall.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: So deputy mayor of community safety, like the first deputy mayor, deputy mayor of health and human services, those are all City Hall staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: And I report to her as other commissioners report to their deputy mayors.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, no, but by creating the OSC, your new management structure, how much, is that 5% of your total budget or we're talking about something else?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: So the Office of Community Safety, the folks who were not part of the others, that's about $2.9 million out of the entire $271 million.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you, Jeff.

chapters.summary: Chair Feliz concludes the OCS panel, thanking the commissioner and team for their testimony. He notes there are about 60 people signed up to testify and announces the hearing will move to public testimony.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz concludes OCS panel and thanks witnesses

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Does anyone else have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Well, I have many more pages of questions, but I think we've covered enough for today.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We have about 60 people signed up to testify, which we obviously want to hear from.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So I think we are going to conclude this panel.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
