utterances.text: Thank you so much for being here.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you for all the work that you've been doing on these issues, and I look forward to continuing.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Wrestler, do you have a second round?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delaney Brumsey
utterances.text: We look forward to continued conversations.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, everyone.

chapters.summary: Chair Feliz opens the hearing for public testimony and reminds attendees that this is a government proceeding and they must remain silent. He explains the two-minute limit for testimony due to the large number of signed-up speakers.
chapters.title: Feliz opens public testimony and sets two-minute limit

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I now open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that the quorum

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that the quorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Please quiet down as you exit the room.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We're going to begin the public testimony, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: If you want to have a conversation, please do it in the rotunda.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the sergeant at arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: For in-person panelists, please come to the table once your name has been called.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Now I'll call our first panel.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Rama Issa Ibrahim from the Center for Anti-Violence Education and Matt Abrams-Gerber.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You may come to the front.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, so the first panel is going to be Rama Issa, Matt Abrams-Gerber, and also Divine Pryor, who is via Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We'll start with Rama.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And also, we have approximately 60 people signed up to testify, so we're going to have to limit testimony to two minutes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'm going to have to strictly enforce that rule.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: If we go over two minutes, obviously we'll be here till tomorrow and some members might not have the opportunity to testify, so we're just going to have to strictly enforce the two-minute rule just to make sure that all the 60 members who have signed up get the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So you may begin when you're ready.

chapters.summary: Rama Issa-Ibrahim, Executive Director of the Center for Anti-Violence Education, testifies about the organization's 52-year history and its work on self-defense and community safety. She urges the city to invest in community-based organizations and include them in designing the Department of Community Safety.
chapters.title: Rama Issa-Ibrahim testifies on community safety and anti-violence education

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: I didn't think I would go first.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: Okay, hi everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: I'm Rauma Issa Ibrahim.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: I'm the Executive Director of the Center for Anti-Violence Education, and I'm here today to testify alongside my peers and colleagues of the New York City Against Hate Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: CAE was founded 52 years ago by a visionary collective of queer women.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: They work tirelessly to equip women and femmes, the LGBT plus community, and survivors of violence with tools for self-defense and self-empowerment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: Today we employ a comprehensive strategy that includes self-defense workshops, community safety education, and youth leadership development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: Before the pandemic, alongside AVP, A&Y, AAF, JFRED, Make the Road, Brooklyn Movement Center, and others, we advocated for city council funding to expand our hate violence prevention work as a coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: A few years later, the coalition helped establish the Office of Prevention for Hate Crimes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: Our collective organizing is proof of what we can bring to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: I share all of this to say that organizations sitting up here with me today have hundreds of years of experience combined in addressing safety in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: Because we see community safety as a framework for healthy and thriving communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: A framework that centers connection, care, and deep investments for those most impacted by unjust systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: A framework that pushes us to rely less on policing and law enforcement and lean on community, each other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: and our neighbors for safety structures and networks of care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: As a collective, we have taught and supported the design and implementation of countless alternatives to punitive and carceral systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: CAE has designed and implemented some of the largest efforts on de-escalation and safety trainings and bystander intervention trainings in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: These trainings have strengthened the capacity of everyday New Yorkers to show up for each other safely and prepare for the unique and ever-changing situations that we come across in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: It builds a network of care and skills simultaneously, and that's why we ask that the city invest more dollars in this education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: Ultimately, building community safety is about connection, love, care, tending to each other and our neighbors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: It's about doing a little bit more every day so that eventually it becomes something that we all embody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: Over the course of this mayoral administration, we have a real opportunity to co-create a community-based safety infrastructure in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: That is rooted in prevention, care, and connection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: Everyone in New York City deserves to be safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: Government and community can coordinate holistic approaches that support the health and well-being of all our people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: I urge the City Council to work hand-in-hand with the current administration and make intentional efforts to include community-based organizations and grassroots organizations like all of us here today in the design and implementation of the Department of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: The Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please conclude.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Sorry, we're out of time.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: It's just one sentence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: The Office of Community Safety is a first step to improving the way we address and prevent violence across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: Much more must be done to ensure that coordination between government and community is deliberate and consistent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: Community buy-in is a vital part of design and implementation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rama Issa-Ibrahim
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, you may begin where you're ready.

chapters.summary: Matt Abrams-Gerber of the Jewish Community Relations Council testifies that anti-Semitism accounts for the largest share of reported hate crimes. He thanks the city for doubling PATH funding and describes the Fellowships Against Hate program operating in all five boroughs.
chapters.title: Matt Abrams-Gerber testifies on hate crime prevention and JCRC

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs Feliz and Brewer and committee members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: My name is Matt Abrams-Gerber.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: I'm the Vice President of the Center for Shared Society at the Jewish Community Relations Council of New York, the primary community relations organization of the New York Jewish community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: Year after year, anti-Semitism accounts for the largest share of reported hate crimes in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: For too many Jewish New Yorkers, fear is part of daily life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: That is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: And we are not alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: Muslim, Sikh, Arab, Asian, Black, Hispanic, and LGBTQIA plus New Yorkers feel it too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: Our safety is bound together, and hate against one of us is hate against all of us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: That is why JCRC is proud to have been an original anchor of Partners Against the Hate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: Thank you to City Council for creating PATH and to the Mayor for doubling its funding for the Office for the Prevention of Hate Crimes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: Because JCRC does not accept City funding, we are grateful to receive this grant through the 67th Precinct Clergy Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: With it, we support community-based organizations who tend to victims

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: of anti-Semitic attacks in Brooklyn, Queens, and across the city, provide educational and arts initiatives for young people and adults, and build partnerships between the Jewish community, the NYPD, and neighbors of every background.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: Our trademark program

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: The Fellowships Against Hate demonstrates what this investment makes possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: It began in Brooklyn five years ago and is now in all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: Leaders from different communities build real relationships across cultures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: They learn how bias and hate operate, and they gain skills in conflict resolution and coalition building to address it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: With hundreds of fellows and alumni, we have an ever-expanding force for peace.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: Thank you for investing in JCRC and all of the PATH anchors to address the immediate needs of responding to hate in our communities, as well as the long-term preventative work of building sustainable relationships that will enable us to eradicate hate once and for all, for that is the only path forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Abrams Gerber
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Divine Pryor, who's joining us via Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You may begin when you're ready.

chapters.summary: Dr. Divine Pryor, President of the People's Police Academy, introduces the organization's work as a bridge between community and law enforcement. He describes their three-day information exchange and public safety council, offering support to OCS.
chapters.title: Divine Pryor testifies on People's Police Academy and community-law enforcement bridge

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: Good afternoon, members of the Committee on Public Safety and Governmental Operations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: Thank you for providing this opportunity for me to speak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: My name is Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: Devine Pryor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: I am the President and Chief Executive Officer of the People's Police Academy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: The People's Police Academy is located within the City University of New York at the historic McGavish College in Crown Heights, Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: Who are we?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: We are a platform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: We are an institution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: We're an organization, but we're a problem-solving enterprise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: For the past 10 years, we've developed a very strong, close working relationship with the law enforcement community and now act as a bridge between the community and law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: We pride ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: And our three-day information exchange experience where we bring people who will otherwise never share the same space, never be in the same room together to problem solve, where they can dialogue, where they can interact with each other, they can get to know each other in a different way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: And our testimony, by the way, has been submitted in writing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: So what I'm saying to you is a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: deviation from the testimony because you already have that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: But what we wanted you to know that we have built over the last five years out of the 10 years we've been in operation, a public safety council,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: which consists of members of law enforcement on all three levels, the federal, state, and city level, as well as nonprofit organizations that actually provide these services to individuals who've been justice impacted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: And our testimony today was simply to introduce to the Office of Community Safety and to members of the City Council who are not aware of us that we are here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: And much of what the new office wants to do, we've begun a lot of that work, and we'd like to be supportive and helpful in any way that we can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: So this was really an introductory testimony to anyone who needs to understand that there is such a platform in existence and that we're not only known citywide, but we're also known statewide and nationally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: We've been called on by folks as far away as Birmingham, Alabama, to come out and use our...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: three-day intervention to show them how to problem-solve it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: We have assembled a team of experts around the city of New York who have skills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: Please conclude.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: So we want to thank you for this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: We are, again, the People's Police Academy, and we're at the City University of New York at Meg Evers College.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Divine Pryor
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you all for testifying.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We're going to call the next panel.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So we have five chairs, so I'll call the first five.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Aaliyah Tejada, Juan Ramos.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Zara Nazir, Hussein Yatabari, and Lina Allen.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: It seems like one person might have left, so I'll call the next one.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Delilah Seligman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: Test.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, so we'll start from left to right.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You may begin when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And again, we're going to have to strictly enforce the two-minute rule, given that we have a lot of people signed up.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You may begin when you're ready.

chapters.summary: Zahra Nasser, Executive Director of the People's Plan, testifies that community safety runs through all their organizing. She supports funding OCS, making it permanent, and making non-police response the default for mental health calls, but recommends amendments to Intro 403.
chapters.title: Zahra Nasser testifies on People's Plan and community safety funding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Brewer, Chair Fleas, and members of the GovOps and Safety Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: My name is Zahra Nasser.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: I'm the Executive Director of the People's Plan, which is a coalition of more than 100 grassroots organizations and unions that fight for a just city budget every year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: Community safety runs through every issue we organize on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: Our members see it in schools where police are still the default responders to children in emotional crisis, on the street where sweeps move people around and criminalize them instead of housing them,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: in homes where people and families hesitate to call 911 for a loved one in crisis, in neighborhoods facing gun and hate violence where community-based prevention reaches people that policing cannot and does not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: We believe safety comes from shifting resources and power away from criminalization and into housing, schools, and care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: That is why funding the Office of Community Safety and holding the NYPD funding flat were top priorities in our FY27 People's Budget Campaign.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: gives that work a home in city government, but today it only exists by executive order.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: We do want this department to be permanent with its own budget and staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: The city should make non-police response the default for mental health crisis calls citywide and 24-7 with infrastructure built up for voluntary care and housing so people have somewhere to go and stay besides the ER.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: The city should also extend that approach to young people, schools, gun and hate violence, and pay its workers and providers fairly and on time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: We also support the goal of Intro 403 and thank Councilmember Ressler

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: for bringing this forward, but recommend amendments, which is to keep the bill focused on establishing the department in law and removing provisions on specific prescriptions around borough offices, safety patrols, et cetera,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: and how, if at all, the department works on law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: Those decisions should come out of a planning process with community partners, and we really look forward to working with all of you to fund this office, scale it, and make it permanent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zahra Nasser
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hussein Yatabari, Executive Director of Muslim Community Network, testifies about the shooting of Javits Frimpong and the need for prevention. He describes MCN's work with OPHC and NGBV and calls for language access and a permanent Department of Community Safety.
chapters.title: Hussein Yatabari testifies on Muslim Community Network and prevention

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairs Felice and Brewer and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: This morning, I actually sat with the father of Javits Frimpong in the South Bronx, the 15-year-old Councilmember Riley and Stephen's name today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: Javits, a recent immigrant from Ghana, should have been in class today at Dream Yard Prep.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: Unfortunately, his father is planning his funeral and asking how this could have been prevented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: My name is Hussein Yadabari.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: I'm the executive director of Muslim Community Network, serving about 8,000 New Yorkers a year for 23 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: I grew up in the South Bronx as a black New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: I know families do not live in crime statistics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: They live with the loss.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: As a Muslim New Yorker, I watch Islamophobia become normalized, at times even from those in power.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: In January, at the city's own Muslim Heritage Month celebration, I had to use my own body to shield community members from agitators, putting MCN's de-escalation training into practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: Prevention is safety, and it only works in partnership with community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: MCN partners with OPHT.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: We've trained city agencies and community members on Islamophobia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: We're launching a Bronx Family Violence Prevention Program with NGBV next year, but none of it works without language access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: When people cannot be understood, they are not counted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: And we see that happen oftentimes across different spaces in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: Language access must be built into.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: to every layer of the cake and delivered by organizations our neighbors already trust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: Gun violence, hate, gender-based violence, and mental health crises reach the same families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: Safety must live in one place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: MCN supports a Department of Community Safety and the intro, but the bill needs stronger community input and clarity on which functions move from the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: Into this new Department of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: We also want to make sure it's written into law so no future administration can undo it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: Police arrive after the harm is done, and our communities carry a history of police brutality and surveillance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: No community should face a hierarchy of harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: Black, brown, Asian, immigrant, and Muslim New Yorkers each deserve a city that names them in its plan and does not leave them out of it, speaks their language, and brings them into the buildings, into building this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hussein Yatabari
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Aaliyah Tejada of the RISE Project at the Center for Justice Innovation testifies about work at the intersection of community violence and domestic violence. She supports making OCS a permanent department and praises new investments in NGBV.
chapters.title: Aaliyah Tejada testifies on RISE Project and community violence prevention

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairs Feliz and Brewer and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: My name is Alia Tejeda.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: I'm the Senior Program Manager of Community Initiatives at the RISE Project, an initiative at the Center for Justice Innovation, and I'm a Native Queens girl.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: The Center strongly supports the Office of Community Safety and its vision for a more comprehensive, community-centered approach to public safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: We have been particularly encouraged by the leadership of Commissioner Delaney Brumsey and Deputy Mayor Francois.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: The creation of OCS presents an opportunity to bring together traditionally siloed areas of violence prevention, and this reflects our work at the RISE project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: RISE works at the intersection of community violence and DV and GBV, developing culturally responsive approaches to preventing harm through initiatives such as barbershop talks, men rising, youth on the rise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: We engage community members in conversations about healthy relationships, accountability, and conflict resolution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: Our partnership with the Mayor's Office to End Domestic and Gender-Based Violence developed Respect First and Respect and Responsibility, two community

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: interventions uplifting a different form of violence prevention through transformative and restorative practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: We applaud the administration's new investment in NGBV, particularly in its support for culturally specific organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: and encourage continued investment in its capacity to support our communities and partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: Finally, we support the goal of making OCS a permanent Department of Community Safety and appreciate Councilmember Rustler's leadership on Intro 403.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: This will help ensure that the department builds upon existing successes, preserves effective programming, and develops a shared definition of safety with clear outcomes and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aaliyah Tejada
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

chapters.summary: Lena Allen of Fountain House testifies about the clubhouse model for serious mental illness. She says community itself is therapy and notes a 21% reduction in Medicaid costs among members, urging OCS to embed intentional communities across care systems.
chapters.title: Lena Allen testifies on Fountain House and clubhouse model

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: Thank you, chairs and members of the committee, for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: My name is Lena Allen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: I'm Policy and Advocacy Manager at Fountain House, and I'm here to speak about the transformative potential of placing community at the center of our continuum of care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: Fountain House pioneered the clubhouse model nearly 80 years ago right here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: It's grounded in the belief that community itself is therapy, and the model brings members and staff together to do work side by side in daily operations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: It works to address often overlooked challenges of serious mental illness, including loneliness, social isolation, and diminished self-esteem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: Through the work-ordered day, members build confidence, agency, and purpose, empowering them to reconnect with the broader community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: Our approach creates a stickiness to jobs, to school, to housing, and it keeps people out of institutional revolving doors and out of crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: One key indicator of this impact is a 21% reduction in Medicaid costs among Fountain House members compared to the highest need population of people with SMI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: The clubhouse model complements and enhances other services and should be accessible to all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: But beyond the ongoing expansion of clubhouses, the practice of building intentional communities should be embedded across municipal care systems and programs to promote safety and health for all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: We're hopeful that the city's new Office of Community Safety will advance a coordinated whole-of-community approach that brings government together with providers, advocates, and those most impacted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: Even with stronger community interventions, crises do happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: We must respond to them more effectively and prioritize non-police approaches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: Our members have intimate experiences with this system, and over 100 of them shared their insights in a published report a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: The recommendations include needing better intra-agency coordination, a strong and dignified workforce, greater public awareness of services and data to support improvements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: Reform has to go beyond acute crisis and connect people to services, benefits, and community supports in the long term.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: We strongly support the Commissioner and Council's commitment to transparent reporting and find peers indispensable in this program and I'll submit written testimony with the rest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lena Allen
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Delilah Seligman of the New York City Anti-Violence Project testifies about their crisis hotline for LGBTQ+ New Yorkers. She describes a historic $26 million increase in OPHC funding that will allow AVP to restore hotline services and urges continued investment.
chapters.title: Delilah Seligman testifies on Anti-Violence Project and LGBTQ+ crisis services

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: Good afternoon, committee members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: My name is Delilah Seligman, and I'm the manager of training and outreach for the New York City Anti-Violence Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: AVP is proud to serve LGBTQ plus New Yorkers through our crisis hotline program, a trauma-informed, anti-oppressive, and culturally responsive community safety service that offers on-call crisis counseling from trained professionals and volunteers,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: and connects survivors of hate violence to vital mental health and legal counseling services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: Recently, due to challenges in the funding landscape, AVP has had to switch to solely operating during business hours, but with a historic $26 million increase in OPHC funding,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: AVP is committed to restoring our hotline services back to scale in the coming months.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: In FY26, AVP was able to serve more than 3,000 clients through our crisis hotline, and we were able to train over 500 professionals and community members through our training and technical assistance program, which offers customized trainings to LGBT New Yorkers and those who serve them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: Through this vital funding provided by OCS and OPHC, we will be able to continue making that level of impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: Services like AVP's Crisis Hotline and training program are more vital than ever.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: The Williams Institute of UCLA reports an increase of 184 to 527 anti-transgender hate crimes between 2018 and 2024.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: Whether it's being attacked on the street, unjustly fired from a job, or navigating a domestic violence emergency, L.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: LGBT New Yorkers have been resilient through a tremendous amount of pain and uncertainty and deserve culturally responsive services that meet their needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: As a survivor and a queer transgender woman myself, I can speak to the truth behind these statistics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: When I was 18 and beginning my gender transition in the early 2010s, I know that I would have been safer had I had access to resources like AVP's crisis hotline.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: LGBT New Yorkers deserve to have access to resources that allow them to live in safety as their authentic selves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: APP thanks OPHC, OCS, and Mayor Mamdani for this historic increase in funding, and we urge committee members to continue expanding funding opportunities for essential hate crime prevention across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Delilah Seligman
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, everyone, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Also, earlier I called Juan Ramos.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Is Juan Ramos with us?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, so we'll call Juan later before we conclude.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The next panel is going to be...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Andrea Ortiz, Raul Soto, Rafid,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: and Keziah.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, you may begin when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We'll start from my left to my right.

chapters.summary: Raul Soto of the Yaya Network testifies that youth cannot wait for safe and supportive schools. He calls for a robust Department of Community Safety that includes school safety and moves police away from schools, citing racial disparities in school policing.
chapters.title: Raul Soto testifies on Yaya Network and school safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: No worries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: Good afternoon, chairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: My name is Raul Soto.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: I'm the co-executive director of the Yaya Network, which is a youth organizing hub on issues impacting young people across the entire city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: I'm proud to represent young people, public high school students from across the city that say today that youth can't wait for safe and supportive schools, and we deeply believe that that includes a robust Department of Community Safety that can help coordinate that and move police away from schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: Police away from schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: For years, our youth have advocated for a vision of safety, not relying on policing of communities, especially our black and brown students, students with disabilities and immigrant communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: When our youth organizers conduct workshops and listening sessions in their schools, they hear time and time again, wishing for an agency, a city coordinated response,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: to youth mental health and to meet their needs before things get dire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: I think of a time working in East Harlem before I joined the IA Network as an educator and community organizer, helping to coordinate rapid response for our young students as part of the program that we were in, where we would help

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: Ensure that there was mental health counseling inside of their school buildings and community centers and coordinating our efforts to curb youth violence with other organizations in the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: We know that a community coordinated strategy can work and will work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: School safety needs to be included in the vision for a new department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: Framing safety as how we can continue to police kids, protect students from each other, from the inevitable violence that they will commit on each other has already failed as policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: Nothing tells us more than the data showing that black students represent 52% of all police interventions in DOE public schools and 56% of the students who are handcuffed in the first half of this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: Our youth have shared experiences where school administrators have used the NYPD as a policy of school discipline.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: So today, let me just reiterate, we want to see a Department of Community Safety that includes school safety, to coordinate youth safety responses in communities,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raul Soto
utterances.text: to pass Intro 460 to eliminate the gang database, and to pass the Curb Act, and to prevent the NYPD from conflicting with the future vision for truly safe communities.

chapters.summary: Keziah Mickle, a student at Fordham University and organizer with the Yaya Network, shares a personal story of a classmate being body-slammed and handcuffed in school. She asks the city to invest in restorative justice and mental health services instead of policing.
chapters.title: Keziah Mickle testifies on school policing and restorative justice

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Keziah Mickle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: I'm a student at Fordham University, an organizer at the Yaya Network, and a supporter of the Dignity in Schools campaign.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: Today, I come to you as a former public school student and a firsthand witness to the injustice faced by students in underprivileged communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: I'm here today because we want Mom Donnie's administration and city council to expand the Office of Community Safety scope to include school safety and mental health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: This office must take action to put strategies in place to ensure safety, academic, and social success of youth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: Without your help, New York City youth, especially those from marginalized communities, will continue to fall vulnerable to mental health crises and criminalization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: Black girls represent roughly 15% of female public school students nationally, but make up around half of exclusionary punishments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: For girls who look like me, being perceived as innocent is a luxury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: We're threats to be disarmed rather than children capable of making mistakes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: When I was a freshman in high school, during lunch, a physical altercation between two black girls broke out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: While it's completely reasonable for the adults in the room to try to break up the fight, extreme measures were taken in the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: Soon my classmates and I watched as a security agent body slammed a 15-year-old girl to the ground and placed her in handcuffs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: I never saw that girl again, and I doubt she ever got the mental health resources or counseling that she deserved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: She was one of many black girls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: Girls who the system simply disappears.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: Now that I am in a place to advocate for myself and other marginalized kids, I ask that the city and the Office of Community Safety invest in restorative justice

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: and mental health services in public schools and for a commitment to work collaboratively to transition schools away from policing and surveillance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: Punitive punishments reinforce the adultification of marginalized youth and halt them from growing past their mistakes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: If this negligence continues, black and brown children will continue to fall out of the public school system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keziah Mickle
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Rafid Al-Arik, a high school student and youth organizer, testifies about a friend who brought a weapon to school after not receiving mental health support. He urges the committee to expand OCS to include school safety and pass Intro 460 to eliminate the gang database.
chapters.title: Rafid Al-Arik testifies on youth mental health and school safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: Good afternoon, members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: My name is Rafid Al-Arik, and I'm a current high school student at Stuyvesant and a previous middle school student at MS-180 in Co-op City and a resident of the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: I'm here as a youth organizer with Yaya Network and Dignity in Schools Campaign New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: I'm here today to urge the Committee of Public Safety to expand the Office of Community Safety to include school safety and invest in youth mental health resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: School should be a place where young people feel safe, supported, and cared for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: Unfortunately, during my time in middle school, that wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: When I was in middle school, a friend and myself started to struggle and our grades suffered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: Our assistant director then gave us a talk about our risk of failure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: And instead of getting the support we needed, we saw how the teachers devoted their time to those whose grades were deemed salvageable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: I was lucky enough to have a mother who was able to support and push me towards my potential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: Regrettably, my friend did not have the same support without the school providing any proactive counseling or any space to process what's going on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: He tried to cope in an unsafe behavior and toxic relationships.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: He tried to find other resources to seek comfort that failed him.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: And it escalated into him making a bad choice to bring a weapon to school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: Being met with police pulling him out of the school, metal detectors installed the next day with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: without anybody asking, hey, what's going on or what do you need?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: When I think about the potential of Department of Community Safety, I think about the city that could have coordinated structures to catch my friend before he fell through the cracks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: Metal detectors and police officers do not solve why students feel unsafe or why they act out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: They just create an atmosphere of fear and criminalization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: We want the city to fully fund protections for young people that offer support for students before they make unsafe choices, like restorative justice and mental health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: We cannot forget that many students are also feeling unsafe because our families are under attack.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: All school staff should receive regular explicit instructions on what to do if immigration officers were to come.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: What we need is an office of community safety that includes school safety, pass and show 460 to eliminate the end.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafid Al-Arik
utterances.text: NYPD's gang database and permanently delete its data to protect young people from being criminalized.

chapters.summary: Andrea Ortiz of the Dignity in Schools Campaign testifies about the over-policing of Black and immigrant students. She calls on OCS to coordinate with DOE on school safety and mental health and supports making OCS a permanent department, with amendments to Intro 403.
chapters.title: Andrea Ortiz testifies on Dignity in Schools and school safety demands

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: Hello, I'm Andrea with the Dignity in Schools campaign of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: Young people in public schools should feel safe to learn, build community, and develop leadership skills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: Unfortunately, New York City youth are increasingly struggling with depression, anxiety, and isolation, violent immigrant enforcement, and NYPD criminalization, yet our elected and educational leaders continue to invest in police and surveillance instead of supportive staff, restorative justice,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: immigrant protections, and mental health access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: Black, immigrant, trans, and gender nonconforming youth and students

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: with disabilities are disproportionately affected by policing and surveillance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: During the first half of the 2025-2026 school year, black students represented 52% of all police interventions and 56% of all students forced into metal handcuffs despite making up less than 20% of the student population.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: The youngest students targeted were black children as young as four years old targeted by the NYPD for child and crisis incidences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: During this time period, metal handcuffs were used on children as young as 10 years old for child and crisis incidences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: We call on the city, we call on the Office of Community Safety to coordinate with the DOE on school safety and mental health and other anti-violence and anti-criminalization interventions for young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: That is why we support the Office of Community Safety and the effort to make it a permanent department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: Yet we want Intro 403 to be focused on establishing the department in law and its structure and programs should be designed in consultation with community partners, providers, labor unions, workers, and the administration and council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: We do not endorse the current bill, which is too prescriptive in its language.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: We are calling on the New York City Council to ensure that DCS can work collaboratively with community and the DOE to design a process for schools interested in transitioning school safety and culture away from policing and surveillance to supportive staff and services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: Collaboratively plan for a three to five year district wide police and ice free schools transition and begin hiring community based civilian school staff to welcome students as they enter schools and deescalate conflicts, move money away from

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: from policing and surveillance, including ceasing all NYPD recruitment and hiring and training of school police, and expand school-based restorative justice and mental health access, including investing $80 million in hiring school climate coordinators in 500 schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Love that last sentence.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, everyone, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to City Hall.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we're going to hear from Sarah Robinson.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I don't know if that's Eamon, Gad, Eva Gray, and Jenna Sherma.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We'll begin when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Please turn your microphone on.

chapters.summary: Sarah Robinson of the Brooklyn Way and Brownsville Safety Alliance testifies about the link between criminalization and substance use among youth. She supports a permanent Department of Community Safety and urges divestment from policing and surveillance.
chapters.title: Sarah Robinson testifies on Brownsville Safety Alliance and youth criminalization

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: My name is Sarah Robinson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: I've been a city resident for the past 17 years, and I'm an engaged community member of Brooklyn and Parent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: I've also worked with Riseburg Community Partnership for the past decade and currently serve as director of the Brooklyn Way, a community coalition working with youth and young adults.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: We're members of the Brownsville Safety Alliance and supporters of Dignity in Schools and the Gangs Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: I'm here today to urge the administration and OCS to work with us in community to expand their scope and mission to include school safety policies and anti-criminalization interventions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: From our local survey and carried out last year, we found that youth and young adults were three times more likely to drink alcohol and four times more likely to use cannabis if they were impacted by criminalization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: Pair this with reported statistics from NYPD's fourth quarter of last year that shows in top five precincts in Brooklyn with most stops, officers engaged with 2,072 youth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: That's the equivalent of 9th, 10th, and half of 11th grade of students currently enrolled at Stuyvesant, with 12% of those under the age of 18.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: That's about 249 kids or 22 and a half 11-a-side soccer teams in three months.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: In their own words, our youth also describe substance use as a way of coping with the stress and trauma tied to systems contact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: I'm in strong support of a permanent department as designated by law and are encouraged to know that those in the office have extensive experience with and have seen the transformative impact of restorative practice approaches to relationship building, community engagement and safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: It truly takes a village and our youth deserve safety policies that not only include them but value and see them as experts of their own experiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: I call on the administration to divest from the policing and surveillance like quality of life enforcement and the gangs database

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: that continues to disproportionately impact black, indigenous and youth of the global majority and demand that the office reinvest that money

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: in expanding access to affirming and culturally relevant mental health supports, restorative and transformative school and community practices and higher pay for non-clinical staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Robinson
utterances.text: I thank you all for your time, engagement and care of our city and urge you to ensure that community safety is a policy priority for New Yorkers of all ages.

chapters.summary: Iman of Girls for Gender Equity testifies about the need for healing-centered community safety and youth mental health. She cites data showing Black students are disproportionately arrested and restrained, and calls for restorative justice and school climate coordinators.
chapters.title: Iman testifies on Girls for Gender Equity and healing-centered safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Feliz, Chair Brewer, and members of the committees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: My name is Iman, and I'm the Policy and Advocacy Manager at Girls for Gender Equity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: We're an organization that works intergenerationally through a back-feminist lens to center the leadership of Black girls and gender-expansive youth of color through advocacy, programming, and narrative shift.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: I am testifying today on behalf of GGE and the Dignity in Schools Coalition to urge the Office of Community Safety to expand their scope and mission to address youth safety and the youth mental health crisis

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: by prioritizing healing-centered community safety initiatives and to underline the need for gender-based violence to be a priority under the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: Currently, the policing and surveillance infrastructure that students are subjected to in their schools stands at a costly $400 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: This is a system that disproportionately targets BIPOC, immigrant, trans, and gender nonconforming youth and students with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: Data collected through the School Safety Act from 2016 to 2023 and analyzed by the New York City Council's data team

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: found that relative to the percentage that black students make up of the population in New York City schools, they are disproportionately more likely to receive any kind of disciplinary intervention, as well as disproportionately more likely to be arrested and restrained in general.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: This pattern was unfortunately stronger among students who were 10 and under.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: Alongside the data, youth in our programs often speak about the lack of safety they feel in their schools and the distrust they have in the current safety infrastructures to keep them safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: In order to make communities and schools safe for all young people, we call on the city to approach safety through healing-centered approaches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: This looks like fully funding and expanding restorative justice practices to all schools and hiring school climate coordinators, expanding mental health access, protecting immigrant students, and expanding the network of supportive staff in schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: Youth also need seats at the table to weigh in on the policies that impact them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: Providing young people with the resources they need and allowing them to grow in communities and schools they trust is the foundation of community safety and a crucial step in ending the criminalization and push out of marginalized youth from our schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman
utterances.text: We'll submit the rest of the testimony in written.

chapters.summary: A special education teacher in Flatbush testifies about a student with disabilities who was suspended after an incident at a metal detector. She calls for social workers, counselors, and restorative justice instead of police and surveillance in schools.
chapters.title: Special education teacher testifies on school safety and restorative justice

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I'm a special education teacher in Flatbush who sees firsthand that youth safety needs to be prioritized by the city in a coordinated way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We agree that we need a Department of Community Safety and ask that the city expand this mission to include youth and school safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Students spend the vast majority of time in schools, and this is where we need to begin with their social-emotional development, and this is where we can best meet their needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Schools need social workers, counselors, more teachers, more caring staff, and supports, not police and surveillance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I've seen in my own students with disabilities get into altercations with school safety officers in our building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: For example, I'm a case manager for a student who has a learning disability and receives counseling services for emotional support and is arguably has emotional and academic needs beyond the scope of my school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Last week, an incident at the metal detector escalated, causing him to lash out in a defensive way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Now he's suspended from school and will face a suspension hearing, and his education is disrupted when he's a senior and reads at a first grade level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: This student is not violent or dangerous in any way, but has emotional needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: That can't be met by the school and needs to be met by trained professionals who understand his background instead of assuming he's a criminal with dangerous intentions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: So I stand in solidarity with Dignity in Schools, campaigning in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: and more UFT calling for restorative justice, mental

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: health access, and police-free schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Jenna Sharma, co-founder of LearnMobo, testifies about the need for consent and healthy relationships education in schools. She calls on OCS to expand its mission to include youth sexual and gender-based violence prevention and fund community-based educators.
chapters.title: Jenna Sharma testifies on consent education and youth violence prevention

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: Hi, thank you for having me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: My name is Jenna Sharma.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: I'm the co-founder of LearnMobo, which is a sex education organization based in New York City and a supporter of Dignity in Schools campaign.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: I'm here because we want the Momdani administration and city council to expand the Office of Community Safety's mission to include youth and school safety, including sexual and gender-based violence prevention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: My team works with youth organizations and schools across the city, including physical education and health teachers who teach sex ed in New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: They tell us about students in their hallways engaging in unhealthy behaviors, often exacerbated by what their hyper-online generation has come to normalize.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: Students track each other's every move, they share passwords, and they give each other unrestricted access to their phones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: This past summer, our intern conducted research with other young people and found that they often understand consent as a way to protect themselves, what if someone does this to me, but they rarely ask, what if I'm the one causing harm?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: The research highlighted just how little young people have been equipped to understand their own role in perpetrating harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: What we are living through right now is a crisis, a crisis of empathy, of bodily autonomy, of boundaries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: Our kids turn to the internet to fill in the gaps of their own bodies and relationships, risking exposure to narratives driven by people who profit from their insecurity and confusion, building entire cultures around the act of hating one another.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: Even with some requirements to teach the basics of consent,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: Teachers have told us that their own capacity and the materials available to them limit their ability to cover these topics thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: We work with young people and they know they need support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: We work with teachers and they know they need support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: Over-policing schools is reactive, not preventative.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: Criminalizing young people doesn't stop the cycle of harm, but better education can help prevent it before it starts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: We're calling on the City Council to expand the Office of Community Safety mission to include youth sexual and gender-based violence prevention, fund community-based consent, empathy, and healthy relationships education in schools and youth programs taught by trained civilian educators,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: not police, and move money from school policing and surveillance into restorative justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Young from the Power in Action Committee, Josiah Gilbert, Stephanie Frias, Marnie Ponce, and Esperanza Vasquez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: Councilmember Felice, if it's okay with you, I'll have Esperanza is going to testify in Spanish, and I can read her testimony in English.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Yeah, that's fine, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Also, sorry, I'm having trouble reading one.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, so we're missing one person in the call.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We have Josiah Gilbert, Stephanie Frias, Marnie Ponce.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, so, and then Esperanza.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, so Marnie isn't with us.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You may begin when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We'll start from left to right, as always, as we've been.

chapters.summary: Stephanie Frias of the Gangs Coalition testifies about the racially discriminatory NYPD criminal group database. She calls for its abolition, increased investment in community-led violence prevention, and a transition to police-free schools.
chapters.title: Stephanie Frias testifies on Gangs Coalition and ending gang database

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: Good afternoon and thank you Chair Felice and everyone else on the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: My name is Stephanie Frias.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: I'm here as a representative from the Grassroots Association for Neighborhood Groups and Solutions, also known as the Gangs Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: We are a coalition supported by more than 60 New York City community-based organizations, advocates, legal professionals, and directly impacted New Yorkers calling for an end to police surveillance of black and Latino communities and the racially discriminatory nature of gang policing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: The Gangs Coalition calls on the City Council and the Mamdani administration to abolish the NYPD criminal group database

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: and racially discriminatory gang surveillance, strengthen and sustain investments in community-led violence prevention, and develop a concrete transition towards police-free schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: We must stop investing in systems that stigmatize and criminalize our communities and start investing in people and resources that make our communities safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: Labeling, surveilling, and harassing young people of color, many of whom have never been convicted of a crime, is a direct...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: odds with the Office of Community Safety's mission of creating safer communities and addressing the root causes of violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: The racial disparities are undeniable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: The Department of Investigation's Office of the Inspector General found that black and Hispanic New Yorkers accounted for 99% of individuals in the criminal group database.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
