utterances.text: These numbers reflect a long-standing approach to public safety that treats black and brown communities as threats to be monitored and controlled rather than communities deserving of investment and care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: Our young people should not have to live under constant surveillance or fear that their relationships, neighborhoods, clothing, or socioeconomic circumstances will be used to label them as criminals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: Intro 460 is supported by a majority of this council and should immediately be held for a hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: We reject the idea that expanding surveillance and criminalization is the only way to keep our communities safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: New York City must invest in the conditions that allow our communities to thrive, including sustainable housing, quality education, and employment opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: Public safety must mean that people have the resources, relationships, and opportunities they need to live dignified lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: We cannot claim to prioritize community safety while continuing to surveil young people in their neighborhoods, criminalize them in their schools, and underfund the very programs that help them thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Frias
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Josiah Gilbert of the Legal Aid Society's juvenile rights practice testifies about the importance of CMS organizations. He shares a story of a young man mentored by CMS staff and urges the city to invest in community-based programs and give young people a seat at the table.
chapters.title: Josiah Gilbert testifies on Legal Aid Society and CMS funding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: Good afternoon, chairs and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: My name is Josiah Gilbert.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: I serve as the client and community engagement manager for the Legal Aid Society's juvenile rights practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: Through my work, I engage with young people from across our communities, including those impacted by the child welfare and juvenile justice systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: I appreciate the council's consideration of Introduction 403, but I want to emphasize that creating another department alone will not make our community safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: What matters is whether we're willing to invest in the people and programs already doing the work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: Our city's CMS sites are a prime example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: Every day, credible messengers and community-based organizations are doing the frontline, elbow-grease work of building trust, mediating conflicts, and intervening before violence occurs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: I saw the impact of this work firsthand when cases partnered with our team on a young man's case, providing support to his entire family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: His younger brother, although not formally enrolled in the program, developed a bond with a staff member who became a trusted mentor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: At the time, he was beginning to follow his older brother's path toward gang involvement, but through the authentic, relatable mentorship, he began focusing on school and pursuing other positive opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: This is the power of community-based intervention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: Its impact reaches far beyond those officially enrolled in a program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: These organizations are doing the difficult work of keeping our communities safe, yet too often face funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: challenges and inadequate support from the very systems that depend on their work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: We cannot claim to prioritize community safety while failing to adequately support those on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: We must also ensure young people, particularly those with lived experience, have a meaningful role in developing and overseeing this department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: Young people cannot continue to be the subject of conversations about community safety without having a meaningful seat at the table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: Ultimately, if we're serious about preventing violence, we must move beyond responding to crisis and invest in the relationships, opportunities, and community-based programs that prevent them in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josiah Gilbert
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Turn your mic on, please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: Sorry, just used to this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: Sorry, really don't need a mic, but it's okay.

chapters.summary: Chauncy Young, director of the New Settlement Parent Action Committee, testifies about the shooting of Javits Frimpong and the need for holistic school safety. He calls for restorative justice, mental health counselors, and community-led safety passage programs.
chapters.title: Chauncy Young testifies on New Settlement PAC and school safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Felice, Chair Brewer, and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: My name is Chauncey Young.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: I'm a parent and Highbridge resident in the Borough of the Bronx for over two decades and the director of the New Settlement Parent Action Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: At PAC, we organize parents and community members to fight for educational equity, support of schools, and safety in the well-being of our children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: I'm here today because true community safety starts with investing in our families, in our schools, and our youth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: For too long, safety in our neighborhoods have been treated as something brought in after harm occurs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: But for parents in the Bronx, real safety means prevention, care, and opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: Along with Hussein and African community leaders today, I too was in the home of Thomas Frimpong in his home while he was mourning the murder of his 15-year-old son, who was just killed yesterday as he was walking to school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: Only a few months ago, we stood with Jacob Kai Freydes'family after he was killed with a stray bullet only one block from our organization's office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: And we just held a community safety town hall with Councilmember Stevens just two weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: We're looking for true change and true community safety, and that looks like for us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: holistic school safety, expanding restorative justice programs, mental health counselors, school social workers in public schools, rather than relying on measures that criminalize children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: We're looking for safety passage programs and community programs, funding local community-led safety passage initiatives so children can travel to and from schools without fear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: Investment in youth and families, sustainable funding for community-based organizations with provide after school care, youth development and housing support and parent leadership programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: We urge the Office of School Safety to prioritize non-collateral community-based solutions and to work with the community in the development of this office, which is so essential for all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Esperanza Vasquez, a parent leader with New Settlement PAC, testifies in Spanish about the need for OCS and investment in healing rather than punishment. She calls for more school counselors and social workers and an end to police and metal detectors in schools. Chauncy Young provides English interpretation.
chapters.title: Esperanza Vasquez testifies in Spanish on school safety, interpreted by Chauncy Young

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Buenas tardes, miembros del Consejo Municipal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Mi nombre es Esperanza Vázquez, soy madre de dos hijos y líder del Comité Padres en Acción del Bronx del 2001.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Aunque yo nací en México, mis dos hijos nacieron en el Bronx y fueron a la escuela del Distrito 9.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: PAC es una organización dirigida por padres.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Ha estado trabajando con padres de la escuela en el Bronx desde el 96.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Para más de 10 años, PAC ha invocado a Grupo de Trabajo de Justicia Escolar en el Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Luego se unió a la coalición de escuelas centradas en sanación.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: El PAC forma parte de diversas coaliciones, entre ellas la campaña para escuelas centradas en sanación, la coalición de la ciudad de Nueva York, justicia educativa y la coalición de dignidad de las escuelas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Y la coalición de escuelas de neoyorquinos y las escuelas públicas raciales juntas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Es una organización compuesta por familias inmigrantes, negras y latinas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Respaldamos firmemente la necesidad de criar.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: de crear

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: una oficina de seguridad comunitaria.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Pedimos el Consejo Municipal que de la ciudad involucre miembros de la comunidad y defensores en la creación.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Como madre migrante que se de la ciudad debe ser más por nuestras escuelas y familias, invertir más en la sanación y apoyo a nuestros estudiantes en lugar de castigar y suspender y

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: incriminalizar injustamente a personas

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: que atraviesan una crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Necesitamos contratar más consejeros escolares y trabajadores sociales para apoyar la salud socioemocional a los estudiantes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Debemos de dejar de desplegar policías en las escuelas y dejar de utilizar los detectores de metales.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Necesitamos implementar técnicas de justicia restaurativas y dejar de tratar a nuestros niños y familias como si fueran criminales.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Necesitamos soluciones, no suspensiones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: De la ciudad de Nueva York debe invertir más en sanación y no daños en nuestros estudiantes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Esperanza Vasquez
utterances.text: Gracias.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Esperanza Vasquez and I'm a mother of two children and I have been a parent leader with the New Settlement Parent Action Committee since 2001.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: Although I was born in Mexico, both of my children were born in the Bronx and went to school in District 9.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: New Settlement Parent Action Committee is a parent-led organization that has been working with parents and schools in the Bronx since 1996.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: Over 10 years, PAC has convened the Bronx School Justice Working Group, which later joined the Healing Centered Schools Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: PAC is a member organization of many coalitions, including the Healing Centered Schools Campaign, the New York City Coalition for Educational Justice, the Dignian Schools Coalition, and the New Yorkers for Racially Just Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: As an organization of immigrant, black, and Latinx families, we strongly support the need for the Office of Community Safety, and we urge the City Council and the City to involve community members and advocates to be involved in its creation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: As an immigrant mother from the Bronx, I know that New York City needs to do more for our schools and our families and to invest in healing and supporting our students, not unjustly punishing, suspending, and criminalizing people in crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: We need to employ more schools counselors and social workers to support students'social-emotional health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: We need to stop deploying police in our schools and stop using metal detectors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: We need to use restorative justice techniques and stop treating our children and families like criminals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: We need solutions, not suspensions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: New York City should invest in healing and supporting our students, not unjustly punishing, suspending, and criminalizing people in crisis.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you, everyone, for testifying today, and thank you for that translation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: We need to employ more schools counselors and social workers to support students'social-emotional health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: We need to stop deploying police in our schools and stop using metal detectors.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we're going to call Laura Aresso, Rosalind Morrison, Jackie Gostigian, Ruth Lowenkron, and Christina Sparrow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: We need to use restorative justice techniques and stop treating our children and families like criminals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: We need solutions, not suspensions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chauncy Young
utterances.text: New York City should invest in healing.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much everyone for joining today.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You may begin when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We'll start with, yeah.

chapters.summary: Laura Araso, a staff attorney with the Legal Aid Society, testifies about her client Jabez Chakraborty, who was shot multiple times by NYPD during a mental health crisis. She describes his shackling in the hospital and prosecution, urging non-police crisis response.
chapters.title: Laura Araso testifies on Jabez Chakraborty police shooting case

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: My name is Laura Araso.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: I'm a staff attorney with the Legal Aid Society's Queens Trial Practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: I, along with my colleague, Shanaaz Chowdhury, represent Jabez Chakraborty, a young man from Southeast Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: As public defenders, we often meet our clients on some of the worst days of their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: We often see how one moment can change the course of someone's life, particularly when police react and respond in extremely aggressive and combative ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: For Jabez, this life-changing moment happened on January 26th of this year, when in the midst of a mental health crisis, he was shot multiple times by NYPD in his own home within 16 seconds of police.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: entering his home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: We first met Jabez in the ICU at Jamaica Hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: We saw the devastation and pain in the faces of his family who had spent days worrying if their son would make it out of multiple surgeries alive, only to find out that he was being criminally prosecuted and might be held at Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: When we entered the ICU room to meet Jabez, we had to pass a uniformed NYPD officer guarding his doorway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: Although Jabez was critically injured at that time with his stomach open and tubes and drains keeping him alive, he was shackled to his hospital bed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: To see someone shackled in that fragile condition was a level of cruelty that I don't think I've ever experienced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: For four days after he was shot, while Jabez was still in the surgical ICU fighting for his life, the Queen's District Attorney's Office filed charges against him by way of secret indictment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: Charging him with a violent felony offense that carries mandatory state prison time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: The officer who shot and almost killed Jabez was never charged.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: On the day of the arraignment on the criminal charges, Jabez appeared virtually from his hospital bed, still in the ICU.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: The Queens District Attorney's Office asked a judge to remand him, meaning hold him at Rikers Island without bail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: Jabez could be seen on the screen crying from his hospital bed while the prosecutor said that we should not forget that the officer who shot Jabez was the real victim.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: Jabez has been dehumanized at every...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: We did submit our written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Araso
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jenna Sharma
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Jackie Gosdigian of Brooklyn Defender Services testifies that constant NYPD presence makes many residents feel unsafe. She supports shifting resources away from policing and towards community centers, programming, and Cure Violence organizations.
chapters.title: Jackie Gosdigian testifies on Brooklyn Defenders and policing poverty

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: My name is Jackie Guzdigian, and I am Senior Supervising Policy Counsel with Brooklyn Defender Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: I want to thank the Council, Chair Felice, Chair Brewer, for holding this critical hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: New Yorkers of all ages want to feel safe, and while some have called for increased policing to address the perception of safety in the city, the people we represent often report that the constant presence of NYPD in their neighborhoods has contributed to why they feel unsafe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: Their movements and relationships in the community and on social media are surveilled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: They are stopped and frisked outside their homes, required to walk through metal detectors in their schools, and are confronted by armed NYPD officers who distrust them simply because they are black or Latin and live in low-income communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: The launch of the Office of Community Safety marked an important first step toward ensuring the communities are met with care, not criminalization, and that strategies to interrupt and prevent violence meet the needs of communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: The Council has the opportunity to strengthen the programs and services that work to keep New Yorkers safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: Policing poverty stands in the way of making New York more affordable because it acts as a force of economic destabilization for low-income communities and siphons resources away from them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: The city should also consider shifting resources away from policing alleged gang or crew members and toward providing the support that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: individuals, families, and communities need to thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: Specifically, we advocate for an increase in funding for community centers, high quality and engaging programming, and organizations using the Cure Violence model.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: NYPD has spent more than $1 billion in military-grade surveillance resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: This mass collection of data from low-income communities of color is used to justify increased police presence in these neighborhoods and represents NYPD's technical justification for broken windows policing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: NYPD's criminal group database is a striking example of how law enforcement data collection leads to harm by systematically wrapping up more youth in the criminal legal system and separating them from their families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: This is why we support Intro 460 and are calling for the complete abolition of the criminal group database.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gosdigian
utterances.text: We hope to see the Office of Community Safety contribute to a shift in resources and approaches, and we thank the Council.

chapters.summary: Rosalind Morrison, Senior Attorney at the Legal Aid Society, testifies about the importance of CMS organizations like Life Camp and 100 Suits. She calls for more investment in CMS, schools, and programs for youth who are not in school.
chapters.title: Rosalind Morrison testifies on Legal Aid and CMS organizations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: I appreciate the opportunity to testify here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: I am Rosalind Morrison, Senior Attorney in the Community Justice Unit of the Legal Aid Society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: CJU was established in 2011 as part of the New York City's Task Force to Combat Gun Violence to serve as a primary legal provider for the city's community violence intervention programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: I've had the honor of being a public defender for over 20 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: While it is important to deal with the current realities, we must also build programs that form the infrastructure to future greatness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: Schools provide a great opportunity to engage our youth, help them see that they have something to live for, and provide them with the tools they need to not only survive but thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: We must also look to engage young people who have aged out of school or no longer go to school because they also need stability and support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: CJU partners with the city CMS system, which is a citywide network of community-based organizations to create healthier and safer communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: CMS organizations are vital to community safety and embody the wisdom that those closest to the issues will have solutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: For example, Life Camp, a CMS organization that developed a tree of life approach, they work to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: Prevent harm before it escalates by understanding and addressing the reasons behind a young person's actions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: In their safe corridor program, violence interrupters accompany youth concerned for their safety to and from school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: They also provide mediation and other interventions to address conflict and connect young people with support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: 100 Suits and King of King Foundations are other CMS organizations that provide ground support to youth throughout Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: What can the city council do to make communities safer?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: More investment in CMS organizations so that they're able to expand their work throughout the boroughs and also increase their work in schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: Just one more sentence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: Schools must also receive additional investments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: We must also bridge the gap to include youths who are not going to school through programs such as summer youth programs and anti-gun violence employment program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: Ultimately, the solution to community violence is in the description.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: We must lean into creating community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: And a substantial part of the city's budget can fund and invest in vision and imagination to create and implement these community building programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: I'm going to be submitting a complete written submission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosalind Morrison
utterances.text: Oh, thank you.

chapters.summary: Christina Sparrock, a mental health advocate and researcher, shares her lived experience of a police wellness check during which she feared for her life. She calls for fully funding a Department of Community Safety and using 988, EMTs, and peers instead of police.
chapters.title: Christina Sparrock testifies on mental health crisis response and police fear

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: Dear Chair Feliz and members, City Council members, my name is Christina Sparrow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: I'm a mental health advocate and an alternative crisis response researcher at the Disability Justice Program at New York Lawyers for the Public Interest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: Due to affordable housing, unaffordable housing, rising health care premiums, Medicaid cuts, unlivable wages, increased gun violence, worsening of climate change, and fear of global war, mental health crisis will worsen in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: We are all vulnerable and seconds away of a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: Mental health crisis response reform is necessary to help decriminalize people with mental health conditions, reduce city liabilities, save taxpayer dollars, and more importantly, save lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: I speak from lived experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: The stigma that I face every day is influenced by the systems that I go through.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: And police officers whose training primarily focused on crime should not be mental health crisis responders at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: When I'm in a crisis, I'm always afraid of police, always afraid of sirens, always afraid of everything involving police.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: During my wellness check in 2020, police pounded on my door, unannounced, to my apartment door.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: I believed it was a violent intruder because I didn't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: So what I immediately did was grab the knife in my kitchen because I was afraid of someone barging into my door.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: It's COVID.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: People were dying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: People were getting killed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: I was in my home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: If my door was unlocked, I would have been dead like Eleanor Bumper, Deborah Danner, Wynne Rosario, Kowalski-Trowick.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: I would have been dead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: in my own home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: This is why we don't need police responding to our homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: We need crisis response workers like EMT workers and peers with lived experience responding to wellness checks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: I could have died, anyone could have died.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: What would you have done if someone was pounding on your door?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: As a New York City,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: In other states and municipalities throughout the country are changing crisis response to compassionate and culturally responsive care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: It's important that we understand language matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: I am the one that changed the terminology from emotionally disturbed person to person experiencing emotional crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: Language matters when we describe people with mental health concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: In addition to that, I asked that we...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: I ask that we fully fund a Department of Community Safety and also follow the outline and proposals that CCIT NYC has of using 988, not police, EMTs and peers, culturally responsive community-based care,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: and have oversight committee with peers, 51% peers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Sparrock
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ruth Lowenkron of New York Lawyers for the Public Interest testifies on transforming mental health crisis response. She criticizes Intro 403 for not sufficiently limiting police involvement and calls for utilizing peers with lived experience as responders.
chapters.title: Ruth Lowenkron testifies on Daniel's Law and mental health crisis reform

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: My name is Ruth Lowen-Kron, also with the Disability Justice Program at New York Lawyers for the Public Interest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: Our office has worked on mental health justice for over 50 years and has worked in the area of what we call transforming mental health crisis response for the last 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: It's a major priority for us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: We're staunch members of Correct Crisis Intervention Today and the Daniels Law Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: My primary testimony is devoted to INT 403, which we think is a good step in the right direction, but we have a number of qualms about it and hope to speak with Council Member Ressler about it further.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: Before I say anything, though, I think it's really important to note there has been a lot of use of the word safety, a lot of use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: The whole topic of the hearing is called reducing violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: And I want to make it absolutely clear that may be appropriate for a lot of the things that were discussed today, but it is wholly inappropriate when we're talking about issues of mental health crisis and individuals with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: mental health diagnoses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: The statistics are such that people with mental health diagnoses are no more likely to be violent than people who don't have such a diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: You would think absolutely otherwise from everything you hear, and this august body should not be perpetrating that concept that we need to be saved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: From people with mental disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: I want to point out that the way to transform mental health crisis can be found in Daniel's Law,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: S3670, A4617, and it is crucial, as some of my fellow panelists have said, we have had people dying and near death at the hands of the police and in their own homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: Since 2015 alone and in New York City alone, we have had 24 individuals, primarily people of color, killed at the hands of police.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: So we want to look towards that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: It's being supported by council members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: If I can have just one more minute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: No, not one more minute, quickly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: Councilmember Epstein, Mayor Mamdani have supported Daniel's law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: Public Advocate is directly aligned with us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: And really critically, we don't have that piece of removing police except in the rarest circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: In INT 403.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: In fact, there says there's no limitation on NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: There is a coordination with law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: That's not the way to do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: The way to do it is to utilize peers, those with lived mental health experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: INT 403 has a much more vague sense of just having individuals who possess the requisite training and experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: That's insufficient, inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: Limit police, and that's the way to go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ruth Lowenkron
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you, everyone, for testifying today.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Leo Ferguson, Donovan Tavares, Daphne Tamasila, Mehta Rahman, and Michael Sositsky.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You may begin when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We'll start from left to right.

chapters.summary: Leo Ferguson of Jews for Racial and Economic Justice testifies in support of a Department of Community Safety. He argues that hate violence has risen even as overall crime declined and calls for investment in data-driven hate violence prevention and community-based reporting.
chapters.title: Leo Ferguson testifies on JFREJ and hate violence prevention

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: Good afternoon, chairs and council members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: My name is Leo Ferguson, and I am the scholar in residence at Jews for Racial and Economic Justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: I am testifying on behalf of our organization and our partners in the NYC Against Hate Violence Coalition in support of creating a Department of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: Jay Fridge wants a Department of Community Safety because we need to change how New York thinks about safety, away from policing and towards the kind of evidence-based, public health-driven solutions that are so much more effective in preventing violence and keeping New Yorkers safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: In the area that we focus on, hate violence prevention, the inability of police to address this crisis is reflected in the terrible statistics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: Hate violence has climbed even as overall crime has declined.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: Anti-Muslim and anti-Jewish hate crimes are up with hate crime up 12.9% overall.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: The existing carceral approach inherited from prior administrations is an abject failure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: This is what led J-Fridge and a coalition of community-based organizations representing a diverse array of New Yorkers to fight in 2019 for the creation of the Office to Prevent Hate Crimes for the Hate Violence Prevention Initiative, which funded community-based prevention for the first time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: and now for the creation of a durable Department of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: We need a partner in government to invest in and scale data-driven evidence-based approaches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: to hate violence prevention, and we need the city to finally demonstrate the vision and competence to implement a single, coherent strategy for reducing violence that sets clear metrics for success and remains accountable to those metrics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: The best available research shows that cooperation between groups reduces hostility and violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: To be successful, the city's strategy should resource intergroup collaborative projects that bring neighbors together around mutual shared interests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: We need to equip ordinary New Yorkers with the tools to keep themselves and their neighbors safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: De-escalation and bystander training should be scaled up and integrated into a targeted, data-driven citywide strategy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: We need to give New Yorkers greater diversity reporting channels, better coordination between agencies and community organizations, and robust access to victim services and restorative justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: And finally, we need to replace inherently flawed NYPD reporting with statistically accurate neighborhood surveys.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: We are committed to partnering with OPHC and hopefully soon DCS on a new strategy for community safety that recognizes that hate violence can't be policed or punished away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: Creating real safety for New Yorkers will require rigor, vision, and long-term investment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leo Ferguson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for the opportunity to testify.

chapters.summary: Donovan Tavares of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund testifies that expanding policing does not make communities safer. He calls for sustained investment in credible messengers, violence prevention workers, and restorative justice, and for OCS to expand its role in school safety.
chapters.title: Donovan Tavares testifies on NAACP LDF and community safety investments

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Felice, Chair Brewers, and members of the Public Safety and GovOps committees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: My name is Donovan Tavares, and I'm a community organizer at the NAACP Legal Defense Fund.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: And on behalf of LDF, we want to thank you for the opportunity to testify on matters as important as our public safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: For decades, LDF has challenged law enforcement violence and racial discrimination against black communities, and through this work we have seen that expanding policing, surveillance, and enforcement does not make our communities safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: And too often, these approaches deepen the very harms they claim to address.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: New York City has an opportunity to choose a different path here through the creation of the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: But the Office of Community Safety cannot simply be another office on an organizational chart.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: If it is going to fulfill its promise, it must be adequately resourced and empowered to invest in the people, relationships, and institutions that communities have been telling us they have needed for generations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: That means sustained investment in credible messengers, violence prevention workers, community-based organizations, youth programming, and restorative justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: It means recognizing credible messengers as essential public safety professionals, providing them with living wages and meaningful workplace protections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: LDF's Thurgood Marshall Institute has found that even with enhanced compensation for community responders, the cities could save $120.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: million annually.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: It also means expanding OCS's role in school and youth safety, investing in restorative justice and mental health supports, and working toward a transition away from policing and surveillance in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: For too long, black and brown communities have experienced over-policing alongside generations of disenfranchisement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: We cannot continue to criminalize our communities while neglecting the resources they need to thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: New York City should not measure public safety by how much policing it can deploy, but by whether people have what they need to learn, live, heal, and thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Tavares
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Daphne Tomasula of the Asian American Federation testifies about the Hope Against Hate campaign and PATH initiative. She urges the city to invest in culturally and linguistically competent community organizations and involve advocates in structural changes.
chapters.title: Daphne Tomasula testifies on Asian American Federation and PATH

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Felice and Chair Brewer, for providing the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: My name is Daphne Tomasula, the Associate Director of Programs from the Asian American Federation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: I'm testifying today as part of the NYC Against Hate Violence Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: For our communities, safety goes beyond policing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: AAF launched the Hope Against Hate campaign in 2021 and joined the PATH initiative to expand our community safety efforts to respond to anti-Asian violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: Through PATH, we work with organizations whose trained volunteers provide safety accompaniment, maintain a protective presence in neighborhoods, and connect residents to support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: In 2026 alone, through funding from OPHC, our partners distributed nearly 9,000 safety resources, trained 479 community members, hosted over 100 outreach events, and provided over 1,000 protective services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: We're encouraged by the city's recent commitment to increasing OPHC funding by $26 million and doubling PATH funding to $6.4 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: Bringing OPHC under the Office of Community Safety recognizes that hate violence prevention is part of a broader, coordinated approach to keeping New Yorkers safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: Although we support establishing a new Department of Community Safety, before establishing, we urge the Council to meaningfully engage organizations and advocates before pursuing structural changes,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: ensuring that the experiences and needs of communities most impacted by violence are reflected in decision-making.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: Recognize and build upon the work already underway through OCS, including its coordination of violence prevention programs and increased investment in

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: community-based safety initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: Sustain and expand direct funding for culturally and linguistically competent organizations that are already providing trusted non-police approaches to violence prevention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: And ensure that increased investments reach frontline organizations, including nonprofits that have historically faced barriers to accessing city funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: As the city considers the future of its community safety infrastructure, we must ensure that existing partnerships, investments, and progress are not overlooked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: Our priorities should remain on strengthening the trusted community programs New Yorkers already rely on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daphne Tomasula
utterances.text: Thank you for your leadership and opportunity to testify.

chapters.summary: Meida Rahman of the NYCLU testifies that the city must invest in credible messengers and violence prevention programs. She calls for ending broken windows policing, passing the Curb Act, and abolishing the NYPD criminal group database.
chapters.title: Meida Rahman testifies on NYCLU and community-based violence prevention

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Meida Rahman and I'm testifying on behalf of the New York Civil Liberties Union.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: For far too long, New York City has relied on policing and criminalization as a solution to community safety issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: This approach fails to address the underlying causes of violence and disproportionately targets black and brown New Yorkers, entangling them with the criminal legal system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: The creation of the Office of Community Safety is an important step towards a vision of public safety that prioritizes prevention and support rather than policing and penalization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: The city must continue to invest in the relationships, resources, and conditions that actually keep communities safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: Credible messengers, violence interrupters, and violence prevention programs play a critical role in addressing violence and preventing crimes before they happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: These programs help build trusted community relationships that address violence, resolve conflicts, and support young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: Unlike police, community-based interventions aim to address the underlying causes of violence, reducing the potential for future harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: Understanding that violence is not one-dimensional and can often be connected to various factors such as poverty, trauma, substance abuse, mental health crisis, and inequality,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: these programs can offer targeted solutions and connect community members with the resources that best meet their needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: Research has already shown positive results from these programs, including significant reductions in gun violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: However, the success of these programs depends on broader policy alignment across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: Any attempts to further community safety through OCS will only be effective if coupled with efforts to curb aggressive and racist policing tactics and policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: This requires, at the least, an end to broken windows policing, passage of the Curb Act, and abolition of the NYPD criminal group database.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: These tactics, which allow the NYPD to surveil, harass, and criminalize everyday New Yorkers, do nothing to enhance community safety and, in fact, make communities less safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meida Rahman
utterances.text: The NYCLU thanks the committee for the opportunity to provide testimony and for recognizing the need for non-police solutions to violence and community safety issues.

chapters.summary: Michael Sosnick of the NYCLU testifies specifically on Intro 403. He urges the council to clearly articulate where a new Department of Community Safety assumes primary responsibility from the NYPD, warning against creating new enforcement patrols.
chapters.title: Michael Sosnick testifies on NYCLU concerns with Intro 403

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sosnick
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sosnick
utterances.text: I'm Michael Sositsky with the NYCLU.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sosnick
utterances.text: I'll focus my comments more specifically on Intro 403.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sosnick
utterances.text: While we share the goals of both the administration and the sponsor in establishing non-carcereal approaches to meeting the needs of New Yorkers, we urge the council to take the time necessary to get the structure and the powers of this new department right as it considers the legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sosnick
utterances.text: For a DCS to succeed, it must not merely replicate past failed outreach efforts that have primarily functioned only to remove already vulnerable and marginalized populations from public view without providing them with the supports that they need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sosnick
utterances.text: To that end, we have substantial reservations about any legislative proposal that would establish new patrol units within a proposed DCS, which, regardless of how well intended, run the risk of being transformed into a new enforcement arm for so-called quality of life issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sosnick
utterances.text: A DCS that is seen as perpetuating broken window style tactics, just with different enforcers, will quickly lose credibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sosnick
utterances.text: And along those lines, it's essential that the statutory authority of a new DCS very clearly articulate where DCS is assuming primary responsibility when intersecting with other city agencies, including and especially the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sosnick
utterances.text: In her testimony before the Council's executive budget hearing earlier this year, Commissioner Tisch indicated that the NYPD had had no discussions about, and apparently no intention of, transferring any responsibilities from the NYPD to OCS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sosnick
utterances.text: The success or failure of the current OCS and any future DCS

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sosnick
utterances.text: will depend on whether either can actually effectuate the removal of crisis response from the NYPD, an agency that was never designed for and, as it has demonstrated time and time again, will never be appropriate for such a role.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sosnick
utterances.text: Without a clear and explicit transfer of specific responsibilities away from the NYPD, which is something that is currently missing from Intro 403, DCS will be unable to fulfill its goal of actually providing a real and better alternative to our current approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sosnick
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you all for testifying today.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Next, we're going to call...

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Rabbi Jason Kleehan via Zoom, also Ray Switlik, Mariama Bach, Bayadir Mohamed Osman, and Nahiyan from the Muslim Community Network.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Glover
utterances.text: Excuse me, did a lot of these people pre-register?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Glover
utterances.text: Because I was here since 1 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: They pre-registered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Glover
utterances.text: I need to get my testimony finished.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Glover
utterances.text: My name is Crystal Glover.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Yeah, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Glover
utterances.text: I'm seeing testifying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Glover
utterances.text: They just came in all late and everything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Glover
utterances.text: I have to get out of here.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Yeah, everyone who's testifying, they registered.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So if you haven't already, you need to speak with them.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: All right, so you should be on the list.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: By the other is peeing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: She's coming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: She had to pop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: But she's literally here.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Okay, so you could start and then she could testify when they get here.

chapters.summary: Nahiyan, a program manager at Muslim Community Network, testifies about culturally specific domestic violence education. She shares a quote from a participant and argues that prevention is safety, calling for investment in community-based services.
chapters.title: Nahiyan testifies on Muslim Community Network and gender-based violence

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: Hi everyone, my name is Nahian and I'm a program manager at Muslim Community Network and today we are here in support of the Department of Community Safety and making sure that we sustain its culturally specific work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: At MCN we focus on culturally specific community education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: Domestic violence is an extremely taboo topic in Muslim communities, yet MCN has reached over 500 women over 23 workshops last fiscal year through our Healthy Relationships workshops.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: So what does that tell us?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: Culturally competent care works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: It's not that our communities don't need this information, they just don't know how to access it or have spaces to help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: In many of our workshops, women finally feel comfortable to share their stories for the first time, and that sharing is the first step in getting help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: When we empower women with the skills to recognize unhealthy relationships, understand their rights, and support one another, that's how we combat gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: One woman said, the problem is that we do not know our rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: If we know our rights and are educated, most of us will not remain in unhealthy situations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: By creating this department, we're finally acknowledging what communities have been saying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: Prevention is safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: When we rely primarily on police to respond to domestic violence, we're responding after harm has already occurred, rather than trying to prevent that harm in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: And for black and brown communities that have historically experienced harm at the hands of police, calling the police is always not a safe or accessible option.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: That's why this office must prioritize prevention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: invest in community-based services, and ensure that culturally specific care is accessible to all of New York's diverse communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: We also need to recognize that gender-based violence doesn't live in a silo.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: It's a gun violence issue, a mental health issue, and a community safety issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: They're all connected, which is why bringing all of these offices together keeps our community safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: And if I had more time, I would tell you so many stories of gender-based violence cases that are tied to mental health and gun violence in all of these.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: I want to leave you with just one final quote from one of the women in our program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: We are passionate about this work because a woman died in our community from physical abuse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: She complained for so long, and she was told to be patient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: She had so many health issues and ended up dying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: That really woke my community up to speak about DV.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: We need a part two to this workshop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nahiyan
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Rae Switlik of the Center for Anti-Violence Education testifies as a self-defense instructor. She describes safety planning for survivors and calls for continued funding of NGBV and community-based gender-based violence education.
chapters.title: Rae Switlik testifies on Center for Anti-Violence Education and self-defense

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: Hello, Council Members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: I appreciate your focus and attention as we begin our Friday evening together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: My name is Rae Switlik, and I am here to speak from my role as Program Manager of Empowerment Self-Defense at the Center for Anti-Violence Education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: As a self-defense instructor, a harrowing part of my job is listening to first-hand accounts from survivors in order for them to regain a sense of agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: Some of these conversations require safety planning for folks who come to CAE after already pursuing orders of protection and other legal recourse and still seeking some sense of safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: This is common in cases of domestic violence, intimate partner violence, stalking, sexual assault, rape, and other gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: When it comes to gender-based and sexual violence, the solution cannot be through law enforcement alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: That process exposes survivors to risk of further harm without sufficient resolution or protection for them moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: There must also be comprehensive community-based initiatives providing easily accessible support and education specific to the various needs of communities across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: Through our work partnered with other community-based organizations, CAE provides these resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: I have personally facilitated trainings on gender-based violence education to various cultural and religious groups, LGBTQIA plus communities, folks with developmental and physical disabilities, human trafficking survivors, at-risk youth,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: health care workers, employees of critical aid organizations, and many.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: other New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: In the wake of renewed public concern about sexual assault, I've been working with our team to bring expansive consent and sexual violence response programming to high school and university students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: From the feedback I've been receiving, these resources are widely and urgently needed, yet insufficiently funded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: New Yorkers deserve access to trainings, rapid response, and ongoing care within their own communities that is attuned to their unique needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: We need continued funding and city support to make that happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: OCS has been a great step in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: When I teach about gender-based violence, an often overlooked aspect is isolation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: We're all safer when we come together, and I urge you to support funding of NGBV to continue to make this happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rae Switlik
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Bayadir Mohamed Osman of Muslim Community Network shares a personal family experience with mental health and gender-based violence. She urges the city to protect and fund trusted community organizations so families do not have to navigate fragmented systems alone.
chapters.title: Bayadir Mohamed Osman testifies on mental health and family support

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: My name is Bayat and Muhammad Ismail, and I'm here representing the Muslim Community Network.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: Mental health is the center of the issues being discussed today, from violence to hate to gender-based violence, trauma, recovery, and healing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: We cannot address these challenges without addressing mental well-being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: I want to share a personal experience with you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: A young member of my family began hurting herself and those around her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: We could have taken what was deemed the easiest route and called the police.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: Instead, our family chose compassion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: We connected her with counseling, social services, and medication.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: Today, she is doing well and healthy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: Only later did we learn that she had been sexually abused and experienced gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: What we initially saw as troubling behavior was connected to a trauma she had experienced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: I want to emphasize that this burden should never fall entirely on families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: We had to navigate a complicated and fragmented system to help find...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: What she needed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: A comprehensive department could have helped identify these needs earlier, coordinated the services instead of having immigrant families do that, ensuring that the families don't have to figure it all out on their own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: At Muslim Community Network, we know that trusted, culturally responsive community organizations are the first place people turn to help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: They need to be recognized, supported, and adequately funded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: I urge the city to protect this department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: Because families should not have to net.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: navigate a broken system to save someone they love.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: The support should have been there before the crisis even happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayadir Mohamed Osman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And also we have Rabbi Jason Kleehan via Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin when you're ready.

chapters.summary: Rabbi Jason Klein of Jews for Racial and Economic Justice testifies in support of a Department of Community Safety. He uses a Torah portion about hospitality to argue that resources to address hate violence are already available and should be invested in prevention.
chapters.title: Rabbi Jason Klein testifies on JFREJ and hate violence prevention

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: Good afternoon, chairs, council members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: My name is Rabbi Jason Klein.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: I live on the Lower East Side of Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: I'm a member of Jews for Racial and Economic Justice, JFREDGE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: I'm testifying on behalf of us and our partners in New York City against hate violence coalition in support of creating this department, community safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: Tomorrow, synagogues around the world read the Torah portion called Vayera, a text whose through line is hospitality and the gravity of sins against hospitality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: The Parsha opens with a divine imperative to welcome guests and continues with the story of a mother and her son who are experiencing homelessness in the scorching desert.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
