utterances.text: The mother can barely look at her son, who is at immediate risk of dehydration, bursts into tears.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: The text tells us that God opened her eyes and she saw a well of water and the boy drank.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: The story reassures us that even in the direst times, the resources to give life and well-being are already there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: We need to only look for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: The awful news is that in New York City, the incidence of hate crimes against Jewish, Muslim, Black, trans New Yorkers has continued to rise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: Yet the good news for our city is that this is one of those dire times when the answers are right here in front of us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: We have heard already today about the details of the social psychology research that has been done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: The evidence is already here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: And we are thankful for the mayor for allocating $29 million for hate crime prevention in all forms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: The well of nourishing water is available and abundant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: We need a Department of Community Safety to proactively center public health for every resident and guest of the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: We know that investing in prevention is more effective than more policing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: As an alumnus of Columbia University, who has been somewhat ashamed of his alma mater's lack of hospitality to its own scholars in recent years,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: I cannot help but imagine an alternative history in which demonstrations with the encampments led the university to call a well-staffed, thoughtful, and permanent department of communities.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: The time has expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: To provide campus with different kinds of opportunities for de-escalation, dialogue, resources in response to those moments rather than military display.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabbi Jason Klein
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you everyone for testifying.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: The next panel, Preston Davis.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Rana Abdel-Hanid, Dina Hadhoud, Rasha Harvey, Charlotte Manwood.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Run it left.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: All right, thank you for joining us.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin when you're ready.

chapters.summary: Dina Hadhoud of the anti-violence nonprofit Malika testifies about providing de-escalation and bystander intervention training across the city. She cites statistics on why survivors do not call police and urges deeper stakeholder input in creating a Department of Community Safety.
chapters.title: Dina Hadhoud testifies on Malika and survivor-centered safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: My name is Dina Hadhood, and I'm the director of programs at an anti-violence and wellness nonprofit called Malika.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: In my role, I've had the privilege of connecting with at least 100 community organizations, public schools, and places of worship across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: To hear about their safety concerns, and offer de-escalatory self-defense and bystander intervention skills to support thousands of New Yorkers in feeling more confident to move around New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: We've seen firsthand how different communities across the five boroughs have different needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: It's also clear that our most vulnerable community members, especially those who are domestic violence survivors, immigrants, and black and brown community members often don't feel comfortable going to the police.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: In 2021, the National Domestic Violence Hotline served survivors who called the police for help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: 55% believed they were discriminated against by the police, 25% were threatened with arrest, and 12% were arrested despite having identified as the victim in the situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: With this, it's no wonder that 92% of survivors who didn't call the police was because they were afraid or concerned about how the police would react.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: Survivors come to organizations like ours after they experience gender and hate-based violence when they don't feel comfortable involving the police or formally reporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: Due to these gaps, the city data is deeply inaccurate, but the stories and need for survivor resources are so, so real.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: Our organizations on the ground are often best equipped to provide trusted care that truly meets people where they're at.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: That's why we're so grateful to work with OPHC under the Community Safety Office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: We support increased investment and urge that the creation of a Department of Community Safety seeks deeper stakeholder input in ideation and implementation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dina Hadhoud
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Charlotte Manwood, a musician and constituent in Upper Manhattan, testifies about street homelessness and drug use near New York Presbyterian Hospital. She calls for a fully funded Department of Community Safety without police co-response to mental health calls.
chapters.title: Charlotte Manwood testifies on street homelessness and police response

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Manwood
utterances.text: Good afternoon, co-chairs Brewer and Feliz and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Manwood
utterances.text: My name is Charlotte and I'm a working musician and constituent of Councilmember de la Rosa in Upper Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Manwood
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity for members of the community to give testimony regarding safety in this city that we love.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Manwood
utterances.text: My neighborhood is Washington Heights, and if you're familiar with the area around New York Presbyterian Hospital, you'll know that there is an unusually high population of street drug users and chronically homeless folks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Manwood
utterances.text: Some of my homeless neighbors have been hanging out and breaking down in the 168th Street subway stop for as long as I've lived in the neighborhood, which began in early 2021.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Manwood
utterances.text: Study after study finds that poverty and untreated mental illness are the primary underlying contributors to street drug use and homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Manwood
utterances.text: Despite this research, New York's first line of quote-unquote treatment for these issues is a police response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Manwood
utterances.text: The police have a disastrous and sometimes deadly track record with regard to escalating situations that involve mental health and addiction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Manwood
utterances.text: Yet officers are still dispatched to respond first and sometimes as the only response to 911 calls involving mental health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Manwood
utterances.text: Earlier this year, in the case of Jabez Chakraborty, police response to a 911 call requesting medical assistance culminated in Jabez being shot four times in the chest while he was experiencing a mental health crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Manwood
utterances.text: The New York City of the 21st century has no place for police violence toward New Yorkers, which is why I'm speaking in support of establishing and fully funding a permanent Department of Community Safety without a police co-response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Manwood
utterances.text: My neighbors and I deserve to be able to call for medical help without fearing misunderstanding or potentially deadly escalation of the situation by responding officers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Manwood
utterances.text: With the creation of a Department of Community Safety, New York City has the opportunity to separate the threat of police violence from its care response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Manwood
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Rashe Harvey, a resident of Forest Hills, testifies that community safety is a public good that comes from investing in conditions and relationships, not adding police. She supports a permanent and fully funded Department of Community Safety.
chapters.title: Rashe Harvey testifies on investing in community safety over policing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairs Feliz and Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: My name is Rashe Harvey.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: I'm a resident of Forest Hills, Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: Today, I'm here in coalition with fellow New Yorkers to build community safety through prevention, not policing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: Community safety is a public good.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: We do not make our communities safer by adding more police.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: We build safety together by investing in the conditions, institutions, and relationships that prevent harm, meets people's needs, and allow our communities to thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: For decades, New York City has relied on policing to respond to social issues such as poverty, homelessness, and mental health crises.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: But these problems cannot be solved through arrests and incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: We need public investments that address their underlying causes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: I think about the generational trauma black New Yorkers have endured, especially black men, at the hands of our current system not fit for humane public safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: For example,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: The rapid rise in NYPD excessive force complaints cost our city real dollars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: We're talking about over $100 million in settlements in 2025 alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: That real money, it's real money, should be invested in the material needs of our people, not city-funded police violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: Building safer communities requires us to rethink what public safety means and who is responsible for providing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: By shifting

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: resources towards prevention, care, and community-led outcomes, we can create approaches to safety that meets people's needs without exposing them to further harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: As a proud New York City resident, I support the creation of a permanent and fully funded Department of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rashe Harvey
utterances.text: Thank you for taking the time to listen, and I appreciate the Council and Administration's work on this bill.

chapters.summary: Preston Davis testifies about trauma and the need to break cycles of police violence. He calls for a permanent Department of Community Safety with authority to bring together mental health experts, violence prevention workers, and peers.
chapters.title: Preston Davis testifies on trauma and need for Department of Community Safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Brewer and Felice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: My name is Preston Davis, and I'm here speaking for a permanent Department of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: Trauma unaddressed is a dangerous thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: For those of us who suffer from it, we recreate it in our other relationships, poisoning them, and thus continuing a vicious cycle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: Our city's relationship with the police is no different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: Millions of our neighbors cannot afford to live in our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: Which makes them more likely to be targeted by police policies and have interactions with officers trained for command and force that have often ended with deadly force.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: Then police leadership refuses to take responsibility for the harm said violence has caused.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: Leaving victims without justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: or support and are then forced to continue to struggle in a city they cannot afford.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: And thus the cycle continues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: The only way to break this cycle is to do something different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: An alternative to the carceral system that claims so many lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: For our city, that alternative is a permanent department of community safety,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: a department that has given the authority to bring together the experts on mental health, violence prevention, and non-police crisis response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: A department given the resources to plan the city's responses to these things with community peers and organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: A department given the mandate to lead the city's crisis response to mental health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: Only then will we have the chance to heal, to break these vicious cycles, and to live.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Preston Davis
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Next, we'll call Brandon Lode, Sarita Daftari.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: A.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Sutton, Haidara, James Innes.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Also, we'll call Loris Weintraub, Christine Noel.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Alba, Laureano.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We have one more seat left.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Mariam Shouai.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Actually, we have one more seat left.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So, Julio Cesar Herrera.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Not here.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Lloyd, Cambridge.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Nicholas Pearson.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: All right, we have a full panel.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You can begin when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We'll start again from left to right.

chapters.summary: Aisha Soumahoro of the Bronx Community Justice Center testifies about Neighborhood Stat and Save Our Streets. She calls for treating community organizers and credible messengers as essential public safety workers with fair compensation and stable funding.
chapters.title: Aisha Soumahoro testifies on Bronx Community Justice Center and CMS funding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairs Felice and Brewer and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: My name is Aisha Suhaidara.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: I'm the Senior Program Manager of Community Initiatives at Bronx Community Justice Center and Initiative of the Center for Justice Innovation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: So our neighborhood safety initiatives support Neighborhood Stat, a resident-driven initiative across 30 NYCHES developments that empowers residents to identify safety concerns and work alongside government and community partners to develop solutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: Whether through improvements to public spaces, youth programming, or expanded opportunities for community engagement, this work recognizes that residents themselves are essential partners in creating safer neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: Save Our Streets complements this approach through direct gun violence intervention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: Using a public health model, SOS employs credible messengers with deep community ties to mediate conflicts, interrupt cycles of retaliation, and connect young people with support services and opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: Both programs demonstrate that effective violence prevention depends on trust, sustained relationships, and the expertise of the people closest to the challenges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: But these relationships cannot be built overnight, and they cannot be sustained through short-term funding alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: For too long, community-based organizations have been expected to address deeply entrenched challenges while navigating unstable funding, delayed payments, and limited resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: So we encourage the city to treat community organizers, credible messengers, outreach workers, and other community-based organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: practitioners as essential public safety workforce with fair compensation, professional development, and opportunities for advancement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: We also urge OCS to strengthen contracting and payment processes so that providers can focus on developing services, delivering services, sorry, rather than managing financial uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: We applaud the administration's initial investments and encourage the city council to advocate for increased, sustained, and flexible funding that represents the scale of OCS's mission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: And if we believe that community-based approaches are essential to public safety, then we must fund them as essential public safety infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aisha Soumahoro
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

chapters.summary: Christine Noel of the 67th Precinct Clergy Council (God Squad) testifies about the PATH initiative. She describes their Another Way program and urges continued expansion of community-led hate crime prevention funding.
chapters.title: Christine Noel testifies on 67th Precinct Clergy Council and PATH

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: Good afternoon and thank you for the opportunity to share.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: My name is Christine Noel and I represent the 67th Precinct Clergy Council known as the God Squad, serving as an anchor organization for Partners Against the Hate in partnership with the New York Office for Prevention of Hate Crimes, now under the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: PAXSS is rooted in one simple truth, prevention begins with connection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: Bringing OPHC into the Office of Community Safety recognizes that hate prevention must be a broader coordinated strategy to prevent violence and protect New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: Through this initiative, we currently support eight community-based vendors and have seed grants to cover 10 organizations and counting representing black and brown communities across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: Together in FY26, we transform funding into meaningful action and partnerships through over 370 hyperlocal events consisting of educational programs,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: impacting over 5,000 youth and teens, community dialogue, safety know your rights training, cultural experiences, and community of over five and collected over 500 hate crime surveys.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: Each sub-vendor brought their own unique expertise and cultural lens to the work, which creates a safe and trusted space for our residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: An example of programming is our Another Way initiative, dedicated to reducing tension, addressing bias, and promoting unity in ethnically and religiously diverse neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: It seeks to foster dignity, reconciliation, and long-term peace in communities that have experienced historical and ongoing divides.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: We are not simply responding to hate after harm occurs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: We are proactively educating communities, creating safe spaces for dialogue, building relationships across differences, and helping all understand how to recognize and address hate and bias.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: PATH is more than a calendar of programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: It really is a movement of partnerships rooted in empathy and the belief that every community deserves to feel safe, seen, and respected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: Doubling PATH funding to $6.4 million is a greater investment in our capacity and will allow God Squad and other community partners already doing the work to strengthen prevention response efforts and expand survivor support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: One last thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: As we look ahead, we ask that you continue and expand investing in community-led prevention because when we invest in communities, we really invest in a safer and more connected New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Noel
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Lori Weintrob, Executive Director of the Wagner College Holocaust Center, testifies about their youth education programs on hate and anti-Semitism. She says more resources mean more young people equipped to stand up to prejudice and asks for expansion to all boroughs.
chapters.title: Lori Weintrob testifies on Wagner College Holocaust Center and hate prevention

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: Is it on?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: Education is our city's first defense against hate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: I testify on behalf of the Wagner College Holocaust Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: Our mission is to empower a new generation with courage, empathy, and ethical leadership to combat anti-Semitism, racism, and prejudice in all forms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: This work relies on critical school and district attorney partnerships, vital funding from the Office for the Prevention of Hate Crimes, and foundational support from our City Council person, Majority Whip Camila Hanks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: My name is Lori Weintraub, and as Executive Director, I can tell you that this investment drives community safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: We have reached over 35,000 youth of all faiths in 12 years, connecting them with survivors of the Holocaust and of the Tutsi genocide in Rwanda.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: Students in our Youth Stand Up to Hate programs analyze how hate escalates and how interfaith alliances enable resilience and hope using peer dialogue, theater, and testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: We link past to present by asking, how are the survivors of the Holocaust received as New York City refugees then, and how do we treat refugees and immigrants today?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: We empower our youth to be upstanders, not bystanders, in the face of rising anti-Semitism and bigotry online and in schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: We deepen this connection by teaching students how to identify, prevent, and report contemporary hate crimes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: We bring OPHC and commissioners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: on human rights representatives into our programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: We are proud that our model combining Holocaust education with cultural competency and interfaith anti-bias work was praised in President Biden's national strategy to counter anti-Semitism and Mayor Montani's municipal strategy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: We are eager to expand this model to all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: More resources mean more young minds equipped to stand up to prejudice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: Let me close with a message from Wagner College's president back in 1938 after Kristallnacht.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: He decried both anti-Semitism and racism on this night of broken glass and challenged Americans to strengthen our democracy, quote, by showing our deep feeling of sympathy for our fellow man.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: Our center is here for that reason, to train ethical leaders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: Thank you for your partnership as we build bridges against hate with support of OCS towards a safer, more empathetic New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lori Weintrob
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Mariam Chabab of the Arab American Association of New York testifies about their PATH anchor work. She says the $1 million grant supports nine sub-organizations and calls for continued investment in community-based hate violence prevention.
chapters.title: Mariam Chabab testifies on Arab American Association and PATH funding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: My name is Miriam Schwab, and I am the coalition organizer at the Arab American Association of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: I want to thank the City Council for giving us the opportunity to share our hate crime prevention work in light of the recent investment in the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: The $26 million investment in the Office of Community Safety has expanded funding for the Office of the Prevention of Hate Crimes and the Partners Against the Hate Forward Initiative.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: As a path anchor organization, the Arab American Association of New York received approximately $1 million to support our work and redistribute funding into nine organizations, investing directly in community-led efforts to address hate violence across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: We are thankful to the Office of Community Safety and the Office for the Prevention of Hate Crimes for our partnership and for continuing to prioritize our community safety across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: Together, we are working to address the lack of visibility of anti-Arab and anti-Muslim hate crimes in NYPD statistics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: The city recognizes that the only right preventative measure to growing hate in our city is to decentralize law enforcement by putting community-based organizations at the center of prevention work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: This investment is going right back to community members where it belongs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: During fiscal year 2026, AAA NY and its sub-anchors engaged in almost 5,000 community members across New York City through community safety initiatives, youth education to combat Islamophobia,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: women's self-defense training, political education, hate and bias prevention, and language accessible app.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: advocacy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: Through programming centered on combating hate violence, centering community safety, our organization's efforts strengthened community engagement, expanded access to culturally and linguistically responsible resources,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: and empowered diverse communities to prevent hate and discrimination and build safer, more inclusive neighborhoods across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: AAA and Y continues to offer drug services to survivors of anti-Muslim hate crimes, such as one that occurred in February, when a woman from Staten Island assaulted three Muslim women, among them a 12-year-old minor on her way home from school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: As hate crimes against our communities continue to rise, it is community-based organizations that initiate solutions that other agencies ignore.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: When community organizations lead this type of work, we know exactly what is needed to make critical information available and accessible to those who need it most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mariam Chabab
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak where we are hopeful that you will continue to support the importance of community-oriented solutions to hate crimes in the city we all call home.

chapters.summary: Nicholas Pearson, a working-class Bronx resident, testifies about his brother who has schizophrenia and is homeless. He supports the idea of specialized responders but warns against sending unarmed workers alone into dangerous situations and asks for law enforcement coordination on calls involving weapons.
chapters.title: Nicholas Pearson testifies on brother's schizophrenia and responder safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: My name is Nicholas Pearson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: I am a working class New Yorker from the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: I am not here as a policy expert.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: I am here as a brother.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: Let me say clearly, this bill has good intentions, the community safety bill, great intentions even.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: The idea that a city this large should have specialized responders for mental health crises, for conflict mediation, for outreach to vulnerable people, that is a good idea.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: I support that idea.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: I want that idea to exist for my brother.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: I have an older brother who is schizophrenic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: As I stand here speaking to you, speaking to this committee, he is wandering the streets with no guidance, no help, no help from my mother, not even from most of my family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: I have gone looking for him.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: I have found him in Washington Square Park, Canal Street, West Village, in the financial district where my brother lives now, on your sidewalks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: I live with one fear above most others, that one day my brother encounters the NYPD in the wrong moment with the wrong object in his hand, and he does not come home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: That fear is why I am here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: That fear is why I actually read this bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: That fear is why I care whether we get this right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: right or we get this catastrophically wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: But I am here to draw a line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: I'm going to draw it plain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: Do not use this department to replace the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: Do not send therapists and bureaucrats alone into the line of fire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: Do not send unarmed city workers to negotiate by themselves with a person who has lost touch with reality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: And who may have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: That is not compassion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: That is a funeral waiting to happen for the responder and for the person in crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: I know because I have fought with my brother.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: I know what can make him snap in a half a second.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: In plain language, this bill makes it so that community safety responders operate with law enforcement, coordination on any call involving a weapon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: I came here today for my brother.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: I want you to make it so that it can save him, because I don't want it to be the reason that it kills a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: therapist or a professional.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Pearson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us and for offering your perspective.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Crystal G., Conrad Blackburn, and Oren.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Chickaster.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Sorry if I mispronounced the last name.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And also, if anyone is here in person and would like to testify, see the sergeant's table in the back.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We're going to move to the Zoom testimonies after this final panel.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So we'll start with Crystal Jean.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you, Crystal, for joining us.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You may begin when you're ready.

chapters.summary: Conrad Blackburn of the Bronx Defenders testifies about clients harmed by police-first response to mental health crises. He shares the story of Ms. P, who was beaten, arrested, and had her children removed after police responded to her crisis, and urges focusing Intro 403 on establishing the department in law.
chapters.title: Conrad Blackburn testifies on Bronx Defenders and police-first response harms

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: And good evening, chairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: I know we're getting to a late hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: I'm Conrad Blackburn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: I'm policy counsel for the Bronx Defenders in a criminal defense practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: And I want to thank you for the opportunity to testify here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: So we support the Office of Community Safety and efforts to make it a permanent department that would outlast this mayoral administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: As a public defender, I stand shoulder to shoulder with clients, defending them from a system that works to strip them of their dignity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: I'm reminded every day that our current system, a system that relies on the police as a default response to our neighbors in crisis, fails us in so many respects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: Our current police first response system results in devastating consequences for my clients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: Consequences like clients who appear in arraignments bloodied and bruised after being beaten up by the police.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: Clients being rendered homeless by an order of protection that their partner didn't want.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: And consequences like homeless clients decompensating or dying at Rikers Island instead of getting the mental health support and treatment that they want and need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: I witnessed just how destructive to my clients and their communities our inability to provide non-police safety responses to crisis is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: And that's exactly why I support an Office of Community Safety that would focus on community-based non-police responses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: And I want to tell a story of my client, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: P is someone who lives with mental health complications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: One night, she was experiencing a brief moment of crisis, and her sister called 911 because she wanted her sister to go to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: Instead of professionals trained to deal with people in crisis, the police showed up, and the police immediately escalated the situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: When Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: P expressed that she no longer wanted to go to the hospital, the police tried to unlawfully arrest Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: P and tried to force her to go to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: They beat her up, they strapped her to the bed, and they tried to force her to take a shot of an unknown substance that she did not consent to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: And Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: P, fearing for her life, bit one of the officers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: She was arrested.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: ACS took her children away from her, and for six long months, we fought her case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: That case was ultimately dismissed, and Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: P had to fight to regain custody of her children.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Please conclude.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: Yes, cases like these are not uncommon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: They're more common than you think, and that's the reality of the system where we rely on a police default response to people in crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn
utterances.text: We support the bill, but we urge the council to ensure that they are keeping the bill focused on establishing the department in law and taking out any prescriptive provisions,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Conrad Blackburn

chapters.summary: Ghada El-Midawi of the Women Empowerment Coalition of NYC testifies about immigrant women and school safety. She shares a story of a 17-year-old girl who translates for her family and faces bullying, and urges expanding OCS to include school safety and youth mental health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ghada El-Midawi

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ghada El-Midawi

chapters.summary: Joanne Kim of the Korean American Family Service Center testifies about serving immigrant survivors of domestic violence. She welcomes the $15.7 million increase in NGBV funding and says culturally specific services are the only access pathway to safety for many survivors.
chapters.title: Joanne Kim testifies on Korean American Family Service Center and NGBV funding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: Good afternoon, well, good evening, chairs and members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: My name is Joanne Kim, and I am the Assistant Director of Community and Volunteer Management at the Korean American Family Service Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: For nearly 40 years, KFSC has provided culturally specific services to immigrant survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault, and other forms of gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: Each year, we serve more than 3,000 individuals, the vast majority of whom are immigrant women facing language, cultural, and economic barriers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: Last year alone, we answered 4,834 calls to our 24-hour hotline,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: provided 2,023 nights of safe shelter, supported 46 women and 21 children through transitional housing, and helped 203 women gain economic independence through workforce development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: This is what community safety looks like to us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: It means ensuring that a woman can leave an abusive relationship without becoming homeless.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: It means helping a survivor access counseling, legal assistance, and employment opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: She can rebuild her life safely and independently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: We commend the Lamdani administration for recognizing that public safety goes beyond policing and for investing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: in community-based prevention and survivor services through the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: We particularly welcome the $15.7 million increase in NGBV funding, including the additional $3 million dedicated to culturally specific organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: This is an important recognition that culturally specific services are not optional.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: For many immigrant survivors, they are the only access pathway to safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: KFSC is also proud to participate in the Partners Against Hate initiative through our anti-hate prevention work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: We have heard directly from immigrant community members who fear harassment, discrimination, and violence, particularly in public spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: Your time has expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much for joining us today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Estella Nguema

summary: The Committee on Public Safety, jointly with Governmental Operations, held an oversight hearing on the Office of Community Safety (OCS) and non-police solutions to violence.
Commissioner Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey testified about OCS's budget, programs, and plans, facing extensive Q&A from council members on topics including Be Heard, NGBV, hate crimes, and youth violence.
Nearly 50 members of the public testified on issues ranging from school safety and mental health crisis response to hate crime prevention and community violence intervention.
title: Committee on Public Safety
topic: Oversight - The Office of Community Safety and Non-Police Solutions to Reducing Violence
